title: The sync workflow proposes churn its own import created
description:
The issue-sync workflow succeeded end to end for the first time and opened a pull request proposing a change nobody wanted.

It held one file, .beads/issues.jsonl, and three beads differing in exactly one field:

  inventory-tng-61b  defer_until 2027-01-05T00:00:00Z -> null
  inventory-tng-9u8  defer_until 2027-02-01T00:00:00Z -> null
  inventory-tng-f8g  defer_until 2026-11-01T00:00:00Z -> null

bd import does not preserve defer_until. The workflow builds a tracker in a runner by importing the committed export, and the import silently drops deferral dates, so exporting again writes them back as null. Merging that would have un-deferred three beads by between two months and eighteen months, putting them into bd ready years early.

NOTHING WAS PULLED on that run -- every GitHub issue already had a bead. So the entire proposal was churn the job created itself, and it would produce the same one every day.

TWO SEPARATE THINGS, and only the second is ours to fix.

1. bd import losing defer_until is a bug in bd, worth reporting upstream and worth knowing about locally: any bootstrap-from-export loses deferrals. Recorded here rather than only in a pull request comment.

2. The workflow decides whether to propose by asking whether .beads/issues.jsonl changed. That is the wrong question. The right one is whether anything was actually pulled -- if no issue arrived, there is nothing to propose whatever the file looks like, and a diff caused by the import is by definition not news.

Gate the proposal on the pull rather than on the diff. pull-new-issues.sh already knows and already says so; have it report the count in a form the workflow can read, and skip the commit entirely when it is zero.

title: A working-tree restore cannot undo what is already staged
description:
The fourth issue-sync failure, and rbvb's fix not going far enough.

rbvb restored the checkout with a checkout of the working tree before committing, so that only the export would be proposed. The next run still carried eight files: .beads/.gitignore, .beads/config.yaml and the five hooks.

WHAT THE DIAGNOSTIC SHOWED, and it is the whole answer. The step ends with a short status, which printed:

  M  .beads/.gitignore
  M  .beads/config.yaml

The M is in the FIRST column. Those changes were STAGED, and restoring a path in the working tree takes it FROM THE INDEX rather than from HEAD. So it restored them faithfully to their staged state and left them staged. Something in bd stages what it rewrites; the run never commits before this point, so no hook did it.

A hard reset to HEAD is what discards the index and the working tree together. The export is saved and put back after, as before.

WORTH KEEPING: the fix looked right, ran, and reported success while doing nothing, because the wrong command was a plausible spelling of the right one. What caught it was printing a short status at the end of the step -- a diagnostic added for a different reason, and the only reason this took one run rather than several.

title: The sync workflow would propose beads scaffolding as a change
description:
Third failure of the issue-sync workflow, and the most serious: the first two stopped the job, this one would have produced a wrong pull request.

The run got as far as committing and pushing a branch. That commit held TEN files, not the one the step adds by name:

  .beads/.gitignore, .beads/config.yaml, five .beads/hooks/*,
  .beads/issues.jsonl, .claude/settings.json, and AGENTS.md

AGENTS.md GAINED 80 LINES. bd init scaffolds a workspace -- it writes its own agent instructions, rewrites the Claude settings, reinstalls its hooks and rewrites its config -- and this repository's AGENTS.md is a deliberate, argued document that CLAUDE.md is a symlink to. A pull request appending beads boilerplate to it is not a proposal anybody would want, and it would have arrived looking routine.

THEY WERE COMMITTED DESPITE  because bd init also sets core.hooksPath, which installs beads' pre-commit hook, which stages the beads directory. The step added one file and the hook added the rest.

TWO FIXES, and the second is the one that matters:

1. bd init --skip-agents stops AGENTS.md and the Claude settings being touched at all.
2. After the sync, restore everything and keep only the export: save it, , , put it back. That undoes whatever bd scaffolded, including anything a future version scaffolds that this issue has not seen.

And unset core.hooksPath before committing -- not to bypass a guard, but to return the runner to the state a fresh checkout has. bd set it; CI never did. The commit message is still held by the one-issue-per-commit job on the pull request.

SEPARATELY, AND NOT FIXABLE IN CODE: gh pr create failed with 'GitHub Actions is not permitted to create or approve pull requests'. That is a repository setting -- Settings, Actions, General, Workflow permissions -- and only the owner can enable it. The branch is pushed either way, so nothing is lost when it is off.

title: Self-signed by default, and the warning said out loud
description:
Ali's call, 2026-08-30, and it changes what docs/decisions/0028-a-certificate-a-phone-will-trust.md chose:

  "I'm okay with self signed cert by default since developers are/should be
  aware that the browser will present a warning. I'd also like that clearly
  indicated in the relevant docs."

WHAT 0028 SAYS TODAY, and why this is a change rather than a clarification. It chose a local certificate AUTHORITY whose root the contributor installs once per device, specifically so that no warning appears. The per-device trust ritual -- three steps in two places on iOS -- is the cost that decision knowingly accepted. Self-signing removes that ritual and puts a warning in its place.

WHY THE SIMPLER DEFAULT IS DEFENSIBLE, which is the part the amendment has to carry rather than merely asserting the new rule. The audience for the local stack is developers, not volunteers: a browser warning on a hostname you typed yourself, on a certificate your own machine made a minute ago, is information rather than a threat, and somebody working on this project can be expected to read it. The trust ritual is real work repeated on every device, and it buys the absence of a dialog that the person seeing it already understands. That trade is the operator's to make, and he has made it.

WHAT MUST NOT BE LOST. 0028's actual subject was not the warning; it was that the CAMERA is the reason any of this exists, and that clicking through a warning may not yield the secure context getUserMedia requires. That claim is still untested -- 0028 says so in as many words -- and the amendment must keep it visible rather than quietly dropping it, because if it turns out that clicking through does NOT give a secure context on iOS, self-signed alone does not achieve the goal and the authority comes back as the answer rather than as an upgrade. So:

* the amendment states the new default and the reason,
* it keeps the local authority as the documented route for anybody who wants no warning, or who needs one because the camera refuses,
* and it keeps the untested claim named, with inventory-tng-dzwu.2 still asked to settle it on a real device early.

WHAT TO CHANGE:

* docs/decisions/0028 -- an amendment section, in the shape decision 0013 already uses for one. Do not rewrite the original points: the reasoning that led to them is what stops somebody undoing this next month.
* inventory-tng-dzwu.2's description, which currently carries 0028's seven points as its specification and would otherwise send the implementer the wrong way.
* Any other document that describes the local TLS arrangement. Established by reading rather than assumed: at the time of filing there is no implementation, so 0028 and the bead are the only places it is described. Check again before closing, because rule 2 is about the state at close rather than at filing.

DONE MEANS the warning is described where a contributor meets it, in the words somebody seeing it would search for, rather than left as a surprise they are expected to have been told about.
close_reason: Decision 0028 amended: self-signed by default with the warning documented, the local authority kept as the way to avoid it. Points 1 and 6 and the decision summary annotated so a reader of the list is not misled. inventory-tng-dzwu.2 rewritten -- the warning is now half that issue, and settling the untested secure-context question on a real iOS device is the FIRST thing it does, because the answer decides whether the new default serves the feature at all. DEVELOPERS.md now says the camera does not work from a phone today, that the failure is silent, and that the certificate will be self-signed and will warn. Established by reading that 0028 and DEVELOPERS.md are the only documents describing this; deployment.md's self-signed mention is about ingress-nginx in a cluster and is unrelated.

title: Batch: a warning we tell people about
description: Holds the amendment to decision 0028 alone. Its own batch epic rather than a child of inventory-tng-dzwu, for the reason inventory-tng-l4ek gives: a stream epic and a batch epic are recorded the same way, so a stream whose other children have not landed cannot be merged in pieces.

title: Batch: the decision behind local TLS
description:
Holds inventory-tng-dzwu.1 alone, and exists because a batch and a stream are different things that the tracker records the same way.

inventory-tng-dzwu is a STREAM -- the local development experience -- and will hold work for months. check-batch.sh reads the parent epic of the landed issues as the batch and then requires every child of it to have landed, which is right for a batch and impossible for a stream: the plan and its implementation are deliberately separate pull requests, so the stream can never be merged in pieces.

So the plan gets its own batch epic and the stream keeps inventory-tng-dzwu.2. The same will apply when that lands.

The friction itself is inventory-tng-l4ek.
close_reason: All children completed

title: Quoting the review marker counts as having posted it
description:
Found while checking inventory-tng-bq6d, which turned out not to be a defect. This one is.

WHAT HAPPENS. record_receipt looks for its evidence marker with a substring test over the whole comment body:

  if mark in (c.get("body") or "")

So a comment that merely MENTIONS the marker is evidence that the pass ran. Quoting it in prose counts. Quoting it in backticks counts. Quoting it inside a fenced block explaining what the marker is for counts.

IT HAS ALREADY HAPPENED, which is why this is filed rather than noted. Pull request 48 merged with no code-review marker on it. The correction comment posted afterwards -- the one reporting that the receipt was missing -- contained the marker text while explaining what had been omitted, and the gate then read that as the evidence. Running record against pull request 48 today prints "code-review 1 on the pull request" and points at the comment saying there was none. A comment reporting an absence created the thing it reported absent.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THE IRONY. The receipt is the one artifact that says a review cycle happened, and the merge guard trusts it completely. Evidence that can be produced by writing about evidence is not evidence. Worse, the failure is silent and in the permissive direction: nobody is told the marker was found in a sentence rather than posted as one.

WHAT TO DO. The marker is documented as going on a line of its own -- .agents/skills/pull-requests/SKILL.md says "carries <!-- review-cycle: simplify --> on a line of its own" -- so match that instead of a substring:

  any(line.strip() == mark for line in body.splitlines())

That is what the documentation already promises, so nothing that follows it breaks, and every accidental mention stops counting. Somebody determined to forge one can still put the marker alone on a line, which is deliberate and out of scope: this closes the accident, not the fraud.

TEST IT with a comment whose body contains the marker inside a sentence and assert it is NOT evidence, alongside the existing case that a marker on its own line is. scripts/landing-gate.test.sh's pr_json helper already builds both shapes.
close_reason: The marker must now be at the left margin, outside any fence, to count. Verified against reality: recording pull request 48, whose only code-review 'evidence' was a comment quoting the marker while reporting its absence, is now refused; pull request 49, where both markers were genuinely posted, still records. Two cases added -- quoted inside a sentence, and shown indented in an instructional block, which is the shape this gate's own refusal message prints.

title: Batch: a gate that cannot be stepped around
description:
Two defects found the same way -- by merging past the gate. Pull request 48 landed with no receipt recorded and nothing refused it.

inventory-tng-mno6 -- the Bash matcher sees a guarded command only in command position, so a wrapper like timeout moves it out of view.

inventory-tng-bq6d -- record refuses clearly and then exits zero, so the documented record-then-merge sequence merges anyway.

They land together because either one alone still leaves a way through: fixing the matcher without the exit status leaves the chained sequence silently merging, and fixing the exit status without the matcher leaves the direct command unguarded.
close_reason: All children completed

title: The landing gate does not see a command behind a wrapper like timeout
description:
FOUND BY MERGING PAST IT. PR 48 was merged on 2026-08-30 with no receipt recorded, and the gate did not refuse. This is not a hypothetical.

WHAT HAPPENS. scripts/landing-gate.sh's Bash matcher finds the guarded command only when it is in command position. A command WRAPPER puts it one word to the right, and the matcher then sees nothing to guard:

  gh pr merge 48 --rebase                -> deny        (correct)
  timeout 180 gh pr merge 48 --rebase    -> allowed     (the hole)
  env gh pr merge 48                     -> allowed

Reproduced directly against the check mode with a hand-built PreToolUse payload; the first denies with "No review cycle has been recorded for pull request 48", the second returns nothing at all.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN THE USUAL BYPASS. Every command an agent runs in this repository is prefixed with a timeout, because the shell guidance asks for non-interactive, non-hanging invocations. So the wrapper is not an exotic shape somebody would have to reach for: it is the DEFAULT shape, and the guarded shape is the exception. A guard whose refusal is skipped by the ordinary way of calling things is not a guard.

WHAT THE FILE ALREADY KNOWS. Its own header records the same class of defect being fixed twice before -- a leading assignment (GH_TOKEN=... gh pr merge 7), and the compound-command keywords ((gh pr merge 7), { gh pr merge 7; }, if true; then ... fi). Wrappers are the third member of that family and were not covered.

WHAT TO DO. Skip a leading wrapper before deciding what is in command position, the way the leading-assignment case is already skipped. At minimum: timeout, env, nice, ionice, stdbuf, time, command, xargs, sudo, doas. Prefer a rule -- "a word that is a known wrapper, plus its own options, then look again" -- over a list that grows one incident at a time, and consider whether the simpler answer is to look for the guarded pattern ANYWHERE in the command rather than only at its head, accepting the false positives that brings and refusing on them.

TEST IT WITH THE CASES ABOVE. scripts/landing-gate.test.sh already builds payloads this way and its "the ways this could stop guarding without saying so" section is where these belong. A fix with no case for the wrapper form is the same fix that was made twice already.

SEE ALSO the sibling issue about record exiting 0 when it refuses, which is the second half of how PR 48 got through: the merge was chained after it with && and the chain did not break.
close_reason: timeout now has its own arm in WRAP, because it takes a positional duration that the options-only pattern could not skip -- adding the word to the existing wrapper list would have looked like a fix and changed nothing. Five spellings tested, including two durations after a flag and one behind a second wrapper, plus a negative case so the matcher still distinguishes naming a command from running it.

title: Make TLS for local development a container that runs itself
description:
Build what docs/decisions/0028-a-certificate-a-phone-will-trust.md decided, AS AMENDED on 2026-08-30. The decision is the specification; this issue does not restate it in full and does not get to overrule it. If building it makes the decision look wrong, that is an amendment argued in the pull request rather than a quiet divergence here.

=== DO THIS FIRST, BEFORE BUILDING ANYTHING ===

ANSWER THE UNTESTED QUESTION ON A REAL iOS DEVICE: does accepting the browser warning on a self-signed certificate give a secure context, so that the camera works?

It is first because it decides whether the documented default serves the feature this whole stream exists for. 0028 states it plainly as untested, and the amendment puts it underneath the default rather than beside it:

* If YES -- self-signed is the right default, the local authority is an optional comfort, and the rest of this issue proceeds as written.
* If NO -- self-signed alone does not achieve the goal on that platform. The authority is the answer there rather than an upgrade, the amendment needs amending, and that is a conversation rather than a decision to take here.

Write the answer into 0028 either way. An untested claim that stays untested through the implementation that depended on it is the worst outcome available.

=== WHAT WAS DECIDED ===

* A certificate made by a CONTAINER, SELF-SIGNED by default.
* THE BROWSER WARNING IS EXPECTED, and is documented where a contributor meets it -- see below, it is half of this issue.
* A local certificate authority stays documented as the way to avoid the warning, for somebody who wants none, who is demonstrating to people who should not be taught to dismiss security dialogs, or whose camera refuses.
* Opt-in through a compose profile, the way the collector already is.
* TLS terminates in a proxy container, NOT in the frontend image.
* Port 8443, because rootless Podman cannot bind 443 here.
* The certificate names the address a phone actually dials, as a SAN.
* A tunnel is the documented alternative for somebody who can do neither.

=== THE WARNING IS HALF THIS ISSUE, NOT A FOOTNOTE ===

Ali asked for it to be clearly indicated in the docs, and it is the difference between a default that works and one that reads as broken. So:

* It appears at the point in the setup where it happens, not in a troubleshooting section somebody reaches after being alarmed.
* It uses the words a person seeing it would recognise -- what the browser actually says on the platforms this is used from -- rather than a paraphrase.
* It says what the certificate is, who made it, and why the warning is the expected outcome rather than a fault.
* It says what to click, on desktop and on the phone.
* It names the local-authority route immediately afterwards, for the reader who does not want to click it every time.

A warning nobody was warned about is the same defect as a camera that fails silently: it teaches the reader that the project is broken at the moment they are deciding whether to keep going.

=== THE STANDING REQUIREMENT, which is the acceptance criterion ===

Ali's words: "I don't want contributors to have to mess around with openssl commands to generate certs. I want the end to end flow to be executable locally, or within containers on a dev machine."

* NO openssl INVOCATION IN ANY DOCUMENT. If a reader has to copy a command with -subj and -addext in it, this is not done, whatever works.
* END TO END means from git clone to a phone with a working camera, with no step assuming a tool the reader has or an account they can create.
* IT WORKS UNDER PODMAN OR IT IS NOT ADDED. Podman is rootless, which is why the port is 8443; test under it before claiming it works.
* IT STAYS OPTIONAL. compose up continues to work untouched for somebody who has not set TLS up.
* NO KEY REACHES A COMMIT. Add the path to .gitignore in the SAME change that first writes to it, never after.
* NEVER WRITE CRYPTOGRAPHY. AGENTS.md rule 3. An established tool generates the key and signs the certificate through its own public interface. The moment the work needs anything resembling implementing a construction, it stops and asks a person.

=== DONE MEANS ===

* Somebody who has never run this project gets a working camera on a phone by following the document, and every step that surprises them -- the warning above all -- was described before they met it.
* Automated checks cover what can be: the certificate's names, the compose wiring, the gitignore entry. A phone's trust decision cannot be, and saying so beats a test that asserts nothing.
* The docs move with it, per rule 2. DEVELOPERS.md#running-it is the main one. Decision 0011's bullet about the camera failing invisibly describes an unsolved problem today, and this change is what makes it out of date -- that sentence moves in the same commit.

=== DELIBERATELY NOT HERE ===

Anything about the deployed environment. docs/deployment.md still requires a real certificate from a real authority and offers no switch to skip it. A change that made local development easier by making deployment less honest is refused rather than traded.

title: Decide how a contributor's phone trusts a locally-made certificate
description:
Asked for by Ali on 2026-08-30: automate TLS for local development so that a contributor never types an `openssl` command. Plan first, implementation second and separately, because the hard part here is a decision rather than a script.

=== WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN "HTTPS IS NICE" ===

The application's reason for existing is scanning a QR code with a phone at a shelf. Decision 0011 already states the trap precisely, and it is worth quoting rather than rediscovering:

  "On an insecure origin `navigator.mediaDevices` is `undefined` rather than
  restricted, so it looks like a bug. `localhost` is exempt; PRIVATE AND LAN
  ADDRESSES ARE NOT, so the app must never be served over plain HTTP at
  `http://10.0.0.5:8080`, which is otherwise the natural way to try it from a
  phone on the mesh."

So the current position is: the camera works on the developer's own machine at http://localhost:8080, and fails on the one device the feature is FOR, in a way that looks like a broken app rather than a missing certificate. A contributor who wants to work on scanning cannot, and the failure does not tell them why.

That is what this stream is fixing. Not a padlock in the address bar.

=== WHAT EXISTS TODAY ===

Nothing. Established by reading rather than assumed:

* frontend/nginx.conf.template has one `listen 8080;` and no `ssl_certificate`, no 443, nothing.
* compose.yaml publishes 8080:8080 and no TLS port.
* No certificate is generated, referenced or gitignored anywhere in the tree.
* docs/deployment.md requires TLS in a cluster and says there is no switch to skip it -- that is the DEPLOYED path and is not what this changes.

=== THE PART THAT IS ACTUALLY HARD ===

Generating a certificate is trivial. Getting a phone to TRUST it is the whole problem, and any plan that does not answer it has not planned anything.

A self-signed certificate, or one from a locally generated CA, is not trusted by an iPhone that has never heard of it. Chrome and Safari will refuse the origin, and -- this is the trap -- a user who taps through the interstitial STILL may not get a secure context in the sense `getUserMedia` requires on all platforms. So "click past the warning" is not a workable answer for the one thing this is for.

The plan has to choose between approaches whose costs land in different places:

1. A LOCAL CA, INSTALLED ON THE PHONE ONCE. mkcert is the well-known tool; a container that runs its own CA is the same idea without a host install. Cost: every contributor's phone needs the CA profile installed, which on iOS is a download, an install in Settings, AND a separate "enable full trust for root certificates" toggle that is genuinely obscure. Once done it lasts. This is honest, offline, and needs no external service -- and its cost is a documented one-time ritual per device.

2. A REAL CERTIFICATE FOR A REAL NAME, via DNS-01 against a domain the project controls, with the certificate and key distributed to contributors. Cost: no phone setup at all and it Just Works -- but it means shipping a private key for a public name to anybody who clones, which is a credential in a repository and is not acceptable. A variant where each contributor gets their own subdomain and their own DNS credential is acceptable in principle and is a lot of machinery, plus a dependency on somebody administering it -- which is the private fiefdom the epic's own framing warns about.

3. A TUNNEL -- cloudflared, ngrok, tailscale funnel. Cost: trivially correct TLS with a trusted public name and zero device setup, at the price of an external account and the traffic leaving the machine. Attractive as an OPTION, poor as the only path, and it fails exactly where NYC Mesh often is: a network with no upstream.

4. TAILSCALE ON THE MESH, or any WireGuard-ish overlay with its own name and cert. Same shape as 3 with different trade-offs; worth naming so it is considered rather than assumed away.

THE RECOMMENDATION TO EVALUATE, not to assume: 1 as the default, containerised, with 3 documented as the escape hatch for somebody who cannot install a CA on their device. That combination keeps the offline case working, needs no account, and leaves an opinionated default that a person may disagree with -- which is what the epic asks for.

=== WHAT THE PLAN MUST DECIDE, EXPLICITLY ===

* Which approach is the default, and what the documented alternative is.
* WHERE TLS TERMINATES. Two shapes: teach the frontend's nginx to listen on 443 as well, or put a small proxy container in front of it in compose. The second keeps the shipped image identical to the deployed one, which matters -- the frontend image is the same artifact in every environment and docs/deployment.md leans on that. A `profiles:`-gated service, the way the collector already is, would let TLS be opt-in rather than a cost every `compose up` pays.
* HOW THE CERTIFICATE IS MADE AND WHERE IT LIVES. A container that generates on first run into a named volume, or into a gitignored directory? The .gitignore question is not optional: a private key committed once is committed for ever, and `.claude/.*.json` was added to that file this week for a smaller version of the same mistake.
* WHAT NAME THE CERTIFICATE IS FOR. `localhost` alone is useless here -- the phone reaches a LAN address or a name. An IP SAN, a `*.localhost` name, an mDNS `.local` name, or a name in the mesh's own DNS are all different answers with different device behaviour, and iOS in particular is fussy.
* WHETHER THE DEV SERVER PATH GETS IT TOO. `npm run dev` on 5173 is the other supported way to run this, and the camera is exactly what somebody iterating on the scanner is working on. Vite can serve HTTPS; whether it should share the same certificate is part of the plan.
* WHAT HAPPENS WHEN IT IS ABSENT. Whatever is built, `compose up` must still work for somebody who has not set TLS up, because most contributions do not touch the camera. Failing closed here would be a tax on everybody for a feature some need.
* IOS IS THE PLATFORM TO TEST ON, and decision 0011 already says so for the camera itself. A plan validated only on desktop Chrome has not been validated.

=== WHAT IT MUST PRODUCE ===

A written recommendation with the trade named, enough for Ali to disagree with. If the answer needs a decision recorded -- and "how a contributor gets a trusted certificate" probably does, because it constrains everything after it -- then docs/decisions/ is where it goes, and 0027 is the recent example of writing down a rule so a later contributor does not undo it.

The implementation is inventory-tng's sibling issue and is deliberately not this one. A plan that is also a pull request is a plan nobody reviewed.

=== DOCS THAT MOVE WITH IT, whichever way it goes ===

* DEVELOPERS.md#running-it -- the three ways to run this, and where TLS fits into each.
* README.md#quickstart -- only if the default path changes; the quickstart is the first thing a stranger reads and should not grow a certificate step it does not need.
* docs/decisions/0011-qr-batch-scanning.md -- its "the camera path requires HTTPS and fails invisibly without it" bullet currently describes an unsolved problem. When this lands it describes a solved one, and rule 2 says that sentence moves with the change.
* docs/deployment.md -- only to say that the local arrangement is NOT the deployed one, if there is any risk of confusing them.
close_reason: Decided and recorded in docs/decisions/0028-a-certificate-a-phone-will-trust.md: a local certificate authority run from a container, opt-in behind a compose profile, terminating in a proxy container on 8443 because rootless Podman cannot bind 443 here, with the root installed once per device and a tunnel documented as the alternative. Four alternatives are named with the reason each was not taken. inventory-tng-dzwu.2 now carries what was decided as its specification.

title: EPIC: a local development setup a contributor can join without asking anybody
description:
Opened by Ali on 2026-08-30, and the reasoning is his and belongs at the top rather than buried in a child:

  "Ensuring a good local dev experience is a key goal since getting
  contributions is and participation in the development is consistent with the
  mesh value of it being a COMMUNITY resource. So development should not be
  done in isolation and the output including the hosting env should not be
  treated as a private fiefdom. There can be opinions, defaults and views, but
  people should be able to disagree and fork if we cannot come to agreement on
  any matters."

That is a design constraint rather than a sentiment, and it has teeth in at least three directions:

* A setup step only the author can perform is a fork nobody can run. Anything this project needs in order to be developed has to be in the repository, reproducible, and runnable by somebody who has never spoken to anybody here.
* "People should be able to disagree and fork" means the hosting environment cannot be a dependency. A fork gets the whole thing -- the stack, the certificates, the seed data -- or it gets an app it cannot exercise.
* Defaults may be opinionated. They may not be mandatory. Where this stream picks a tool, it picks a default and says what to do instead, rather than building the tool into the only path.

=== WHAT THIS EPIC HOLDS ===

The friction between "I cloned it" and "I am usefully changing it". Its first children are about TLS, because that is the sharpest instance: the application's central feature cannot be exercised on the device it was designed for without it. What else belongs here will accumulate; candidates already known and NOT yet moved in, because each is filed and doing its job where it is:

* inventory-tng-nre8 -- a test that deadlocks on a small pipe, so the suite hangs rather than fails on a busy machine. A contributor's first `pytest` is exactly when that bites.
* The Podman friction recorded in DEVELOPERS.md#podman -- the API socket that has to be started before `podman compose` works at all. Documented, not automated.

=== WHAT IT IS NOT ===

Not the deployed environment. docs/deployment.md is a different reader with a different problem, and a change that makes local development easier by making deployment less honest is refused rather than traded.

Not a rewrite of the three ways to run this. DEVELOPERS.md#running-it describes Docker, native, and a devcontainer, and all three have reasons. This stream removes friction from them rather than replacing them.

title: Batch: a dev environment that works
description:
The rest of inventory-tng-o1uj that does not need a decision from the project owner, formed 2026-08-29 after PR #40 made writes work again.

Four issues: the Django admin rendering unstyled (o1uj.1, P0), nginx holding a dead upstream address after the backend restarts (o1uj.2), a configurable trusted-origin list (o1uj.7), and the missing test that would have caught o1uj.6 in the first place (o1uj.8).

TWO OF o1uj's CHILDREN ARE DELIBERATELY NOT HERE. o1uj.3 amends decision 0013 point 3, which is a security decision and a person's to make; o1uj.4 decides whether a cross-origin arrangement is supported at all, which changes what configuration this project ships. Both were put to Ali rather than guessed at. o1uj.5 is not here either: it closes on documentation that already landed in PR #40, so it has no commit to contribute and check-batch reads commits.

The parent of each of the four moved here from o1uj, because scripts/check-batch.sh reads parentage as batch membership and o1uj holds issues this pull request does not land.

title: Batch: make the writes work again
description:
Two issues, formed on 2026-08-29 out of one sitting spent trying to run the application on the project owner's own machine.

inventory-tng-o1uj.6 is the defect that made it unusable: nginx forwarded the host without its port, so Django rebuilt a different origin from the browser's and refused EVERY write with a CSRF origin failure. The other is the documentation that sitting produced -- Podman as an equal to Docker, a heading for the first sign-in, corrected ports, and three worked examples to follow.

They ship together because they came from the same afternoon and neither is much use without the other: the walkthroughs cannot be completed while writes are refused, and the fix is hard to notice without a session to run against it.

BOTH ISSUES' PARENT WAS MOVED HERE from inventory-tng-o1uj, the dev-environment epic, which holds five further issues that are NOT in this batch. scripts/check-batch.sh reads parentage as batch membership, so an issue cannot be in both at once.

The guard half of o1uj.6's original description -- making CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS configurable -- was split out as inventory-tng-o1uj.7 rather than landed here. It touches settings, .env.sample, compose.yaml, the chart and their docs, and none of it is needed to make writes work.
close_reason: All children completed

title: Every write is refused: nginx drops the port, so Django's CSRF origin check fails
description:
Found on 2026-08-29 by driving the volunteer flow end to end in a browser
against the compose stack: pick a volunteer, scan the location label, scan an
item label, press Save. This is almost certainly what the project owner
reported as a CORS error after signing in -- the message Django returns says
"Origin checking failed", which is what most people would call that.

THE SYMPTOM. Every write fails. Reads all work, sign-in works, TOTP works, the
batch builds correctly on screen, and then Save answers:

    POST /api/stock/transactions -> 403
    {"detail":"CSRF Failed: Origin checking failed -
      http://localhost:8080 does not match any trusted origins.","code":"forbidden"}

So the single-page app cannot save a batch, which is the thing the application
is for. Decision 0011's whole QR flow -- scan, cart, Save -- is unusable on the
stack the README tells a new contributor to run first. Nothing else in the
inventory can be changed either: the same check refuses every POST, PUT, PATCH
and DELETE, so the administrative screens cannot write either.

THE CAUSE, proven rather than reasoned. Three facts.

1. frontend/nginx.conf.template proxies with `proxy_set_header Host $host` in
   all three of its proxying locations (lines 92, 119 and 129 of the rendered
   config). nginx's `$host` is the host WITHOUT the port -- that is its
   documented behaviour, and `$http_host` is the variable that keeps it.
   So Django is told the Host is `localhost`, not `localhost:8080`.

2. Django builds the origin it will accept from its own view of the request.
   Asked directly, inside the running container:

     Host: 'localhost'       -> good_origin http://localhost        match: False
     Host: 'localhost:8080'  -> good_origin http://localhost:8080   match: True

   against the browser's Origin of http://localhost:8080.

3. CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS is [] at runtime, and the name appears NOWHERE in this
   repository -- not settings.py, not .env.sample, not compose.yaml, not the
   Helm chart. So there is no second chance after the host comparison fails.

Together: nginx drops the port, Django therefore computes the wrong origin, and
nothing is configured to forgive the difference.

WHY IT WAS NEVER CAUGHT, which is the part worth keeping. On a deployment the
browser reaches the ingress on 443 and the Origin header carries no port, so
`$host` and the origin agree and every write succeeds. The bug only appears
when the port is not the scheme's default -- which is every local setup and no
deployed one. The browser integration suite does not catch it either: its specs
sign in and read, and nothing in frontend/integration/ posts a batch.

TWO FIXES, and they are not alternatives so much as one fix and one guard.

* `$http_host` in place of `$host` in the three proxy_set_header lines. This is
  the actual defect and the one-line correction. The template's own comment
  block already says the Host header has to stay the browser's, so the
  intention was right and the variable was wrong; correct the comment with it.
  Check the same reasoning against vite.config.ts, which documents the same
  requirement for the dev server and gets it right by not overriding the host
  at all.
* Make CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS configurable and set it explicitly in compose.yaml
  and .env.sample. Even with the header fixed this should exist, because the
  moment anybody runs the frontend on a host name that is not what Django sees
  they will land here again with no knob to reach for. It also belongs with the
  sibling issue about Access-Control-Allow-Credentials, since a genuinely
  cross-origin arrangement needs both and neither is present.

TESTS, and this is where the real gap is. The unit tests drive Django's test
client, which does not go through nginx and so cannot see this at all. What
would have caught it is a browser test that SAVES -- the integration suite has
the fixtures for it already (seed_integration_data mints a volunteer, an item, a
location and a label). Add one spec that scans the location, scans the item and
presses Save, and asserts the ledger moved. The nb8 epic's notes make the same
point about asserting things that happen outside Django: drive the real stack,
not the test client.

VERIFY BY RUNNING IT. After the change, the manual walkthrough is: sign in at
:8080, pick a volunteer, scan DEM0000002 (the seeded location label), scan
DEM0000001 (the seeded item label), press Save, and the batch should clear and
the on-hand count for LiteBeam AC Gen2 should move. Today it 403s at the last
step.
close_reason: nginx now forwards $http_host, so Django rebuilds the origin the browser actually used. Verified end to end: the same Save that answered 403 answers 201, and the ledger moved.

title: The Django admin loads with no styling at all under compose
description:
Found by the project owner running the app on 2026-08-29, reported as "the
admin page has NO styling at all", and reproduced and root-caused the same day
against the compose stack on this machine.

WHAT IT LOOKS LIKE. http://localhost:8080/admin/ (and :8000/admin/) renders as
raw browser-default HTML. Measured in the page rather than described: the
computed font-family on body is "Times New Roman" and the computed background
is rgba(0, 0, 0, 0). All five stylesheets the admin asks for answer 404:

    /static/admin/css/base.css
    /static/admin/css/dark_mode.css
    /static/admin/css/nav_sidebar.css
    /static/admin/css/dashboard.css
    /static/admin/css/responsive.css

WHY. Three facts that are individually reasonable and together are the bug.

1. compose.yaml sets DJANGO_DEBUG to true by default (the ${DJANGO_DEBUG:-true}
   on the backend service).
2. settings.py adds WhiteNoise to MIDDLEWARE only under `if not DEBUG`. The
   comment above it says why -- in development Django's staticfiles app serves
   them and collectstatic has not run, so WhiteNoise would only warn about a
   missing directory.
3. The compose stack runs gunicorn, not runserver. The staticfiles app only
   serves anything through runserver's handler.

So the one arrangement the comment in settings.py does not account for is the
one the quickstart ships: DEBUG on AND gunicorn. Nothing serves /static/ and
every admin asset 404s. The files themselves are present and correct --
backend/Dockerfile runs collectstatic at build time, and
/app/src/staticfiles/admin/css/base.css is in the image at 24538 bytes.

PROVEN BOTH WAYS on this machine, same stack, same image:

    DJANGO_DEBUG=true   (the shipped default)  -> /static/admin/css/base.css 404
    DJANGO_DEBUG=false                         -> /static/admin/css/base.css 200

That is the whole diagnosis; there is nothing left to investigate.

WHY IT IS WORTH MORE THAN IT LOOKS. The admin is not decoration here. Decision
0013 routes admin/login/ to allauth, and guides/administrator.md sends an
administrator into the admin for the things the app cannot yet do -- notably
identifiers, which inventory-tng-gz2 records are reachable from nowhere else.
An unstyled admin has no sidebar, no nav and no layout, so those tasks are hard
to complete rather than merely ugly, and it is the first impression anybody
gets of the project.

THE FIX IS A DECISION, NOT A LINE. Options, and the trade is real:

* Add WhiteNoise unconditionally and let it serve from STATIC_ROOT whenever the
  directory exists. Closest to what the deployed image already does, and makes
  the compose stack resemble production, which is what compose.yaml says it is
  for. Costs a collectstatic in any DEBUG-on flow that wants admin CSS.
* Key the condition on the server rather than on DEBUG -- the real distinction
  is runserver versus gunicorn, and DEBUG is standing in for it badly.
* Set DJANGO_DEBUG=false in compose.yaml. Smallest edit, but it trades the
  Django error page away, and that page is worth a lot in the stack somebody is
  using to find bugs. Probably the wrong one.

Whichever is chosen, settings.py's comment states the reasoning that is now
wrong and has to be corrected with it, and DEVELOPERS.md's Option A is where a
developer would look for the consequence.

A TEST IS WHAT KEEPS IT FIXED. Assert that a request for an admin static path
answers 200 under the settings the compose stack actually runs. The unit tests
drive Django's test client, which never exercises WhiteNoise, so this one has
to go through inventory_tng.wsgi.application -- the same trap the nb8 epic's
notes record as the iqff.1 defect recurring.
close_reason: WhiteNoise now loads when STATIC_ROOT exists rather than when DEBUG is off. Verified in the stack: the admin renders styled under the compose default, and all five stylesheets answer 200.

title: EPIC: An app the owner can run and use on their own machine
description:
Raised by the project owner on 2026-08-29 and given priority over the feature work in flight. The reasoning is theirs: the project is at the point where USING the app is the cheapest way to find the usability and cosmetic faults that matter, and that is only true if it runs on their laptop without a fight. Every child here is something that was hit while trying to do exactly that, in one sitting, following the repository's own documentation.

Nothing in this epic is speculative. Each child was reproduced against the compose stack on that machine and root-caused before it was written down, and each says what was observed as well as what to change.

WHAT WAS ALREADY DONE in the same sitting, so it is not duplicated as a child: README's quickstart was rewritten to cover Docker and Podman as equals, to give both command sets, to add a Sign in for the first time section, and to send people to port 8080 for everything; DEVELOPERS.md gained a Podman section carrying the one prerequisite Podman has that Docker does not. scripts/check-docs.sh passes on both.

THE ORDER IS BY WHAT BLOCKS USE. The admin having no styling is first because an administrator cannot do the identifier work guides/administrator.md sends them into the admin for. The 502 is second because it punishes the develop-and-restart loop every time. The rest are smaller.
close_reason: All children completed

title: Backend pods can never become Ready: the probe's Host is refused
description:
Found by a deployment review of docs/deployment.md on 2026-08-22, reading the chart rather than a cluster.

infra/helm/inventory-tng/templates/backend-deployment.yaml probes /api/healthz with a plain httpGet and no Host header, so the kubelet sends 'Host: <podIP>:8000'. DJANGO_ALLOWED_HOSTS is set from django.allowedHosts, which names the ingress host and not the pod IP, and settings.py has no wildcard. Django answers 400.

Verified against the real settings module: DJANGO_ALLOWED_HOSTS=inventory.nycmesh.net gives ALLOWED_HOSTS = ['inventory.nycmesh.net'], and a probe carrying 'Host: 10.42.0.17:8000' is refused.

CONSEQUENCE, and it is the whole deployment: every backend pod starts, fails readiness at once, never joins the Service, and is killed by liveness at roughly 70 seconds. CrashLoopBackOff for ever. The ingress answers 503 because the frontend can proxy to no endpoint. 'kubectl exec' to make the first administrator lands in a container that is killed mid-command. The logs show 400 with no explanation, because DisallowedHost is only visible with DEBUG on, which must not be on.

It is silent, it looks like a database problem, and it is not.

FIX: set the probes' Host header to an allowed host -- the first entry of django.allowedHosts -- on BOTH probes. Then say so under 'Health checks' in docs/deployment.md, because the next person to edit django.allowedHosts will otherwise re-break it.
close_reason: Closed

title: The backend job has been red since before this batch
description:
CI's backend job sets only DJANGO_SECRET_KEY and DATABASE_URL, so DEBUG is False and settings.py selects CompressedManifestStaticFilesStorage. collectstatic never runs in that job, so every test that renders /api/docs, /admin/... or the MFA pages dies on 'Missing staticfiles manifest entry'.

Reproduced locally with DJANGO_DEBUG=false: test_only_an_existing_administrator_can_reach_the_grant and test_the_admin_can_still_be_read both fail. With the repository .env, which sets DJANGO_DEBUG=true, all 446 pass.

main has been failing this job since 'Require one issue per commit', and it is a required check, so nothing can merge until it is fixed.

The integration job already sets DJANGO_DEBUG: true for the same reason. The settings comment says the DEBUG split exists because collectstatic has not run in a development checkout, which is what the backend job is.
acceptance_criteria: The backend job passes on main without weakening what the suite covers.
close_reason: The backend job sets DJANGO_DEBUG so the suite runs against a checkout's storage rather than the built image's manifest, which is what the integration job already does.

title: Rework the local landing gate
description: .claude/hooks/landing-gate.sh blocks publishing until a review has been recorded, which is the opposite of the new ordering: quality gates then publish, and review afterwards against the pull request. It also assumes one review per change rather than one per batch. Move the gate onto the merge instead. Separately, its textual test matches any command whose text contains 'git' followed by the words it guards, so prose about this very workflow trips it.
close_reason: The gate now guards the merge rather than the push, keyed on the pull request head, and its command matcher no longer trips on prose. Local file, gitignored.

title: Document how work reaches main
description: New canonical section in DEVELOPERS.md covering the branch, the pull request, publishing before review, the review cycle against the PR, and why rebase is the only merge. Update its Commits section for the trailer and summary rules, replacing 'Several issues at once'. Record the reasoning in docs/decisions/0017. Everything else links here and restates nothing.
close_reason: DEVELOPERS.md gained a canonical Pull requests section; Commits updated for the trailer and summary rules; ADR 0017 records the reasoning.

title: Make Django settings environment-driven
description: Scaffold settings hardcode SECRET_KEY, DEBUG=True, ALLOWED_HOSTS=[] and sqlite. Production deploy is impossible until settings read from env. Add django-environ, .env.sample, Postgres via DATABASE_URL, and wire DRF/CORS/spectacular into INSTALLED_APPS (DRF is installed but unregistered).
acceptance_criteria: No secrets in source; DEBUG defaults False; DATABASE_URL drives Postgres; .env.sample documents every var
close_reason: Closed

title: An anonymous throttle bucket is the forgeable reading of the header
description:
Filed under decision 0029 point 4: a weakness may be described in the open
while it is unreachable, and the reachability argument is at the bottom. No
recipe here -- decision 0023's own Context already carries the measurement, and
this adds nothing to it.

THE PREMISE THAT CHANGED. Decision 0023 keeps two readings of X-Forwarded-For
on purpose. The throttles keep DRF's hop count (NUM_PROXIES), and
forwarded.client_address is the sound one. 0023 argues that trade explicitly:
"Believing a forger in a throttle costs one bucket; believing one in an
admission decision costs the roster." That was priced on a premise the record
states in its own Consequences -- every endpoint asks for a session, so nothing
anonymous reaches the throttles at all.

inventory-tng-gnhl removed that premise. Under VOLUNTEER_ACCESS=open a caller
with no account reaches roughly six endpoints, and AnonymousReadThrottle
buckets them by DRF's reading of the address whenever no device header is
carried.

WHAT IT COSTS, AND WHY "ONE BUCKET" NO LONGER DESCRIBES IT. A forger does not
get one bucket. They get a fresh one per value they write, which is not a
bounded cost. That matters for exactly one claim: ANONYMOUS_READ_RATE is
documented -- in roster.py, in throttling.py's own docstring, and in the
published consultation brief -- as being close to useless against copying the
catalogue and decisive against the membership question, turning ten thousand
lookups from seconds into an hour of conspicuous traffic. Bucket rotation is
what that argument does not survive. The limit's headline value is the thing at
risk, not the roster.

WHAT THIS IS NOT. Not an admission bug: nothing decides who gets in on an
address, decision 0030 point 1 forecloses that outright, and Device.enrolled_from
already uses the sound reading. Not a reason to move the throttles over without
thinking -- 0023 says why that is worse today, since with the empty default
every volunteer behind the ingress would share one bucket and a packing night
would go down. The decision is which of those two costs is worth paying once an
open posture is real, and it is a decision rather than a fix.

WHY IT IS SAFE TO SAY THIS IN PUBLIC, per 0029 point 4, on three independent
counts:

* VOLUNTEER_ACCESS defaults to session, so no deployment answers an anonymous
  caller unless an operator opts in.
* No deployment exists. docs/deployment.md says the procedure has never been
  run through to the end against a cluster.
* Decision 0030: the intended deployment is admitted at the network, so the
  population that could reach the throttles at all is mesh members rather than
  the internet.

0029 POINT 4 ALSO SETS THE TRIGGER, and it is quoted here so nobody has to go
looking: if that changes, the fix stops being optional. An open posture over
real volunteers requires this settled first, not this description hidden. That
makes this a blocker on any deployment that sets VOLUNTEER_ACCESS=open over
real people, and it should be weighed as part of inventory-tng-81f7 rather than
after it.

title: A pull request can say "do not merge" and have it enforced
description:
A pull request can be marked "do not merge" only in prose today, and prose is
not read by anything. inventory-tng-81f7.3's spike -- pull request 28 -- says
so in its bead, in its title and twice in its body, and none of that is a
barrier. What is currently stopping it is draft state and a branch 102 commits
behind, and both come off in one command each.

THE HAZARD IS AN AGENT OBEYING THE RULES, not an accident. AGENTS.md puts
merging a batch/* pull request on the side that needs no permission once it is
green, and pull request 28 is a batch/* branch. A session that finds it, marks
it ready -- which .agents/skills/pull-requests/SKILL.md instructs as a step --
rebases, runs the cycle and merges is following the documented flow exactly.

THE SHAPE, and it reuses what inventory-tng-x0jp built rather than inventing:

* A marker, `<!-- do-not-merge -->`, posted on a line of its own in the pull
  request body. scripts/review_cycle.py already reads exactly this idiom, and
  its `carries` already distinguishes a marker POSTED from one written about or
  shown in a fence -- so a body may explain why it is blocked without
  disarming itself. Measured before filing: posted -> True, in prose -> False,
  fenced -> False.
* A job in .github/workflows/ci.yml that fails when the marker is posted. It
  has to be in THAT file: scripts/repo-settings.sh derives the required
  contexts from its job names and would remove anything added by hand.
* Nothing else. No new triggers are needed, and that is worth stating because
  it looks like an omission. The only two ways a blocked pull request becomes
  mergeable are being marked ready and being pushed to, and `ready_for_review`
  and `synchronize` are both already in this workflow's trigger list. Editing
  the marker out without pushing leaves the last verdict standing, which fails
  in the safe direction.

WHY A REQUIRED CHECK RATHER THAN A LABEL OR A HOOK. enforce_admins is true, so
a required context binds the owner as well; it covers the GitHub web interface,
which no local hook can see; and it cannot be routed around by spelling the
merge differently. A label would want `labeled`/`unlabeled` added to ci.yml's
triggers, which would re-run the whole suite -- and cancel it, since
cancel-in-progress is set -- every time somebody tags a pull request.

AGENTS.md WANTS A ROW WITH IT, because an agent that meets a red check it has
no rule for will try to make it green. The rule it reads has to match the check
it hits: a pull request carrying this marker is never merged, whatever its
state.

NOT THE WHOLE ANSWER FOR 28. Once inventory-tng-81f7 is settled and the demo
has been given, the spike is better preserved as a tag with the pull request
closed -- a closed pull request cannot be merged at all, and a tag cannot be
merged by one. This issue is what protects it in the meantime, and what
protects the next spike.
close_reason: Closed

title: Batch: a demo that can be shown, and a system that always has an admin
description: Batch membership for batch/a-demo-that-can-be-shown. Holds inventory-tng-w2f6 and inventory-tng-s8dk.

title: A setting the sync workflow needs is declared nowhere
description:
scripts/repo-settings.sh declares the repository settings this project's workflow depends on, and checks for drift. It does not declare the one the issue-sync workflow needs.

"Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests" is off, so gh pr create in .github/workflows/issue-sync.yml is refused and the job fails at its last step every run. Confirmed twice: the API reports can_approve_pull_request_reviews false on repeated uncached reads, and a live run failed with "GitHub Actions is not permitted to create or approve pull requests".

The project owner turned it on in the web interface on 2026-08-31 and it did not take -- both signals still say off afterwards, which is most likely the Save button under Workflow permissions not having been pressed.

THAT IS THE SMALLER HALF. The larger half is that a setting this repository's automation depends on was not declared anywhere, so nothing would have noticed it being off, or being turned back off later. The whole point of settings-as-code is that the checker fails rather than the workflow.

So declare it: read can_approve_pull_request_reviews from the actions permissions endpoint, compare it to true, and set it when applying. Same shape as the merge-method block above it, including the "this token cannot read it" path -- the scheduled check runs with a token that may lack Administration access, and "nobody could look" must not report as "nothing is wrong".

Note that default_workflow_permissions is deliberately NOT declared. It reads "read", and the workflow sets contents: write in its own permissions block, which is proven to work -- every failing run still pushed its branch. Declaring the repository default would be asserting something this project does not depend on.

description: Batch membership for batch/a-proposal-that-holds-only-the-tracker.

title: bd init in CI tries to clone over SSH and cannot
description:
The second failure of the issue-sync workflow, found by running it after t3w9 fixed the first.

.beads/config.yaml is committed and carries sync.remote: git+ssh://git@github.com/lotia/nycmesh-inventory-tng.git. So  in a runner does not initialise a local database -- it tries to CLONE that remote over SSH, and a runner has no key:

  Error: failed to clone remote: dolt clone ...: Permission denied (publickey)

WHY THE LOCAL TEST MISSED IT, which is the part worth keeping. The check before cwpa.3 landed ran  in an empty temp directory with only issues.jsonl in it. No config.yaml, so no remote, so nothing to clone. And re-running it on this machine still passes, because this machine HAS an SSH key -- the reproduction needed GIT_SSH_COMMAND=/bin/false as well as the config present. A local test that does not carry the committed config is not testing what CI does.

THE FIX: move .beads/config.yaml aside before init. A runner needs none of what it holds -- the prefix is given on the command line, export.auto is irrelevant to a job that exports explicitly, and the sync remote is for a developer's machine pushing Dolt history. Nothing commits the config, and the commit step adds only .beads/issues.jsonl by name.

Verified under reproduced CI conditions: config moved aside and GIT_SSH_COMMAND=/bin/false, bd init succeeded and bd import brought in 382 issues with both external_refs intact.

title: The issue-sync workflow cannot install beads
description:
Found by running the workflow, which is the only way it could be found: inventory-tng-cwpa.3 landed unverified because verifying it required merging it.

The first run failed at 'Install beads'.  compiles the whole of Dolt, and the run died verifying one of its modules:

  github.com/dolthub/dolt/go@v0.40.5-...: verifying module: reading
  https://sum.golang.org/tile/8/0/x215/552: stream error; INTERNAL_ERROR

That particular failure is transient -- a checksum-database read -- but the fragility is not. Building from source pulls and compiles a database engine to get a CLI, on every run, and depends on sum.golang.org being reachable and healthy each time.

BEADS PUBLISHES BINARIES, which makes the whole step unnecessary: beads_1.1.2_linux_amd64.tar.gz and a checksums.txt are on the v1.1.2 release, which is the exact version the sync behaviour was measured against. No Go toolchain, no compile, and a published checksum to verify against rather than a promise.

Verify the download against checksums.txt rather than trusting the tarball. This step installs a binary that then writes to the tracker, so it is worth the two lines.

title: Decide whether RFC 9421 signing clears the never-write-crypto rule
description:
FIRST CHILD OF jro, AND IT COMES BEFORE ANY CODE. Not a design task and not a spike: a written determination under AGENTS.md rule 3, made by a person, recorded in docs/decisions/.

jro's shape is a WebCrypto keypair the browser cannot export, registered against a code, signing every request under RFC 9421. The stored project memory names this exact case: 'RFC 9421 message signatures, non-extractable WebCrypto keys and anything resembling a bespoke token format all sit squarely under this rule.'

THE QUESTION, in the rule's own order.

Route 1, an established library. WebCrypto is route 1 for generating a keypair and producing a signature, and is not in doubt. The doubt is the SIGNATURE BASE: RFC 9421 requires canonicalising the covered components into a string both ends derive identically. Python has maintained implementations. The browser half would be assembled by hand unless a maintained, widely deployed, independently audited one exists. Find out whether it does, and name it.

Route 2, a thin wrapper. A wrapper arranges calls and validates inputs. Building a signature base is not arranging calls -- it is implementing the construction, and canonicalisation is exactly where an implementation is wrong in a way that produces output the same shape as output that is right. Weigh that honestly rather than describing the work as thin because it is short.

Route 3, stop and say so. If the browser side has no library worth the name, this is where it lands, and that is the rule working rather than a setback. It does not mean jro is impossible; it means the next step is a person deciding what to do about it, with the reasoning in a decision record, and NOT an agent prototyping to see.

WHAT ELSE THE ANSWER DEPENDS ON, so it is not made in a vacuum: inventory-tng-2jzx may conclude the network is the control, which changes what signing is for; inventory-tng-izbm can deliver a testable enrolment flow with no new cryptography at all; and inventory-tng-dzwu.2 is a precondition for developing any of it on a phone, because WebCrypto needs a secure context and a handset reaching a laptop over the LAN does not have one.

title: Find the GitHub issues beads has never seen
description:
Phase 1, and the only part bd does not do. Without it there is no two-way sync, only a one-way mirror.

bd pulls by explicit reference and never enumerates. Measured: a contributor opened issue #62, 'bd github sync --pull-only' reported nothing, and 'bd github pull 62' created the bead. The argument must be a bare number -- '#62' and the issue URL are both rejected.

WHAT TO BUILD. Something that lists GitHub issue numbers, subtracts the ones already named by an external_ref in .beads/issues.jsonl, and hands the difference to bd github pull. It is small:

  gh issue list --state all --json number --jq '.[].number' | sort > /tmp/gh
  python3 -c "import json;[print(r['external_ref'].split('/')[-1]) for r in map(json.loads,open('.beads/issues.jsonl')) if r.get('external_ref')]" | sort > /tmp/known
  comm -23 /tmp/gh /tmp/known | xargs -r bd github pull

Read the external_refs from the COMMITTED export rather than from the database, so it gives the same answer in a fresh clone and in CI, where there is no Dolt database at all.

Belongs in scripts/ beside the other checkers, in their shape, with their report.sh output. It is run by phase 2 and phase 3 both.

title: The demo cannot be seeded with the roster its own numbers describe
description:
Found while rewriting the presenter run of show on 2026-08-31.

Every figure the consultation rests on is measured against a roster of 86 distinct folded names -- one letter returns 54 of them, six searches sweep the lot, 13 names carry more than one address, 5 of those 13 collide when blurred, about 45% have no address at all.

seed_demo_data creates TWO volunteers. _seeding.VOLUNTEERS is (PACKER, INSTALLER), and nothing else in the repository builds a roster. So there is no shipped way to stand up the database the demo is written against.

The old run of show asked the presenter to seed 'around 80 names, with two pairs deliberately sharing a display name, and one of those pairs on the same mail provider with the same first initial'. Nothing behind that instruction exists. Anybody following it would have to invent a method minutes before a meeting, and the two-Seans beat -- which is the whole cost argument -- cannot be shown at all without a colliding pair.

The rewritten guide now tells the presenter to decide and rehearse a method rather than pretending a command exists, which is honest but is not a fix.

WHAT IS NEEDED: a way to seed a demonstration roster of invented people with the shape the argument needs -- a couple of deliberate display-name collisions, one pair sharing a mail provider and first initial, and roughly the real proportion carrying no address at all.

MUST NOT use real volunteers: the run puts the pick-list on a shared screen and the call may be recorded. inventory_tng.roster says why that matters and PUBLIC_VOLUNTEER_DETAILS is the safety net rather than the control.

Blocks any delivery of inventory-tng-81f7.3.

title: Every deferred-decision setting says what would let it be deleted
description:
The project owner, 2026-08-31: config flags must be clearly documented and their behaviour tracked so they can be pruned when making them default is prudent, because an explosion of flags even with safe defaults leads to overly complex code.

Three settings now exist purely to defer a decision: REQUIRE_SECOND_FACTOR, PUBLIC_VOLUNTEER_DETAILS and VOLUNTEER_ACCESS. Each is documented in .env.sample and docs/deployment.md, and check-config already fails when one is not. What NOTHING records is the exit: which decision each is waiting on, and what would have to be true to delete the flag and make one value the behaviour.

Without that, the flags accumulate. Each is individually justified and none is ever removed, because nobody can tell later which were provisional and which are real operator choices.

Add the marker to each module, collect them in one register, and enforce it: a fourth deferred-decision setting must declare its own exit or fail the build, and docs/deployment.md must name every one that exists. inventory_tng.console and inventory_tng.redaction are deliberately NOT in this class -- they are ordinary adaptation an operator chooses between, with no decision pending and nothing to prune.

title: Batch: one walk, and an audit that asks about admission
description:
Holds inventory-tng-s047 and inventory-tng-2hbv, which the owner chose to do together rather than in sequence.

They are one piece of work seen twice. s047 found six hand-rolled walks over urlpatterns that disagree about what counts as a route; 2hbv found that the audit riding on one of them asks about permission CLASS NAMES rather than about whether an anonymous request is admitted, and that it sees 20 routes of 203. Building the audit first would add a seventh walk for s047 to unpick; building the walk first and repairing the audit on top of it is one shape rather than two.

Its own batch epic rather than sitting under inventory-tng-hfv2, for the reason inventory-tng-l4ek gives: the stream epic holds gnhl and 81f7 too, and check-batch.sh would refuse a merge for siblings this work has nothing to do with.

title: Withholding a volunteer's identifiers does not stop them being guessed
description:
Found reviewing inventory-tng-81f7.5 (PR #55), which withholds a volunteer's email and slack_id from anonymous callers.

THE GAP. Withholding the fields from the RESPONSE BODY does not withhold them from a QUERY. VolunteerFilter.by_name_or_identifier in backend/src/inventory/views.py matches email__iexact and slack_id__iexact, so a caller who cannot read an address off a row can still send ?search=sean@nycmesh.net and learn from a hit that it belongs to a volunteer. That is confirmation of membership of a named organisation from a guessed address, arrived at without the field 81f7.5 removed.

Second route, same class: VolunteerListCreateView answers a POST whose identifier is taken by an unshowable record with a 409 (VolunteerConflictSerializer, decision 0015). The nested VolunteerSerializer does inherit 81f7.5's trimming correctly, so what leaks is the existence of the clash rather than the address -- but the existence is the whole of the oracle.

NOT REACHABLE TODAY, and that is why this is its own issue rather than a fix to 81f7.5. VOLUNTEER_APPEND is [IsAuthenticated, DeviceNotRevoked], so both endpoints still require a session and a signed-in caller is entitled to the identifiers anyway. This becomes live the day inventory-tng-gnhl opens them, which is the same day PUBLIC_VOLUNTEER_DETAILS starts mattering -- so it wants deciding alongside gnhl rather than after it.

WORTH KNOWING BEFORE DESIGNING A FIX. Exact matching on identifiers is deliberate and argued in VolunteerFilter's own docstring: a volunteer who types their own address and is shown nobody adds a duplicate, which is the one outcome the endpoint exists to prevent. So the answer is not simply to drop the identifier lookups -- that trades a confirmation oracle for the duplicate-spelling problem decision 0008 point 5 counts. The plausible shapes are gating the identifier half of the search on the same setting, or on being signed in, or throttling it hard enough that guessing is not worth doing.

81f7.5 also left VolunteerFilter's docstring saying identifier matching is 'not a privacy measure' because the pick-list already shows identifiers to anybody who may read it; that clause was corrected in 81f7.5's own commit, but the reasoning it pointed at is what this issue reopens.

title: Batch: a roster a demo may publish
description:
Holds inventory-tng-81f7.5 alone.

Its own batch epic rather than sitting under inventory-tng-81f7, for the reason inventory-tng-l4ek gives: check-batch.sh reads the parent epic of the landed issues as the batch and requires every child of it to have landed. 81f7 is a QUESTION with several children in flight, so a single issue landing beneath it would be refused for the siblings it has nothing to do with.

The relationship to 81f7 is not lost -- 81f7.5's own description opens with what that question is and what this settles of it.

title: EPIC: a volunteer uses this without an account
description:
The largest remaining thing between this repository and an application somebody who has not cloned it can use.

Decision 0012 point 3 is accepted and not built: volunteers do not sign in. inventory-tng-gnhl states the consequence in its own first line -- "Volunteers cannot use this application without an account, which is the reason it cannot be put in front of anybody yet." Everything under here exists to make that sentence false.

=== WHY IT IS AN EPIC RATHER THAN THREE LOOSE ISSUES ===

Because the ORDER is the difficult part, and it was only visible once all three were read together.

The obvious plan -- open the endpoints, then tidy up -- is the wrong one, and measurably so. inventory-tng-2hbv found that the audit which is supposed to catch a credential-free endpoint asks about permission CLASS NAMES rather than about whether an anonymous request would be admitted. `permission_classes = [StaffWrites, RecentlyAuthenticated]` -- the project default minus one token -- serves every read to an anonymous caller while `open_to_anybody` answers False and the audit records nothing. Two further spellings escape identically, and the walk sees 20 of 203 routes.

gnhl is precisely the edit that writes a permission list. So opening six endpoints while that audit has a hole in it means relying on a safety net already measured not to hold, at the exact moment it matters most. The audit is repaired first, and that is the whole reason these are grouped.

=== WHAT IS IN IT ===

* inventory-tng-2hbv -- repair the audit so it asks about admission rather than spelling, and so it sees every route. Both halves already exist in this repository and are named on the issue; this composes them rather than inventing anything.
* inventory-tng-gnhl -- open the reads a volunteer needs, which is more than the two writes: the catalogue and its balances, the pick-list, the label map the client prefetches, and the resolver for one scanned code.
* inventory-tng-81f7 -- MEETING INPUT, and not this repository's to answer alone: what an anonymous caller may learn about a person. It carries its own children.

=== WHAT IS DELIBERATELY NOT IN IT ===

inventory-tng-jro, device enrolment. Decision 0012 point 4 is explicit that enrolled devices are the NEXT step and not the first, deferred until this flow is in real use and the cost of enrolment friction is known. It is also, today, no gate at all: DeviceEnrolmentView mints a token to anybody who asks, and its own docstring says the guard is the throttle rather than the signature.

=== WHAT "DONE" LOOKS LIKE ===

Somebody who has never had an account opens the app, says who they are by picking a name, scans, and saves -- and the audit that says which endpoints take no credential is one that cannot be spelled around.

=== THE PART THAT IS NOT ENGINEERING ===

inventory-tng-81f7 needs a person, not a pull request. inventory-tng-81f7.5 makes a DEMONSTRATION honest by letting one full of invented people publish them; it settles nothing about a deployment holding real volunteers. This epic can be finished for a demo without that conversation and cannot be finished for production without it, and conflating the two is the mistake this paragraph exists to prevent.

title: Let a demo publish the roster, and default to withholding it
description:
Settled by the owner on 2026-08-30, in the brief at inventory-tng-81f7.

THE DECISION, and its scope is the whole of it: for the DEMONSTRATION environment an anonymous caller sees a volunteer's display_name, email and slack_id, exactly as a signed-in one does. No work, and the app behaves for a visitor the way it will behave for a volunteer.

WHAT MAKES IT SAFE IS THE DATA, NOT THE DESIGN. The demo is seeded with invented people -- seed_demo_data writes them and every name in it is made up. There is no real volunteer, no real address, and therefore none of the harm the brief argues about. The owner's words: "I will demo with fake data ... there is 0 risk."

The reasoning does not travel, and that is why this issue exists rather than a one-line config change.

=== WHAT TO BUILD ===

A SETTING WHOSE DEFAULT IS THE CAREFUL ANSWER. The same shape as REQUIRE_SECOND_FACTOR, and for the same reason -- decision 0021 point 11's pattern: the safe value in the code, the intended one written explicitly in every file this repository ships, so the deployment nobody thought about is the private one.

  code default          personal details WITHHELD from anonymous callers
  compose / .env.sample WITHHELD, because a laptop is not a demo
  the chart's default   WITHHELD
  examples/onboarding   PUBLISHED, with the reason in a comment beside it

So publishing the roster requires somebody to write a line that says so, in a file named for a demo, next to a comment explaining that it is safe only because the people are invented.

ANNOUNCE IT AT STARTUP, like the second-factor setting does, on stderr, when it is on. Decision 0021 point 5: adaptation is never silent. An operator who turned this on gets a line every start reminding them the roster is public.

=== THE THREE PITFALLS, which the brief now carries and which the implementation must answer ===

1. THE SETTING OUTLIVES THE FAKE DATA. The failure is not somebody arguing for a public roster in production; it is nobody arguing anything, and the demo values file being copied to a real deployment because it is the one known to work. The default above is the answer, and it is why the default is not merely conventional.

2. REAL DATA ARRIVES IN THE DEMO. A demonstration that becomes useful attracts real entries -- somebody adds themselves, or a real spreadsheet is imported "just to see". The fiction ends on a day nobody marks. WORTH CONSIDERING: whether the startup line should also say how many volunteer rows exist, so "invented people only" is something an operator can check rather than assume.

3. IRREVERSIBLE IN FACT. Tightening later is a small change in code and no change at all to a roster somebody has already taken. Nothing to build; it is the reason the default points the other way.

=== WORTH DOING WHATEVER ELSE IS DECIDED ===

slack_id is serialised and rendered by NOTHING. Removing it from VolunteerSerializer costs one line and loses no feature. It is not part of this decision and should not wait for it.

=== WHAT THIS DOES NOT SETTLE ===

The real deployment. inventory-tng-81f7 stays open: the question of what a volunteer's device may read about people when there is no login still needs the people it is about. This issue only makes a demo possible without answering it.

=== RELATED ===

inventory-tng-81f7.4 already exists to prune the demo flags once 81f7 is settled, and this adds one to its list.
close_reason: PUBLIC_VOLUNTEER_DETAILS decides whether an anonymous caller reads a volunteer's email and slack_id, defaulting to withholding in the code and stated explicitly in .env.sample, compose.yaml, values.yaml and both example files. examples/onboarding.yaml is the only file that turns it on, with the reason -- seed_demo_data invents everybody -- beside the line. roster.py carries the argument and the stderr announcement made at every start where the roster is public; it deliberately does not count volunteers, and says why. No request in serializer context is read as anonymous. Mutation-checked five ways: the declared default, the permission check, the environment read, the example file, and the chart template each kill a distinct test.
