title: The burst test cannot fail, because select calls EOF readable
description:
Found while fixing inventory-tng-nre8, by trying to prove the test it repairs still catches the defect it was written for. It does not, and it never did.

THE TEST: test_a_burst_arriving_in_one_write_is_one_post_rather_than_sixty, in backend/src/inventory/tests/test_shipping.py. Its subject is the whole reason shipping.reading exists -- sixty lines already sitting in a buffer must become ONE post, not sixty, and the way that is achieved is holding the undecoded remainder so that "has more arrived?" is asked only when the stream has genuinely gone quiet.

WHY IT PROVES NOTHING. Every pipe helper in that module closes the writing end before the reader starts. select() reports a descriptor at END OF FILE as READABLE -- that is what tells a reader to go and get the zero-length read. So shipping.waiting, which is select with a timeout, can never return False once the writer has closed:

  os.write(w, b"one\\n"); os.close(w)
  ...drain it...
  select.select([f], [], [], 0.2)[0]   ->  truthy

So the quiet path in reading() -- the `yield None` that makes a batch boundary -- is never reached in this test at all. The single batch of sixty comes from the `if held: yield held` at the END of iteration, which happens whatever reading() did on the way. Correct code and defective code produce the same answer.

PROVEN, not argued. reading() was replaced with the original defect -- lines off a TextIOWrapper, so select asks about a descriptor whose data is already decoded into Python's buffer -- and the whole module still passed, 32 of 32.

WHAT TO DO. The writer has to stay OPEN long enough for the reader to observe a quiet moment, and close afterwards so the stream ends. A writer that writes the burst, waits longer than QUIET, then closes gives:

  correct code   one batch of sixty, then the boundary
  defective code a boundary after nearly every line, so dozens of batches

That is the first arrangement in which the assertion means anything. It costs the test about a fifth of a second, which is what asking a timeout-based question honestly costs.

CHECK THE SIBLINGS at the same time. Only this test passes shipping.waiting -- the others call reading() with no ready function, or drive batches() over a literal list that already contains None. So the blast radius is one test, but the reason it went unnoticed applies to any future test that tries to exercise waiting through a closed pipe.

WHY IT MUST NOT BE DEFERRED: the commit for inventory-tng-nre8 is about this exact test, and it argues in its own message that a test which cannot fail is worse than no test. Landing that message over a test that cannot fail would be the same fault it names.
close_reason: The burst test's writer now stays open, idle, for longer than shipping.QUIET before closing, so select can genuinely report a quiet moment. Proven meaningful: restoring the original defect -- lines off a decoded text stream -- now fails it with [36, 24] != [60], where before the same mutation left the module green at 32 of 32.

title: Batch: a suite that finishes, and a test that can fail
description:
Two issues in one test module, found one after the other.

inventory-tng-nre8 -- the module deadlocked on a pipe smaller than it assumed, so the suite hung rather than failed.

The second -- found while proving the first fix kept the test honest -- is that the test in question could never have failed, because select reports EOF as readable and every helper closed the writing end before reading.

They land together because the second was found by doing the first, and because the first's commit message argues that a test which cannot fail is worse than no test.

title: landing-gate.sh record exits 0 when it refuses to record
description:
The second half of how PR 48 was merged with no receipt on 2026-08-30.

WHAT HAPPENS. scripts/landing-gate.sh record refuses correctly and says so clearly -- "Nothing on pull request 48 shows the code-review pass ran", with the marker to post and a pointer to DEVELOPERS.md -- and then exits 0.

So a caller cannot tell a refusal from a success, and the documented sequence in .agents/skills/pull-requests/SKILL.md, which is

  scripts/landing-gate.sh record <pr>
  gh pr merge <pr> --rebase

chained with && merges anyway. The refusal scrolls past above the merge output. That is exactly what happened: the refusal is in the transcript, three lines above "MERGED".

WHY IT IS WORTH FIXING RATHER THAN SHRUGGING AT. Everything else in this file is built on the principle that a guard which cannot see must refuse, and its header says so twice. Exiting 0 on a refusal is the same failure in the reporting channel rather than the decision: the check is right, and the answer is thrown away. It also makes the shell idiom that WOULD have saved this -- chaining with && -- silently useless, which is worse than not offering it.

WHAT TO DO. Exit non-zero when nothing was recorded. Keep the message exactly as it is; only the status changes. Check the other subcommands for the same thing while there.

ONE THING TO GET RIGHT: this must not make the PreToolUse hook refuse commands it should permit. The hook's contract is a JSON decision on stdout, and its exit status means something different -- the header at the top of the file is explicit that a non-zero exit from the hook path is not how a permission is expressed. Only the record subcommand, invoked by a person or an agent from a shell, should change.

TEST: scripts/landing-gate.test.sh, in the section on the ways this could stop guarding without saying so. A case that records with no evidence and asserts a non-zero status, and one that records successfully and asserts zero.

SEE ALSO the sibling issue: the Bash matcher does not see a guarded command behind a wrapper like timeout, which is why the merge was not refused independently.
close_reason: Withdrawn: not a defect. record_receipt exits 1 when a stage has no evidence, the shell carries it, and landing-gate.test.sh has asserted it since it was written. What I measured was a pipeline into tail, so the status was tail's. The real hole found while checking is inventory-tng-egh4.1.

title: Four helpers that already existed, written again
description:
Found by the simplify pass on PR 48. It belongs to no single issue in this batch -- each copy was made by a different commit, and removing them means touching test modules owned by three -- so it is its own, which is what DEVELOPERS.md's third row is for.

FOUR, and none of them is a judgement call:

1. rendered() -- environment(backend_container(**overrides)) -- is now written out identically in test_second_factor.py and test_trusted_origins.py, with a third call site in test_chart.py and no shared name. charts.py exists for exactly this, and its own docstring says so: two tests ask the same question and a second answer to it is the drift that module exists to prevent.

2. The session wind-back in test_second_factor.py reproduces conftest.py's stale fixture line for line -- the same time.time() minus ACCOUNT_REAUTHENTICATION_TIMEOUT minus one, the same comprehension over AUTHENTICATION_METHODS_SESSION_KEY, the same save(). Its own docstring admits it. What genuinely differs is WHICH client is wound back: conftest's builds on the editor fixture, which has TOTP, and the new test needs a password-only one. The mechanism is not the difference.

3. helpers.shipped() reads a repository file. test_second_factor.py spells the REPO_ROOT join and read_text by hand, twice, while test_static.py in the same branch imports the helper.

4. asks_for() in test_accounts_pages.py wraps a join-and-decode under a name that reads as a predicate, sitting two lines from asked_for(), which IS one. Its own docstring says the responses are always ordinary rendered ones -- which is the condition under which response.content.decode(), what twenty other places in this suite use, is correct.

WHAT TO DO: rendered() into charts.py with its three callers; wind_back(client) into helpers.py, with conftest's stale fixture becoming a call to it; shipped() used where it applies; asks_for inlined.

NOT IN SCOPE, and recorded because the same pass raised it: the "does .env.sample or compose.yaml mention this setting" assertion now exists in nine modules, each spelt slightly differently. That is a real generalisation and a larger one than this; it wants its own issue if it grows again.

title: Let a demo deployment be seeded, behind an acknowledgement it cannot inherit
description:
Found by a state review on 2026-08-30, asking what stands between this repository and a demo deployment people can use. Ali chose this route over a demo-only image and over typing the catalogue in by hand.

THE GAP. seed_demo_data refuses when settings.DEBUG is off. Its own docstring gives the reason and the reason is good: the command ships inside the backend image, so it is one wrong kubectl context away from a production pod, and the half of it not guarded by ledger_is_ours() writes into whatever database DATABASE_URL names.

DEBUG must be off in a cluster -- infra/helm/inventory-tng/values.yaml says false is the only supported answer and docs/deployment.md agrees. So the two rules meet and a deployed demo cannot be given anything to look at. Every list is empty, which README already says makes every page below it useless.

WHAT TO BUILD, and the shape is already in this repository rather than invented. seed_integration_data takes --i-know-this-creates-a-published-login, and its comments argue at length why a FLAG rather than an environment variable: a variable is ambient, so one Helm value switches the guard off for every invocation in that cluster from then on and nobody afterwards has to know it did. A flag is spent per invocation, cannot be turned on in advance by configuration, and shows up in the command that ran. That argument carries here unchanged.

So seed_demo_data gains a flag of its own -- something like --i-know-this-writes-invented-data -- which admits it when DEBUG is off. Without the flag the DEBUG refusal stands exactly as it does today, so nothing about a development machine changes and the path README hands a newcomer keeps working with no extra words.

WHAT THE FLAG HAS TO SAY WHEN IT REFUSES, because the refusal is the interface: name the flag, say the data is invented, and say it writes into whatever DATABASE_URL names. Somebody reaching for this on a real deployment should be told what they are about to do rather than which switch to flip.

AND IT WANTS DOCUMENTING WHERE A DEPLOYER LOOKS. docs/deployment.md's ten-step path from an empty cluster to a first sign-in has no step for data at all, because until now there could not be one. A demo deployment is a real case and the document is where somebody standing in front of an empty cluster reads.

TESTS: refused with DEBUG off and no flag; admitted with DEBUG off and the flag; unchanged with DEBUG on; and the refusal names the flag. The existing suite for this command is backend/src/inventory/tests/test_seed_demo_data.py.
close_reason: seed_demo_data takes --i-know-this-writes-invented-data, which admits it where DEBUG is off. The DEBUG path is unchanged, the refusal names the flag, and docs/deployment.md gained the step it never had.

title: A ship-logs test deadlocks on a pipe smaller than it assumed
description:
Found on 2026-08-30 while running the suite during inventory-tng-8ljy. Present on main, unrelated to any batch in flight, and it hangs FOREVER rather than failing -- the suite stops at 93% and never returns.

THE TEST: test_a_burst_arriving_in_one_write_is_one_post_rather_than_sixty, in backend/src/inventory/tests/test_shipping.py. It writes sixty records into an os.pipe(), closes the writing end, and only then reads:

    reading_end, writing_end = os.pipe()
    os.write(writing_end, (sixty records).encode())
    os.close(writing_end)
    with os.fdopen(reading_end, 'rb') as stream:
        lines = list(shipping.reading(stream, shipping.waiting))

NOTHING DRAINS THE PIPE WHILE IT IS BEING FILLED. One thread writes, and the read that would empty it is on the line after the write completes. So the write blocks as soon as the pipe is full, and nothing will ever empty it. A textbook single-threaded pipe deadlock.

THE ARITHMETIC, measured rather than estimated:

  one record serialised          229 bytes
  sixty of them, with newlines   13,800 bytes
  the pipe on this machine        8,192 bytes
  a default Linux pipe           65,536 bytes

13,800 fits in 65,536 and does not fit in 8,192. That is the whole bug.

WHY IT IS A FLAKE RATHER THAN A CONSTANT FAILURE, which is the part worth keeping. Linux shrinks newly created pipes once a user is over fs.pipe-user-pages-soft. On this machine that limit is 16,384 pages and the user was holding 988 pipes at sixteen pages each -- essentially at the limit -- so new pipes came back at two pages instead of sixteen. Earlier in the same session, with fewer pipes open, the identical test passed in seconds.

So it passes on a quiet machine and on CI, and deadlocks on a developer's machine after a long session with containers, subprocesses and background jobs. The worst shape: green everywhere it is watched, hanging where somebody is working.

PROVEN, not inferred:

  the single test, on this branch   hangs (timeout)
  the single test, on main          hangs (timeout)
  test_shipping.py alone, earlier   passed in seconds
  fcntl F_GETPIPE_SZ on a new pipe  8192

THE FIX IS NOT TO SHRINK THE TEST. Sixty is the number the test is about -- the defect it guards is sixty posts where one was wanted, and the docstring says so. Writing fewer records to fit a small pipe would keep the test green while removing what it tests.

Drain and fill at the same time instead. A writer in a thread, or a child process, so the reader empties the pipe while it is being filled; the assertion afterwards is unchanged. A temporary file would also work and would lose something real -- the reading() helper exists because select answers about a descriptor and a text stream buffers in front of one, and a regular file is not the descriptor that behaviour is about.

WORTH CHECKING AT THE SAME TIME whether any sibling in that module writes to a pipe the same way. The three around it are smaller and pass, but they pass for a reason nobody chose -- they happen to fit -- and the same shrunk pipe would take them too if a record grew.

AND IT EXPLAINS SOMETHING THAT SHOULD BE SAID PLAINLY: while this was hanging, three separate 'the full suite passes' claims were made in this session on runs that had actually timed out at 92%. The guardrail suites and the targeted runs were real; the full-suite claims were not. A test that hangs rather than fails is exactly what turns a timeout into a misread.
close_reason: All three pipe-filling sites now fill from a thread, so the reader drains while the writer runs. The pipe is also deliberately shrunk to one page, which turns the deadlock from a bug that appears on a loaded machine into one that appears on every machine -- proven: 13800 bytes into a 4096-byte pipe hangs deterministically in the old shape, and the new shape passes in 0.34s. A test asserts the shrink took, and goes red both when SMALL is raised and when the fcntl call is removed. The full suite now runs to completion with nothing deselected: 1330 passed.

title: A checker that refuses an undocumented config value
description:
Split from inventory-tng-xi9w on 2026-08-30, because documenting the values and guarding them are two commits.

Read xi9w for the audit. This issue is only the guard, and it lands after the documentation it would otherwise refuse.

WHAT IT CHECKS, and the fourth is the one that matters most:

1. Every assignment in .env.sample has a comment above its contiguous group.
2. Every environment entry in compose.yaml does.
3. Every leaf value in infra/helm/inventory-tng/values.yaml does.
4. Every variable the chart renders into a container appears in docs/deployment.md's environment-variable table.

The measure for 1 to 3 is the one a reader uses: a comment block directly above the group, no blank line breaking the two apart. A naive 'comment on the line above' rule reports three times as many failures and is wrong -- group comments covering a coherent block are correct and must keep passing. xi9w records that mistake being made and corrected.

Rule 4 is what found CLIENT_REPORT_RATE: set in .env.sample, rendered by the chart, absent from the document that lists what an operator may set. It is the rule that catches the gap mattering to somebody deploying rather than somebody reading, and it is the reason this is worth building rather than fixing the values once.

WHERE IT GOES: scripts/check-config.sh with scripts/check-config.test.sh beside it, and a line in CI's 'Guardrail checkers' job with the others. That job runs each checker's own suite and then, for the commit hook, runs the checker itself -- the same shape applies here.

AN ALLOWLIST IS WANTED, following scripts/check-docs.allow and check-telemetry.allow. Some values genuinely need no prose and the local-only variables are legitimately absent from the deployment table. Those files' own headers argue that an entry is a decision to justify rather than a way to make a build pass, and that argument carries.

TESTS, in the shape the other checkers' suites use -- a throwaway tree, a value with a comment, a value without one, a group comment covering several, a chart variable missing from the table, and an allowlisted exception.
close_reason: scripts/check-config.py with its wrapper, allowlist and a 12-case suite, wired into CI's Documentation and Guardrail jobs, and documented in DEVELOPERS.md#documentation-rules.
