title: One posture setting, one register entry, not a fourth copy of four tests
description:
Simplify pass on PR #57.

test_second_factor.py, test_roster_visibility.py and test_volunteer_access.py each carry the same four tests with different constants: the setting appears in compose.yaml and .env.sample; each Helm example carries the value it is named for; the chart's default is the cautious one; and a second render proves the chart reads the operator's answer rather than hard-coding the safe value. Eleven tests, one idea.

A fourth posture setting means a fourth copy, and whoever adds it will write two of the four and not notice the others are missing, because nothing says what the full set is. check-docs already caught four prose duplications between two of these files during this batch -- the same signal from another direction.

inventory_tng.postures.REGISTER already enumerates every posture setting. Give each entry its chart value and what each shipped example is expected to say, and one parametrized test in test_postures.py covers all of them; a new flag gets the coverage by being registered.

DJANGO_LOG_LAYOUT is the exception -- no chart renders it -- so it carries no chart value and the parametrization skips it, which is worth recording in the register anyway.

Only the 'is this written down everywhere it ships' family moves. The behaviour tests stay in their own files.

title: The hand-written client types promise three fields the API may omit
description:
frontend/src/api/types.ts declares email, slack_id and held_by as always present:

  Volunteer.email: string | null
  Volunteer.slack_id: string | null
  Location.held_by: number | null

All three are omitted entirely for a caller with no account -- email and slack_id since inventory-tng-81f7.5, held_by since inventory-tng-gnhl. backend/openapi.yaml already has all three as optional, so the SCHEMA is right and the hand-written types disagree with it. That file's own header says the schema is the contract these must agree with.

Nothing breaks today: the only readers are the admin screens, which are signed in. It bites the first time a volunteer-facing component reads one, and it will read undefined rather than null, so a  check passes straight through.

Spans a merged commit and this batch, so it is its own issue.

Make the three optional, and check whether anything in the integration suite can hold this -- a type cannot, as that header notes, so if the answer is nothing then say so where somebody will look.

title: Decide 'is it a DRF route' and 'what does it answer' once each
description:
Simplify pass on PR #56. Four consumers of helpers.routes() each spell 'view is None or not issubclass(view, APIView)' for themselves, in three different spellings, and three each spell the offered-methods narrowing (name.upper() for name in view.http_method_names if hasattr(view, name)).

This is s047's defect one level down: the walk stopped six callers disagreeing about what a route is, and then four went on to disagree about what a DRF route is. The comprehension spelling at test_capabilities.py:159 inverts the filter, which is the one that is easy to get backwards -- and backwards it audits nothing and passes.

Add helpers.drf_routes() and helpers.offered(view) beside routes(). The credential-free audit keeps its own branch because it must act on the non-DRF case rather than skip it; it just stops spelling the test itself.

Spans all three commits in the batch, so it is its own issue per DEVELOPERS.md 'One review pass'.

title: Route decides what a route is, so its consumers stop reaching around it
description:
Review of PR #56 found two audits going back to the raw URLPattern for what the walk should have decided once: `getattr(route.pattern.callback, 'view_initkwargs', None) or {}` and `route.pattern.callback`.

view_initkwargs is not incidental. as_view(permission_classes=...) is legal and DRF applies it per request, so a route that deliberately opened its view reads as CLOSED to anybody who instantiates the class bare -- a failure in the permissive direction, which is the class of bug this batch exists to close. It is part of what a route is.

Spans both commits in the batch: the dataclass is s047's and one consumer is 2hbv's, so per DEVELOPERS.md 'One review pass' this is its own issue rather than a widened commit.

Also here, because it is the same few lines: admits_anonymously builds its URL from Route.arguments and then tells the view it received none (args, kwargs = (), {}). No permission reads view.kwargs today, but an object-level one would raise rather than answer. And routes() re-imports `reverse`, which helpers.py already has at module scope.

title: Seed the first admin at deploy time, and never have none
description:
The owner's design, 2026-08-31, arrived while deciding what to do about /accounts/signup/ in inventory-tng-2hbv.

  "can the initial admin account be specified during deployment? ... admins
  should only be invited/allowed/created by the initial admin created during
  setup. Additionally, the admin user created during setup should NOT be a
  special admin. They are a normal admin, they just happen to be created
  during initial deployment. It should be possible to delete this admin user
  just as it should be with any other admin user. However the system MUST have
  a safeguard. It MUST do either one of the below: prevent the last admin user
  from deletion unless another admin is added; allow the deploy time
  initialization functionality that seeds the first admin user to be rerun in
  some way (init container) -- to ENSURE that the system ALWAYS has an admin
  user."

=== WHAT IS ALREADY TRUE ===

Read rather than assumed:

* SELF-SERVICE SIGNUP IS ALREADY CLOSED. AccountAdapter.is_open_for_signup
  returns False -- "Local accounts are issued, not registered" -- so
  /accounts/signup/ renders a refusal page and creates nothing. Any framing of
  this issue as "shut the open signup" is already done.
* A NON-INTERACTIVE ADMIN IS ALREADY POSSIBLE. `createsuperuser --noinput`
  with DJANGO_SUPERUSER_PASSWORD is what CI does. Nothing needs inventing to
  make one without a terminal.
* THE FIRST ADMIN IS ALREADY ORDINARY. createsuperuser writes a plain User row
  with is_staff and is_superuser. There is no privileged-first-account concept
  to avoid building, which is the owner's second requirement satisfied by
  construction rather than by care.

WHAT IS NOT TRUE: docs/deployment.md step 8 tells a person to run
createsuperuser interactively through `kubectl exec`. That is the weakest step
in the procedure and the one people are most often stopped by -- it is called
out as such in the procedure's own preamble.

=== 1. SEED THE FIRST ADMIN AT DEPLOY TIME ===

A Job or init container running createsuperuser --noinput, with the username,
email and password supplied from a Secret alongside the ones the deployment
already needs.

IT MUST BE IDEMPOTENT. createsuperuser --noinput fails when the username
exists, so a re-run must treat "already there" as success rather than as a
failed deploy. That is the difference between a step that can be repeated and
one that can be run once.

IT MUST NOT WEAKEN THE PASSWORD STORY. A password in a Secret is a password in
a Secret; docs/deployment.md#secrets already argues what may and may not live
in a values file, and this follows that rule rather than making a new one.

=== 2. THE SAFEGUARD: AT LEAST ONE ACTIVE ADMINISTRATOR ===

RECOMMENDED AS A DATABASE TRIGGER, and decision 0016 is the reason: an
invariant that must hold regardless of which client wrote the row belongs in
the database. The writers here are the Django admin, a shell, a fixture and
any future API -- four, and only one of them is code this project reviews.

THE SUBTLETY THAT MAKES IT REAL WORK: DELETION IS ONE OF THREE DOORS. An
administrator also disappears by having is_staff cleared, or is_active set
false. A guard on DELETE alone is bypassed by demoting yourself, which is the
likelier accident anyway. The invariant is "at least one user with is_staff
and is_active remains", enforced across delete, update-that-clears-is_staff,
and update-that-clears-is_active.

IT MUST NOT BLOCK A HANDOVER, and it does not: adding the incoming
administrator before removing the outgoing one satisfies it at every step. The
refusal only fires on the last one.

DECIDE WHAT COUNTS AS AN ADMINISTRATOR. Decision 0013 point 5 says the staff
flag is what makes one, so is_staff is the field -- but is_superuser exists
too and the two can disagree. Whichever is chosen, it is the same predicate
the safeguard and the admin screens must use, or they will disagree about
whether the system has an administrator.

=== 3. AND THE RE-RUNNABLE INIT AS RECOVERY, not as the guard ===

The owner offered these as alternatives. They are better as a pair, and the
distinction is what each is for:

* The trigger is the GUARD -- it stops the system reaching a state with no
  administrator through any ordinary path.
* The re-runnable init is the RECOVERY -- for when the state is reached anyway:
  a restore from a backup taken before the first admin existed, a direct SQL
  session, a migration that rewrote the table.

A guard with no recovery means the one failure it cannot prevent needs
somebody editing the database by hand at exactly the worst moment. Point 1
already provides the recovery if it is built idempotent, so this costs nothing
extra -- it is a property of point 1 rather than a third piece of work.

=== WHAT THIS IS NOT ===

Not an invitation system. "Admins should only be created by the initial admin"
is already how it works: signup is closed, and decision 0013 point 5 says an
existing administrator grants the staff flag. Nothing here adds invitations,
and inventing them would be scope this does not need.

=== DOCS THAT MOVE WITH IT ===

docs/deployment.md step 8 and its First administrator section, which currently
describe the interactive command as the only way. Decision 0013 point 5 is
worth re-reading while changing this, since it is what makes "an ordinary
admin" the right answer.

title: Stop serialising a Slack ID nothing renders
description:
Raised in the brief for inventory-tng-81f7.5 and deliberately kept out of it. 81f7.5 is closed, so without its own issue this instruction is lost in a closed bead.

THE OBSERVATION, in 81f7.5's own words: slack_id is serialised and rendered by NOTHING. Removing it from VolunteerSerializer costs one line and loses no feature. It is not part of that decision and should not wait for it. Confirmed again while reviewing PR #55: nothing in frontend/ renders it.

WHY IT IS WORTH DOING. It is the cheapest possible reduction in what the API hands out, and it is the field PUBLIC_VOLUNTEER_DETAILS now has to reason about. A field nobody displays is one nobody notices being published.

WHAT MAKES IT MORE THAN ONE LINE, and the reason it needs looking at rather than doing blind:

- VolunteerFilter matches slack_id__iexact, so it is a SEARCH key even where it is not a displayed field. That is deliberate -- the whole point of the identifier search is that somebody typing their own identifier is shown themselves rather than adding a duplicate. Dropping the field from the response need not drop the lookup, but the two decisions want taking together.
- VolunteerConflictSerializer.field is a ChoiceField over ['email', 'slack_id'] and the 409 path names which identifier clashed (decision 0015). That stays meaningful whether or not the field is rendered.
- It is a WRITE field as well as a read one: self-registration can submit it. Removing it from Meta.fields removes both directions.
- backend/openapi.yaml is regenerated, and 81f7.5's PERSONAL tuple in VolunteerSerializer shrinks to one field, at which point its 'two fields' comment and the tests naming both want revisiting.

So the shape is probably: keep the column, keep the lookup, stop rendering and stop accepting it -- but that is the thing to decide rather than assume.

title: Follow an item's journey to retirement, and reference MeshDB rather than copy it
description:
The owner's framing, 2026-08-30, refined over three exchanges. This is a DIRECTION plus the decisions it needs; the implementable slice is inventory-tng-35zr.1.

  "start location -> in a person's custody -> end location ... the eventual
  idea being to integrate with meshdb and enrich the records to fully follow
  the journey of an inventory item from where it was initially shipped to the
  location where it is in production and in use e.g. a hub, or an
  end-user-location."

  "the journey does not end until an item is explicitly retired from the
  inventory."

  "Ideally it should be a MeshDB reference since I really want to avoid
  duplicate data that may drift. But I haven't yet figured out a way to
  integrate with meshDB yet."

=== MOST OF THE MODEL IS ALREADY THERE ===

Read from the code: StockMovement is (item, quantity, from_location,
to_location); Location.Kind already has HUB; Location.parent nests places;
decision 0008 is the ledger as an append-only transfer graph. So
warehouse -> Sean's custody -> hub is three rows in tables that exist.

CUSTODY IS CONFIRMED, NOT CHANGED. location_one_custody_per_volunteer -- one
custody location per person -- is right under this framing: custody is a LEG of
a journey, not a place to store things. "Which of Sean's three rooms" is not a
question the ledger needs, because the next movement takes it somewhere that is
not Sean. Recorded because the constraint carries no comment saying so, which is
why it was questioned.

=== 1. WHY A BOOLEAN CANNOT DO WHAT AN INSTALL LOCATION CAN ===

Asked whether `installed` / `in_use` should replace the NULL destination, so a
thing can be recovered and re-used.

IT HAS NOTHING TO ATTACH TO. Item is a TYPE, not a unit: `name` is unique, it
carries minimum_stock and reorder_quantity, quantities are decimals, and there
are no serial numbers anywhere in the schema. The system knows "40 x LiteBeam
AC Gen2" and never "that LiteBeam". So `installed = true` on an Item says "this
product is installed", which means nothing.

A LOCATION SERVES THE SAME GOAL BETTER. Install is a movement TO the place;
recovery is a movement FROM it; the balance there says what is sitting at that
install. Both directions, no new concept, and unlike a boolean it says WHERE to
go and get it.

THE DISTINCTION IS ALREADY HALF-BUILT AS TRANSACTION KINDS. CONSUMPTION is
`required=(from_location,), forbidden=(to_location,)` -- "stock used at a job
comes out of somewhere and does not arrive anywhere". That is the dead end, and
it is deliberate. What is missing is the split between CONSUMABLE and DURABLE:
a zip tie is genuinely consumed, a router is installed and recoverable, and
today both go through CONSUMPTION. Under this framing, installing a router is a
TRANSFER to an end-user location, and CONSUMPTION keeps only what truly does
not come back. Item.unit_of_measure (each / metre / foot) is already a hint at
that split and may be the wrong axis to lean on -- decide rather than assume.

=== 2. RETIREMENT AS THE ONLY ENDING ===

If a journey ends only at explicit retirement, the destination NULL goes away
entirely. Retirement is then most naturally a movement to a retirement
location: no new machinery, and the trail stays whole.

THE ARRIVAL SIDE IS NOT THE SAME QUESTION, and the owner's follow-up is what
showed it. The two NULLs are not symmetric:

* A DESTINATION null means the item still physically exists -- on somebody's
  roof -- and may be wanted back. Information is genuinely lost, and that is
  the end worth closing.
* An ARRIVAL null means the item did not exist here before. There is no
  earlier leg to lose. Closing it recovers nothing, because there is nothing
  behind it.

A SUPPLIER MUST NOT BECOME A LOCATION, and the owner's own example is why: the
same item -- an SXT -- is sold by several vendors. That is already modelled.
Vendor is a first-class row, and VendorOffer is one vendor's listing for one
item, carrying url, unit_price, units_per_order, observed_at and a constraint
of one is_preferred per item. Three suppliers for one SXT is three offers
against one Item, today.

Making a supplier a Location would break two things. A Location is WHERE STOCK
SITS, so it would assert that a vendor's warehouse holds this organisation's
inventory and corrupt every balance. And it would stand a second, weaker
representation of vendors beside the one already holding the price history --
the duplicate-that-drifts this issue exists to avoid, arriving from inside.

SO THE SHAPE, if purchase provenance is wanted, is a reference from the
RECEIPT TRANSACTION to the Vendor. "Who we bought this from" is a fact about
the purchase, not a place in the journey.

THE DATA-ENTRY BURDEN IS SMALL AND IS NOT THE VOLUNTEER'S PROBLEM. RECEIPT is
already one of the four kinds the volunteer app offers -- "Receiving a
delivery" -- and it requires only to_location, which has to be given anyway. A
vendor would be ONE OPTIONAL FIELD PER DELIVERY rather than per line;
deliveries are rare beside check-outs and check-ins; and VendorOffer.is_
preferred already names one supplier per item, so the field can be pre-filled
and usually only confirmed.

RECOMMENDATION TO ARGUE WITH: keep the arrival null as a deliberate BOUNDARY
and write it down as one, rather than inventing a place for the item to have
been. Add an optional vendor to the receipt if provenance is wanted. The
journey then has one open end on purpose, which is more honest than a fictional
supplier location.

NOT THE SAME AS Item.active / Location.active. Those retire a CATALOGUE ROW.
Retiring stock is a movement; retiring a product is a flag. Conflating them
would be easy and wrong.

=== 3. MESHDB: STORE THE REFERENCE NOW, RESOLVE IT LATER ===

The integration does not have to be solved to avoid the drift. An opaque MeshDB
identifier on Location costs nothing, copies no data, and needs no API to
exist. Until something can be asked, the identifier IS the truth -- only the
friendly name is unavailable.

WHAT DOES NEED SETTLING WITH MESHDB'S MAINTAINERS: which identifier. Install
number, node number, something else. Picking wrong is the expensive part; the
plumbing is not.

AND IT AGREES WITH THE PRIVACY ARGUMENT, which is worth using. A Location per
end-user home means member addresses in this database -- the same personal data
inventory-tng-81f7 is about, for a larger population. A MeshDB reference stores
an opaque id instead. Anti-drift and anti-exposure point the same way here.

=== WHAT IS STILL MISSING, IN ORDER ===

* An end-user location kind, and the decision above about what it references.
* A retirement destination, and the arrival-side decision beside it.
* The consumable/durable split, which decides which kind an install uses.
* Nothing shows a journey: the rows exist, reading them as a story does not.
  That is the one piece needing none of the above -- inventory-tng-35zr.1.

title: A demo that tracks development has no story for staying current
description:
Found by reviewing the board against the owner's second demo goal on 2026-08-30: "deploying to a demo server where people who don't want to mess with the source code and clone the repo can still use the system AND SEE THE CHANGES AS WE CONTINUE DEVELOPMENT."

The last clause has nothing behind it. Established by reading the board and the workflows rather than assumed: no open issue mentions redeploying, and .github/workflows/ has release.yml, which publishes images on a tag, and nothing that installs or upgrades anything.

SO THE CURRENT STORY IS: push a tag, wait for two images, then somebody with cluster credentials runs `helm upgrade --install` by hand with their own values file. Every time. For every change anybody wants a demo audience to see.

That is fine for the FIRST install -- docs/deployment.md walks it, and inventory-tng-qe7 made the images exist -- and it is the wrong shape for a demo that is meant to track development. The failure mode is not an outage; it is a demo that silently falls a month behind while everybody assumes it is current, and feedback arriving about behaviour that was already changed.

WHAT TO DECIDE, because the answers differ a lot in cost and in who has to hold credentials:

* A DOCUMENTED ONE-LINER and nothing else. `helm upgrade` with the release's tag, in docs/deployment.md under a heading about keeping a demo current, plus saying out loud that somebody has to run it. Honest, costs nothing, and does not pretend.
* A WORKFLOW THAT DEPLOYS ON A TAG. GitHub Actions holding a kubeconfig or a token for the demo cluster. This is the real one, and the cost is a long-lived cluster credential in repository secrets -- which is a security decision rather than a convenience one, and belongs in docs/decisions/ if it is taken.
* PULL RATHER THAN PUSH. Something in the cluster watching the registry or the chart -- Flux, Argo, or a cron that reconciles. No credential leaves the cluster, which is the better posture, and it is a second system to run and understand for one demo environment.

WHAT MAKES THIS NOT URGENT YET, and worth saying so nobody starts it too early: nothing has been deployed even once. No tag has been pushed, docs/deployment.md still opens by saying the procedure has never been run end to end against a cluster, and inventory-tng-gnhl means a visitor cannot use the app without an account anyway. Automating a redeploy of an environment that does not exist, for an audience that cannot sign in, is work in the wrong order.

DO IT WHEN: the first install has happened and somebody has been annoyed by the second one. Until then the documented one-liner is the honest answer and the other two are speculation about a cadence nobody has measured.

title: Show an admin what needs fixing, derived rather than tracked
description:
Asked by the owner on 2026-08-30: a simple list of things an administrator needs to fix, seen on signing in. Explicitly NOT a ticket tracking system -- "I don't want to build a ticket tracking system just to support this use case".

That constraint is the design, and there is a way to honour it exactly.

=== DERIVE, DO NOT TRACK. THIS IS THE WHOLE IDEA ===

A ticket tracker stores state: open, closed, assigned, snoozed. State has to be groomed, goes stale, and disagrees with reality -- a closed ticket for a problem that came back, an open one for a problem somebody fixed quietly.

Every item on this list is instead DERIVED from data the system already holds, and has no state of its own. An entry appears because a condition is true and disappears because somebody made it false. Nothing to close, nothing to groom, and it cannot lie: if the row is on the list, the problem is live right now.

That single decision is what keeps this from becoming the thing the owner does not want, and it should be the first line of whatever is built.

=== THE PRECEDENT ALREADY IN THE TREE ===

UnresolvedItemString, in inventory/staging.py, is this idea built once for one case. Its docstring: "a list an administrator can read, decide, and clear by adding a catalogue row or a line to that rule's alias table". Read-only in the admin, cleared by fixing the cause rather than by editing the row.

So the pattern is established and endorsed; what is missing is that it is import-specific, it is one model among about fifteen in the admin, and NOTHING BRINGS IT TO ANYBODY'S ATTENTION. The admin index is Django's stock app list -- verified, there is no custom AdminSite -- so an administrator signing in sees a list of tables, not a list of things to do.

=== WHAT GOES ON IT, drawn from what already exists ===

Each is a query, not a table:

* CODES SCANNED THAT RESOLVED TO NOTHING -- needs inventory-tng-f5la first, which is what records them. A dead sticker on a shelf, and the reason this conversation started.
* UNRESOLVED ITEM STRINGS -- the existing table, surfaced where somebody will see it.
* ITEMS BELOW MINIMUM STOCK -- minimum_stock and reorder_quantity are already on Item and nothing reads them for this. Arguably the single most useful row on the list for an inventory nobody is watching.
* ITEMS WITH NO IDENTIFIER -- inventory-tng-w4dg fixed the create path, so this is the historical tail rather than a growing set, and it will not clear itself.
* VOLUNTEERS THAT LOOK LIKE DUPLICATES -- the trigram index on display_name already exists and this is what it is for; decision 0012 point 2 is the merge operation that clears one.

None of these needs a new writable table. All of them are questions asked of rows that are already there.

=== WHERE STATE CREEPS IN, AND THE ANSWER FOR NOW ===

One case genuinely needs it: "these two volunteers look like duplicates and are two different people". That cannot be derived -- the condition stays true for ever and the entry never clears, so the list grows a permanent row somebody has to learn to ignore, which is how a list stops being read.

DO NOT SOLVE IT IN THE FIRST VERSION. Ship the four that clear themselves, leave duplicates off, and see whether the list gets used. If it does, a single suppression table -- what was dismissed, by whom, when -- is a small and well-understood addition. Building it up front is building the tracker the owner ruled out, in order to serve the one row that needs it.

=== WHERE IT LIVES ===

The admin, because that is where an administrator already goes and decision 0014 keeps it complete on purpose. A custom AdminSite index template, or one read-only page reachable from it. Not the volunteer app: none of this is a volunteer's to fix, and decision 0027 says the two surfaces should look different for exactly this kind of reason.

=== WHAT MAKES IT SUCCEED OR FAIL ===

An empty list has to be the normal state. If the ordinary condition of a healthy system is four rows nobody can clear, the list is furniture within a month. So every entry must name what to DO, not just what is wrong -- "add a catalogue row or an alias" rather than "unresolved string" -- which is the standard UnresolvedItemString already sets.

title: Tell a scanner from a person, without fighting for focus
description:
Asked by the owner on 2026-08-30: a hidden box the scanner writes into, and a separate visible box for a person, with the fuzzy narrowing on the visible one only. The aim is to be strict when a machine is reading and helpful when a person is typing.

The aim is right and is the rule this repository should follow. The MECHANISM needs to be different from a hidden box, for a reason that is not obvious.

=== THE CAMERA HALF IS ALREADY DONE ===

Established by reading Scanner.tsx: the camera does not go through the text box at all. CameraScanner takes an onCode callback and calls it with the decoded string. So for a phone at a shelf there is already no box in the path, and nothing needs adding.

=== WHY A HIDDEN BOX DOES NOT DO WHAT IT LOOKS LIKE IT DOES ===

FOCUS IS SINGULAR. A wedge scanner is a keyboard: it types into whichever element has DOM focus and presses Enter. So

* if the hidden box holds focus, the visible box cannot -- and a person cannot type into it;
* if the person clicks the visible box to type a name, the scanner's characters go there instead.

The two boxes do not coexist; they take turns, and the turn-taking is the whole problem. Any code that steals focus back to the hidden box will do it while somebody is halfway through a word.

AND ON A PHONE IT IS WORSE. Focusing any text input opens the on-screen keyboard. A focused hidden input raises the keyboard over an interface showing nothing to type into, which is a worse experience than the one being fixed.

=== WHAT DOES WORK: RECOGNISE THE MACHINE BY HOW IT TYPES ===

A document-level keydown listener, independent of focus, that recognises a scan by its signature and hands it to the exact-resolution path. Everything else falls through to whatever the person is doing.

The signature is unusually reliable HERE, and that is the point worth keeping. A label code is ten characters of Crockford base32 -- CODE_PATTERN in models.py -- so a scan is:

* exactly ten characters from that alphabet, and
* terminated by Enter, and
* delivered faster than a person types, tens of milliseconds apart rather than hundreds.

All three together. A person typing an item name produces none of them: names are longer or shorter, contain letters the alphabet excludes, and arrive at human speed. The false-positive shape -- a human typing exactly ten Crockford characters at machine speed and pressing Enter -- is not a thing that happens.

So the visible box can be an ordinary item search with fuzzy narrowing, focused, typed into normally, and a wedge scan still resolves exactly without the person doing anything.

ONE ROUGH EDGE TO DESIGN FOR, honestly: the scanner's characters land in the focused field on their way past, because the listener cannot know a burst is a burst until several characters in. The field is cleared when the burst completes and matches. That is a brief flicker of nonsense in the search box, and it is the price of not fighting for focus. Worth prototyping before committing -- if it reads badly, the fallback is two visible fields with the scan one focused by default, which is what the app effectively has now.

=== WHAT THIS IS NOT ===

Not a loosening of code resolution. The burst goes to the same exact lookup it goes to today; the listener decides WHICH path, never WHAT matches. inventory-tng-816n's note has that boundary.

=== DEPENDS ON ===

inventory-tng-816n, which is what makes the visible box worth typing into. Doing this first would give a person a strict box and a search that still cannot forgive a typo.

title: A scanned code that resolves to nothing tells nobody
description:
Raised by the owner on 2026-08-30, while drawing the line between scanning and typing: "If an item is not found then that is an issue for admins to sort and the user should get a clear error."

The volunteer's half is already right. A code that resolves to nothing gives a 404, and the app says so and offers the search instead -- which is decision 0011's degradation rather than a dead end, and DeepLink.test.tsx holds it.

THE ADMIN'S HALF DOES NOT EXIST. Nothing records that somebody scanned a code which resolved to nothing. LabelResolveView is a DetailView and the 404 is the base class's; there is no log line, no counter, and no report. Established by reading views.py rather than assumed.

So the sentence "that is an issue for admins to sort" is not true today: no admin is ever told there is anything to sort. A volunteer meets a dead sticker, works around it through the search, and the sticker stays dead on the shelf for the next person.

WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN IT SOUNDS. A code that resolves to nothing is not a typo -- the codes are ten characters of Crockford base32 and a mistyped one is overwhelmingly likely to resolve to nothing rather than to something wrong, which is exactly why exact matching is safe there. So an unresolvable scan means one of a small number of REAL things, and every one of them is an administrator's job:

* a sticker printed from a database that has since been restored from an older backup;
* a label deleted from the admin while its sticker is still on a shelf -- inventory-tng-6pr made that PROTECT, so it is historical rather than ongoing, but the stickers it already produced are still out there;
* a sticker from another deployment, or a test one that escaped;
* a QR generated for an item that was never saved.

None of those is visible from the volunteer's side and none of them fixes itself.

WHAT TO DO, and the size of it is the point -- this is small:

* Count it. inventory.telemetry already has the REFUSALS counter and a reason label; an unresolved code is a reason.
* Log it once, at WARNING, with the normalised code. The code is not personal data and is printed on a sticker anybody can read.
* Decide whether it needs more than that. A report an administrator can open -- "codes scanned in the last month that resolved to nothing" -- is the fuller answer and is a bigger piece of work; the counter and the log line are what make the problem visible at all, and they are worth having first.

WHAT NOT TO DO: nothing here loosens the lookup. Decision 0011 and 0026 both rest on a scanned code resolving to exactly one item or to nothing, and the whole point of this issue is that "or to nothing" should be audible rather than silent.

title: A typo in one word of a volunteer's name scores below the threshold
description:
Found while researching fuzzy matching for the item search, and measured rather than reasoned.

VolunteerFilter uses display_name__trigram_similar, which compiles to the % operator: similarity over the WHOLE string, against a threshold of 0.3. A multi-word name dilutes that, so a misspelling of ONE word can score below the threshold and return nothing.

Measured against 'Ubiquiti NanoStation M5' -- a longer string than most display names, chosen because it shows the effect plainly:

  typed 'Nanostatoin'   similarity 0.286 (below 0.3, no match)   word_similarity 0.667 (match)

Display names are shorter, usually one or two words, so the dilution there is milder than that example -- but it is the same effect and it grows with every name that carries a middle name, a nickname in quotes, or an organisation.

WHAT TO DO. Django registers display_name__trigram_word_similar, which compiles to %>, and the EXISTING GinIndex with gin_trgm_ops serves it -- verified with EXPLAIN, no new index needed. The threshold for %> is its own setting and defaults to 0.6.

WORTH DECIDING RATHER THAN SWAPPING: %> matches a run aligned to word boundaries, so it is more forgiving of a typo inside one word and LESS forgiving of a string that is merely short. 'nano' scores 0.800 by word similarity and 0.160 by plain similarity; whether that is an improvement depends on whether somebody typing four characters should see a match at all.

The measurements and the full table are on the item-search issue this came from.

title: Let a misspelt item name still find the item
description:
Researched on 2026-08-30 at the owner's request, and measured against the running PostgreSQL 18.6 and Django 6.1 rather than recalled. Everything below was run.

=== THE CORRECTION THAT MATTERS FIRST ===

A trigram index does NOT tokenise into words and does NOT stem. That is full-text search -- to_tsvector, a dictionary, a language -- and it is a different tool that answers a different question.

pg_trgm splits a string into overlapping THREE-CHARACTER sequences and ignores what a word is, except to pad the edges:

  show_trgm('NanoStation')
  {"  n"," na",ano,ati,ion,nan,nos,"on ",ost,sta,tat,tio}

So matching WITHIN a word is exactly and only what it does. Measured:

  similarity('NanoStation','Nanostatoin')  0.500   transposed letters
  similarity('Ubiquiti','Ubiquity')        0.636   wrong last letter
  similarity('Mikrotik','Microtik')        0.500   c for k

And the contrast with stemming, which it cannot do:

  similarity('running','run')                            0.333
  to_tsvector('english','running') = to_tsvector('english','run')   true

=== WHAT THE APP ALREADY DOES, WHICH IS MORE THAN IT LOOKS ===

pg_trgm has been installed since the first migration -- TrigramExtension() in 0001_initial -- and one finder uses it:

  VolunteerFilter, in views.py. display_name__trigram_similar, ORed with icontains and two exact identifier lookups, then annotated with TrigramSimilarity and ordered by it descending.
  Volunteer.Meta.indexes carries GinIndex(fields=["display_name"], opclasses=["gin_trgm_ops"]).

Its own docstring explains the choice to index the bare column rather than Lower(display_name), because pg_trgm lowercases while building trigrams and an expression index would not serve the query. That reasoning is correct and worth keeping.

=== THE WEAKNESS IN THAT EXISTING USE, WHICH IS THE FINDING ===

`%` -- which is what __trigram_similar compiles to -- tests SIMILARITY OVER THE WHOLE STRING, and a multi-word name dilutes it. Against 'Ubiquiti NanoStation M5', with the default threshold of 0.3:

  typed                     similarity   word_similarity   strict_word
  Nanostatoin                    0.286             0.667         0.500
  NanoStation                    0.500             1.000         1.000
  nanostation m5                 0.625             1.000         1.000
  Ubiquity NanoStation M5        0.846             0.846         0.846
  nano                           0.160             0.800         0.308

The first row is the whole point. A volunteer who misspells ONE word of a multi-word name scores 0.286, which is BELOW the threshold, so `%` returns false and the item is not found. word_similarity scores it 0.667 and finds it, because it looks for the best matching run aligned to word boundaries instead of comparing the whole string.

Volunteer display names are one or two words, so the dilution is milder there; item names are three and four. Whatever is done for items, this is a real and measurable weakness in the volunteer search as it stands.

=== POSTGRESQL: YES, AND THE INDEX ALREADY EXISTS IN THIS SCHEMA ===

GIN with gin_trgm_ops. GiST is the other option and is worth less here: it is smaller and slower, and its advantage -- ordering by distance through the index -- is not something a catalogue of this size needs.

ONE index serves all of it. Measured with EXPLAIN over 30,000 rows:

  name % 'x'      similarity          Bitmap Index Scan
  name %> 'x'     word similarity     Bitmap Index Scan
  name LIKE '%x%'                     Bitmap Index Scan
  name ILIKE '%x%'                    Bitmap Index Scan

fuzzystrmatch is available too -- levenshtein, soundex, metaphone -- and is the wrong tool: no index can serve it, so every one of them is a full scan with a function call per row. Soundex is also English-phonetic, which a catalogue of manufacturer part numbers is not.

=== DJANGO ORM: YES, FULLY, AND IT IS ALREADY IMPORTED ===

Three lookups registered on CharField, verified against the installed Django 6.1:

  __trigram_similar              ->  col %   term
  __trigram_word_similar         ->  col %>  term
  __trigram_strict_word_similar  ->  col %>> term

Four expressions in django.contrib.postgres.search: TrigramSimilarity, TrigramDistance, TrigramWordSimilarity, TrigramStrictWordSimilarity. GinIndex takes opclasses. TrigramExtension is the migration operation, already applied.

Also confirmed: annotating with TrigramSimilarity and ordering by it survives .distinct(), which matters because ItemFilter.search now uses distinct() for the identifier join. Run, not assumed.

=== THE TRAP, WHICH IS THE SAME ONE THIS REPOSITORY ALREADY MET ONCE ===

Django's __icontains compiles to UPPER(col::text) LIKE UPPER(...), and an index is over a column rather than over a function of one. Measured against a 50,000-row table carrying a gin_trgm_ops index:

  upper(name) like upper('%NanoStation%')   Seq Scan
  name ilike '%NanoStation%'                Bitmap Index Scan
  name like '%NanoStation%'                 Bitmap Index Scan

This is exactly what identifiers.matching() already documents for __istartswith, one lookup along. So ItemFilter.search's icontains half cannot use a trigram index however the index is built; the fix has the same shape as the existing one -- spend the case-folding somewhere other than SQL, or use the trigram operators, which lowercase themselves.

=== SCALE, WHICH DECIDES WHY RATHER THAN WHETHER ===

The catalogue is 52 items -- docs/architecture.md, and sheet/items.py counts 145 strings for those 52. Measured:

  52 rows, Django's icontains shape       0.031 ms   Seq Scan
  50,000 rows, same shape                15.465 ms   Seq Scan

So PERFORMANCE IS NOT THE ARGUMENT and will not be for years. Anybody proposing this for speed has the wrong reason. The argument is entirely that a volunteer standing at a shelf typing "Nanostatoin" or "Ubiquity" or "Microtik" currently finds nothing, and that is the same failure the spreadsheet had -- a name that did not match matched nothing at all -- arriving through a nicer interface.

=== WHERE IT FITS, AND WHERE IT MUST NOT GO ===

FITS -- ItemFilter.search, the name half. Typo tolerance for a person at a shelf, at a size where the cost is irrelevant. VolunteerFilter is the worked precedent, including the index and the ordering.

FITS, WITH A HUMAN IN THE LOOP -- the sheet importer's resolve() in sheet/items.py, which today is exact, then case-folded, then a hand-maintained table of 27 aliases. Trigram could PROPOSE the remaining unresolved strings to whoever maintains that table. It must not resolve them automatically: those rows post stock movements, and decision 0016 makes movements unremovable, so a wrong guess is permanent.

MUST NOT -- identifiers.matching(), and label code resolution. Both are no, and MEASURED, because the first version of this note asserted a reason that turned out not to hold.

WHAT DID NOT HOLD: the claim that label codes would collide with each other. Two thousand real minted codes -- ten characters of Crockford base32 -- produced ZERO pairs above the 0.3 threshold, and two hundred codes each corrupted in one character produced two hundred matches and NOT ONE that resolved to a different label. Random codes over a 32-character alphabet are well separated under trigram similarity. Anybody arguing the collision case for CODES should be shown these numbers rather than believed.

WHY CODES ARE STILL NO, on the argument that survives: the failure fuzzy would be reaching for is already solved exactly. TYPO_FOLDS maps I and L to 1 and O to 0, and Crockford excludes those four letters precisely so the fold is unambiguous -- no minted code can contain them, so there is never a question of which character was meant. 'DEMOOOOOO1' folds to 'DEM0000001' deterministically and losslessly. Fuzzy matching would replace a correct answer with a probable one, for a failure that has no remaining instances.

WHY IDENTIFIERS ARE NO, and this is the case that does hold, measured on real part-number shapes:

  UBB-LB-AC-GEN2   vs  UBB-LB-AC-GEN1     0.765   above threshold
  LBE-5AC-GEN2     vs  LBE-5AC-GEN1       0.733   above threshold
  TL-WR841N-v14    vs  TL-WR841N-v13      0.750   above threshold
  NBE-5AC-GEN2     vs  NBE-5AC-16-GEN2    0.813   above threshold
  0847101099965    vs  0847101099966      0.750   above threshold

Manufacturer part numbers are not random. They are a shared stem plus a generation, a revision or a check digit -- so the character that distinguishes two DIFFERENT products is exactly the character trigram similarity discounts. Every pair above is two different things that sit on adjacent shelves, and fuzzy matching calls all of them the same.

AND THE COST IS ASYMMETRIC, which is what makes "rare" not good enough. A wrong search result is corrected by the next keystroke. A wrong identifier resolution posts a stock movement against the wrong item, and decision 0016 makes movements refuse UPDATE and DELETE -- so the error is silent, permanent, and discovered at a count months later. Exact matching answers "not found", which a person can act on.

=== WHAT A CHANGE WOULD ACTUALLY BE ===

  1. GinIndex(fields=["name"], opclasses=["gin_trgm_ops"]) on Item, and a migration.
  2. ItemFilter.search ORs in name__trigram_word_similar rather than relying on icontains alone, and annotates TrigramSimilarity or TrigramWordSimilarity to order by.
  3. The identifier half stays exactly as it is -- prefix, exact, unchanged.
  4. Tests: a misspelling finds the item; a string that resembles nothing finds nothing; the identifier half is not made fuzzy by the change.
  5. The threshold is a decision, not a default to accept quietly. 0.3 for %, 0.6 for %>. Too low offers noise to somebody in a hurry; too high is the current behaviour.
notes:
CORRECTION, same day: the first version of this issue argued that label codes would collide under fuzzy matching. Measured, they do not -- 2000 random codes gave zero pairs above threshold, and 200 one-character typos gave zero wrong resolutions. The reason codes stay exact is TYPO_FOLDS, which already fixes the real failure losslessly. The identifier case is the one that holds, and it now carries the measurements.
SCOPE, settled by the owner on 2026-08-30 and narrower than the description above assumes in places.

FUZZY APPLIES TO ONE THING ONLY: a person typing an item NAME into a search box, where the job is to help them type less and watch a list narrow. Nowhere else.

IT MUST NOT REACH CODE RESOLUTION, and that is a rule rather than a preference. A QR code is generated to stand for an item, so a scan either resolves exactly or it does not resolve -- and 'does not resolve' is a clear error for the volunteer and a job for an administrator, which is inventory-tng-f5la.

ALREADY TRUE, and worth recording so nobody 'fixes' it: LabelResolveView.get_object calls Label.normalise_code and then does an exact unique lookup. normalise_code is strip, upper, and the I/L/O fold -- all lossless and deterministic, none of them fuzzy. The scan flow posts to /api/labels/<code> and never touches ItemFilter.search, so the two paths are already separate surfaces rather than one box that would need splitting.

WHAT THE IMPLEMENTATION OWES THIS: a test asserting that no fuzzy lookup can be reached from code resolution. The two are separate today by construction rather than by a guard, and the guard is what stops a later 'why not make scanning forgiving too'.

title: Batch: why the admin stands out
description:
One issue: the decision record for why the Django admin is deliberately not themed (inventory-tng-srs3), asked for by Ali on 2026-08-30.

Shipping on its own rather than with inventory-tng-u1am, which does the /accounts/ styling. They are counterparts and the record says so, but the record is what u1am has to be written against -- landing them together would mean writing the rule and the work that depends on it in the same breath, and the rule is the one somebody has to be able to disagree with first.
close_reason: All children completed

title: Record why the Django admin is deliberately not themed
description:
Asked for by Ali on 2026-08-30, in as many words, when told the rule probably earned one.

THE DECISION TO RECORD, and it is the rule rather than the styling: the Django admin is NOT styled to resemble the volunteer app, deliberately, and looking like Django is a feature. An administrator in there is editing rows directly, where nothing validates on their behalf and nothing is undoable -- decision 0024 is the no-hard-delete rule and 0008 is the append-only ledger, and both of those are about consequences the app's own screens keep you away from. Being able to SEE that you have left the app is part of how that safety works.

WHY IT NEEDS WRITING DOWN RATHER THAN LEAVING TO TASTE. Nothing about an unstyled Django admin looks intentional. The next contributor to meet it will read it as unfinished and improve it, with entirely good intentions, and the loss will be invisible: a themed admin does not break anything, it just quietly removes the signal that you are somewhere different. That is exactly the shape docs/decisions/ exists for -- an argument future work is held against rather than rediscovered.

It also has to be written down BECAUSE OF the sibling work. inventory-tng-u1am styles /accounts/ to match the app, and it lands in the same area for the same reason. Without this record the obvious next step after that one is 'and now the admin', which is precisely wrong and would look like finishing the job.

WHAT IT SHOULD SAY, beyond the rule itself:
* The contrast is the point, and it only reads as deliberate because the other surfaces are consistent -- which is why u1am is its counterpart rather than its opposite.
* The boundary is where the app's guarantees stop. Name 0024 and 0008 as what is on the other side of it.
* This is not an argument that the admin should be unusable. o1uj.1 fixed it rendering with no stylesheet at all, which was a defect; Django's own styling is not.
* And say what would reopen it: an admin that volunteers rather than administrators are routinely sent into would be a different situation, and guides/administrator.md is where that would show up first.

The next number is 0027, and docs/decisions/README.md carries the index row. scripts/check-docs.sh will refuse prose that repeats what u1am's own write-up says, so the two have to link rather than restate -- which is the usual discipline and worth expecting here because the subjects are adjacent.
close_reason: docs/decisions/0027-the-admin-is-meant-to-look-different.md, indexed in the decisions README.

title: Take django-cors-headers out, now that nothing can configure it
description:
Raised by the code-review pass on PR #42, 2026-08-29, and filed rather than folded into that batch: the decision there was to stop advertising cross-origin reads, which is done and true, and removing the library is a separate change that should be made deliberately.

WHAT IS LEFT BEHIND. inventory-tng-o1uj.4 dropped CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS from settings, .env.sample, compose.yaml, the chart and docs/deployment.md. The library it configured is still wired in:

* 'corsheaders' in INSTALLED_APPS
* 'corsheaders.middleware.CorsMiddleware' in MIDDLEWARE, running on every request
* CORS_ALLOW_HEADERS assembled from corsheaders.defaults plus four names
* django-cors-headers==4.9.* in backend/pyproject.toml

None of it can do anything. django-cors-headers emits nothing without an allowed origin, and there is no longer any way to give it one.

THE PART THAT MISLEADS, which is why this is worth doing rather than leaving. The comment above CORS_ALLOW_HEADERS explains that the W3C trace headers must be named or a cross-origin request carrying one is refused at the preflight. There are no preflights now, so it describes a failure that cannot occur. And two tests -- test_debugging.py's assertion that debugging.HEADER is in CORS_ALLOW_HEADERS, and test_devices.py's pair asserting the same for its own header and that one -- still pass while asserting nothing: either header could be dropped from that list with no effect on any request, and both tests would stay green.

A test that cannot fail for the reason it was written is worse than no test, because it is read as coverage.

WHAT TO WEIGH BEFORE DELETING THE TESTS. They were written for a real concern: a header the browser adds has to survive whatever sits between it and Django. That concern is now answered by the arrangement rather than by configuration -- one origin, no preflight -- and the thing that would break it is not a missing CORS entry but a proxy that strips headers. If there is a test worth keeping here, it is that one, and it belongs with the nginx assertions in test_origin.py and test_upstreams.py rather than in a CORS list. Decide that rather than deleting three lines and moving on.

AND IT IS REVERSIBLE ON PURPOSE. If cross-origin reads are ever wanted, inventory-tng-o1uj.4's close reason and the comment now in settings.py say what supporting them takes: the credentials header, a trusted-origin list for writes, and a decision about which origins may hold a volunteer's session. Removing the library does not foreclose that; it just stops the half-built version sitting in the tree looking finished.

title: Make CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS configurable, so a host mismatch has a knob
description:
Split out of inventory-tng-o1uj.6 on 2026-08-29 when that issue was cut down to the defect it names. Read o1uj.6 first: it is the proof that Django's CSRF origin check compares the browser's Origin against the host Django was told it has, and that nothing in this repository configures a second chance.

WHAT IS TRUE. CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS is [] at runtime and the name appears nowhere in this repository -- not settings.py, not .env.sample, not compose.yaml, not infra/helm. So when the host comparison fails there is nothing to reach for, and the only route to a working stack is to correct whatever is rewriting the host.

WHY IT IS STILL WANTED once o1uj.6 has landed. The header fix makes the comparison succeed for the arrangement this repository ships. It does nothing for any arrangement it does not: a frontend reached on a hostname that is not what Django computes, a tunnel, a second port, a colleague running the SPA on a machine name rather than localhost. Every one of those lands on the same 403 with the same message and no configuration to answer it with. CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS is the answer Django itself intends, and the only reason it has never been needed here is that nobody has yet run the stack anywhere but localhost.

WHAT IT TOUCHES, and this is why it is not part of the defect fix: settings.py reads it through Env like its neighbours; .env.sample documents it beside CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS, which is the variable people will confuse it with and the place to say how they differ; compose.yaml sets it explicitly rather than relying on a default, following decision 0021 point 11's pattern of the safe value in code and the intended value in every shipped file; and the chart needs it for the same reason it needs ALLOWED_HOSTS.

DO IT WITH inventory-tng-o1uj.4, which is the missing Access-Control-Allow-Credentials. A genuinely cross-origin browser client needs both -- the credentials header to be allowed to read the response, and a trusted origin to be allowed to write -- and settling one without the other leaves .env.sample still describing an arrangement that half works. That comment in .env.sample already names both in one sentence, and it is the sentence that becomes true or is corrected when these two land.
notes:
FROM THE CODE-REVIEW PASS ON PR #40, 2026-08-29, and it widens what this issue is for.

settings.py sets USE_X_FORWARDED_HOST = True, so Django prefers X-Forwarded-Host over the Host header whenever one is present. The frontend's nginx does not set it, which is why correcting the Host header in inventory-tng-o1uj.6 fixed the local stack outright. An ingress in front of a deployment may well set it, and where one does, the host Django compares the browser's Origin against is the ingress's rather than the one that fix corrects.

So o1uj.6 is a correct fix for the arrangement this repository ships and NOT a general guarantee, and this issue is what would make it one: a configured trusted-origin list is the only thing that answers a host Django computed from a header some other component chose. Say that in .env.sample beside the variable, because the next person to meet a 403 in a cluster will read that file and not this tracker.
close_reason: CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS is read from the environment, empty in every shipped configuration, rendered by the chart, and documented in .env.sample and docs/deployment.md.

title: Signing in on port 8000 lands on a Django 404
description:
Found on 2026-08-29 by following README's own quickstart table on a fresh
compose stack, and reproduced in a browser end to end.

WHAT HAPPENS. The README's service table sent people to
http://localhost:8000/accounts/login/ as the place to start. Sign in there with
a real account, complete the TOTP challenge, and allauth redirects to
LOGIN_REDIRECT_URL, which settings.py sets to "/". Port 8000 is Django with no
nginx in front of it, and inventory_tng/urls.py has no pattern for the empty
path. So a correct sign-in, with a correct second factor, ends on Django's
yellow "Page not found at /" debug page listing every URL pattern in the
project.

It is the first thing a new contributor sees after doing exactly what they were
told, and it reads as "the app is broken" rather than "you are on the wrong
port".

WHY IT ONLY BITES ON 8000. On :8080 nginx serves the single-page app at / and
proxies accounts, api, admin and static to Django, so the same redirect lands
on the app and everything works. Verified: /, /accounts/login/, /api/docs,
/api/healthz and /api/livez all answer 200 there and /admin/ answers 302 to the
sign-in page.

ALREADY DONE, and this issue is what remains. The README quickstart has been
rewritten to send people to :8080 for everything, including sign-in, and to say
that 8000 has no page at / so signing in there lands on a 404. That removes the
trap from the documented path but leaves the trap.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY LEFT TO DECIDE. Django on :8000 answering 404 at / is not
wrong in itself -- there genuinely is no page there, and the port is published
for reaching the API without nginx in the way. The question is whether a person
who arrives at it should be told where to go. Options:

* A view at / that redirects to the frontend, or renders one short page naming
  the two ports. Needs a way to know the frontend's URL, which in a deployment
  is not this process's business, so it would have to be configuration that is
  allowed to be empty.
* Leave / alone and change LOGIN_REDIRECT_URL to something that exists on both
  ports. Smaller, and it fixes the sign-in case specifically rather than the
  general one.
* Decide it is documentation's job only, and close this having done the README.
  Defensible -- say so explicitly rather than leaving it implied.

Worth settling alongside the sibling issue about the missing
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials, because the reported CORS error may turn out
to be somebody on :8000 rather than a header problem at all.
close_reason: Documentation was the fix, and it landed in PR #40. Decided deliberately rather than left implied: the three options in the description were a redirect view at Django's root, changing LOGIN_REDIRECT_URL, or documentation alone. A redirect needs to know the frontend's URL, which in a deployment is not this process's business and would mean configuration that is allowed to be empty -- more surface than the problem is worth. Django answering 404 at / is correct: there genuinely is no page there, and 8000 is published for reaching the API without nginx in the way. What was wrong was the README sending people there to sign in, and it now sends them to 8080 and says outright that 8000 has no page at /.

title: An item created in the app has no identifier, so nothing but its name can find it
description:
Found while implementing decision 0026, by tracing the admin create flow against the search work in inventory-tng-gz2. Measured on main at 485626f.

frontend/src/admin/CreateItem.tsx asks for Name, Category, Counted in, Minimum stock and Reorder quantity. It does not ask for an identifier, and it has nowhere to. ItemSerializer and ItemDetailSerializer carry no identifier field, and ItemIdentifier appears nowhere in views.py at all. So an item created through the app has ZERO ItemIdentifier rows.

That contradicts two things the repository already states. ItemIdentifier's own docstring says every string that has ever meant an item is a row in it, and docs/data-model.md says mint_items writes an identifier for every catalogued name so that after an import almost every item has one. An item made by the importer and an item made in the app are therefore in different states, and only one of them keeps the promise.

It is not urgent on its own, because decision 5 of docs/decisions/0026-what-makes-two-strings-one-identifier.md settles that search reads names AND identifiers, so nothing is unfindable today. It becomes urgent the moment anybody narrows that search to identifiers alone -- the record says why that ordering matters.
acceptance_criteria:
An item created through the API has an identifier for its own name, of kind alias, exactly as mint_items would have written.

THE COLLISION IS A CLEAN CONFLICT, NOT A 500. value_normalised is unique across the whole table, so a new item whose name folds to an identifier already held by a DIFFERENT item must be refused the way decision 4 of the record requires and inventory-tng-udz6.2 builds -- naming the item that holds it. Note this collision arrives from the opposite direction to a duplicate identifier, so it needs its own test rather than leaning on that one.

A RENAME IS A DECISION, NOT AN ACCIDENT. Deciding what happens to the alias when an item is renamed is part of this issue: keeping the old one is defensible, because every string that has ever meant the item is what the table is for, but the new name must also become findable, and neither can be left to fall out of the implementation. Whatever is chosen goes in the record.

A test creates an item through the API with exactly the fields CreateItem.tsx sends, and then finds it by typing its name.
close_reason: An item created through the API now mints an alias for its own name, exactly as mint_items would have, in one transaction with the item. A name another item is already known by arrives as decision 0026 point 4's clean conflict naming the holder, reached from the opposite direction to a duplicate identifier and so tested separately. THE RENAME DECISION, which the issue required: the old alias stays and the new name gains one too, recorded as an amendment on decision 0026 -- the new one is minted even though name search would find it anyway, because leaning on that would put the trap back the day search is narrowed to identifiers alone. The try-insert-then-ask-the-database primitive moved to inventory.identifiers.hold so the importer and the serializer share it. Both mutations caught.

title: DATA: spell the catalogue the way its manufacturers do
description:
Decision 7 of docs/decisions/0026-what-makes-two-strings-one-identifier.md, and the one part of it no code change can do.

The project owner asked that the spelling shown be the one the manufacturer intends. It is not, in at least six places: Tp-Link should be TP-Link, OmniTikPOE should be OmniTIK PoE, Hex POE should be hEX PoE, Netpower should be netPower, ToughCable should be TOUGHCable. And the catalogue contradicts itself in two more, carrying both Ubiquiti J-Pole and Jpole Umount Extender, and both RJ45 and RJ-45.

Eleven names carry intercaps a fold would visibly destroy if it were ever used for display; ten more are casually typed (mast straight, RJ45 passthrough, W-mounts).

DELIBERATELY NOT DONE BY AN AGENT, and not folded into the normalisation work. Deciding what a manufacturer's spelling is takes somebody who knows, and a guess writes a wrong spelling into the column every later screen reads. This needs an owner who can say what each one is.
acceptance_criteria:
Each of the names above is either corrected in the catalogue or recorded as deliberately left alone, by somebody who can say which.

Renaming an item does not need an identifier to be added for the old spelling: mint_items already writes one per catalogued name, so check the old spelling survives as an identifier before the rename lands.

title: Nothing offers a raw identifier where an item's name belongs
description:
Decision 5 of docs/decisions/0026-what-makes-two-strings-one-identifier.md, and the rule that answers the project owner's actual concern: a control offering a choice is populated from Item.name, and identifiers are matched against rather than rendered.

The codebase survey of 2026-08-22 found nothing violating it, so this is a guard to be written rather than a bug to be fixed. What it guards against is known: the natural way to implement search-by-identifier in DRF is to annotate the matched value so the interface can show why a row matched, and that annotation rendered as an option label is the bug.

Nothing in the repository would stop it today. No test asserts an item list carries no identifier value, and the frontend list test drives from a fixture, so a fixture holding one would pass.
acceptance_criteria:
A backend test beside the existing search test mints a mis-cased identifier and scans the response JSON recursively for it. Recursively rather than against a field allowlist, because an allowlist passes a future field called matched_on.

A frontend test stubs a row carrying both a name and an identifier value and asserts only the name is rendered.

Not a browser test: those run one worker against a shared seed and sit outside the coverage thresholds.
close_reason: Landed: a recursive substring scan on the API and a stubbed extra field on the list, both mutation-checked

title: A prefix search an index can actually serve
description:
Decision 6 of docs/decisions/0026-what-makes-two-strings-one-identifier.md.

Measured on 6000 rows: the unique btree with default operator classes cannot serve a prefix query in an en_US database -- sequential scan, 5900 rows filtered. A second index with text_pattern_ops turns it into a bitmap index scan.

Django's __istartswith compiles to UPPER(col) LIKE UPPER(pattern), which matches no index under any design, and it is the spelling somebody reaches for by default. So: add the text_pattern_ops index, lower the term in Python, query with __startswith.

Depends on inventory-tng-udz6.1: the index is on the column that issue rewrites.
acceptance_criteria:
A text_pattern_ops index exists on value_normalised and the query plan shows it being used, rather than a test asserting that it is.

A test holds the generated SQL so __istartswith cannot come back to this path.
close_reason: Landed: item_identifier_prefix with text_pattern_ops, and identifiers.matching as the only spelling of the lookup

title: A fold disagreement is a conflict, not a 500
description:
Decision 4 of docs/decisions/0026-what-makes-two-strings-one-identifier.md.

PostgreSQL's lower() and Python's str.lower() disagree in both directions -- U+0130 folds one way in the database and another in Python, Greek final sigma goes the opposite way -- and they cannot be reconciled, because one is collation dependent and the other is not.

There is exactly one load-bearing site today. _identifiers.py keys its dictionary by the database's fold, read back off value_normalised, and looks it up with items.normalised(). Where the two differ the lookup misses, create() fires, the unique index raises, and because minting runs in one transaction the whole catalogue import aborts rather than one row of it.

Two things to do: make that path treat IntegrityError as a reported outcome naming what already holds the string, and say next to items.normalised() that it is a speed-up rather than an authority.
acceptance_criteria:
The catalogue import cannot abort wholesale over a fold disagreement; whatever it does about one is a number in its report.

items.normalised() carries, in the code, the statement that the database constraint decides and this function only makes the common case fast.

A django_db test pins the disagreement against PostgreSQL itself rather than asserting it from memory -- the two existing tests that claim to pin Python/SQL agreement query no database at all.
notes:
FROM THE SIMPLIFY PASS ON PR 38. inventory/sheet/items.py normalised() is wrong twice over, and appending decision 4's sentence without touching the rest leaves a docstring that contradicts itself in six lines:

1. It gives as the reason the function is public that the importer 'has to know whether two strings are one identifier before it inserts the second'. That is the exact proposition decision 4 forbids. The honest reason is that the importer wants to AVOID a round trip for the strings where the two folds agree, and finds out from the database when they do not.
2. It describes value_normalised as a Lower(Trim()) generated column, which inventory-tng-udz6.1 ends.

Same for the comment on ItemIdentifier.value_normalised in models.py -- 'so normalisation cannot drift between the write path, the import and the scan endpoint' -- and the sentence docs/data-model.md carries after it. The research for decision 0026 measured the drift and named its one load-bearing site; those two sentences are now false and are in the two places a reader looks first.
close_reason: Landed: _hold makes the refusal an answer, and items.normalised says it is not the authority

title: The normalised column folds the whitespace TRIM does not
description:
Decision 2 of docs/decisions/0026-what-makes-two-strings-one-identifier.md.

ItemIdentifier.value_normalised is Lower(Trim(value)). TRIM strips the ASCII space and nothing else, and the expression is blind to Unicode normalisation, so three kinds of duplicate are accepted today and were demonstrated against a replica of the real table: the same string with a decomposed accent, the same string padded with a tab or a no-break space, and the same string with a doubled internal space.

Replace the expression with, in order: NFC normalise, strip the whitespace TRIM does not, collapse internal whitespace runs to one space, lower. Every function needed is IMMUTABLE and legal in a generated column; unaccent() is only STABLE and is foreclosed.

Decision 3 bounds this: case and whitespace only, no punctuation folding.
acceptance_criteria:
The generated expression is the four-step chain and a test proves each of the three duplicates is now refused.

THE MIGRATION REPORTS RATHER THAN DIES. Changing the expression rewrites the column, and rows that are legal under the old rule can collide under the new one. The migration finds them first and reports them by primary key and value, and stops with that report -- it does not fail part way through a rewrite leaving half a table converted and no list of what to fix.

docs/data-model.md agrees with the new expression.
notes: ALSO MOVES WITH THIS ISSUE, found in the review of PR 38: docs/briefs/sheet-classifiers.md section 1 ends by asserting that case is compared as Lower(Trim()), 'which is what ItemIdentifier.value_normalised is'. Decision 2 makes that sentence wrong, so the brief is part of this change rather than a follow-up.
close_reason: Landed: Canonical replaces Lower(Trim()), migration 0018 reports collisions before rewriting

title: A field refusal shows the status code and none of what the API said
description:
Found by the review of PR #35, and its own issue because neither commit in that batch caused it.

detailOf in frontend/src/api/client.ts reads body.detail and otherwise answers "The inventory service answered {status}." DRF answers a FIELD refusal with a field-keyed map and no detail at all -- {"name": ["item with this name already exists."]} -- which is what POST /api/items sends for the commonest mistake there is, Item.name being unique. So an administrator who types a name already in the catalogue is told a number, and so is every field refusal EditItem can provoke: a negative minimum stock, a reorder quantity of zero, a category that would make a loop.

IT WILL GET WORSE BEFORE IT GETS BETTER. inventory-tng-2oba.2 adds location and category writes, whose refusals are almost all field ones -- location_held_by_iff_custody, the tree-cycle guard, the unique name within a parent. inventory-tng-2oba.4 adds merging, where the sentence that matters most is a NON-field error: "X still holds the custody location 'Y'. Move the stock recorded there and retire it, or hand it to somebody else, before merging or retiring them." guides/administrator.md warns an administrator about that exact case, and the app would answer it with "The inventory service answered 400."

WHAT TO DO. Widen detailOf to read the shapes DRF actually sends, in one place rather than in each screen: a string detail where there is one; otherwise the messages under non_field_errors; otherwise the messages under the fields, which is what names the field the person has to go back to. The batch endpoint keeps its own shape (BatchRejectedSerializer) and is not this -- SubmitBar reads errors[] itself and must go on doing so.

WHAT TO PIN. A test per shape, in api/client.test.ts, and one in administrator.test.tsx that refuses a create with the body the server really sends rather than one carrying detail. That second one is the point: the existing test "says the other kind of no as a sentence" stubs a detail body, so it is green over a screen that says nothing.
close_reason: Closed

title: The app carries a device token and never acts on what the server says about it
description:
Raised by the simplify pass on PR #34 and filed rather than folded in: the
server half is inventory-tng-t9of and it landed complete, and this is a client
change that could not have been written before it.

WHAT IS THERE. frontend/src/device/credential.ts mints once from main.tsx and
api/client.ts sends X-Device on every request. GET /api/me answers a "device"
field with one of four words -- none, enrolled, revoked, unknown -- and NOTHING
IN THE APP READS IT. frontend/src/api/capabilities.ts's Me type does not even
declare the field.

THREE THINGS TO DO, and they are separable:

1. ACT ON "unknown". This means the browser is holding a string this server has
stopped honouring -- a key rotated away from, a row deleted, a mangled copy.
credential.forget() already exists, is exported, and is imported by nothing;
calling it on this answer and letting the next load mint again is the whole
fix. Without it the browser presents a dead string for ever and the attribution
this feature exists for is silently off for that device.

2. SAY SOMETHING ON "revoked". inventory_tng/devices.py and
permissions.DeviceNotRevoked both argue that a wall and a "this device was
removed" want opposite screens, and the server does its half: the refusal
carries code=device_revoked rather than the general forbidden, and /api/me
answers before anything has been refused. The client draws neither. Decide what
it draws -- a sentence with a way to enrol again is the obvious one -- and do
NOT replace the app with a gate: a revoked device still holds a batch in the
outbox, and losing that is the thing this system exists not to do.

3. SEND THE HEADER ON THE FAILURE-REPORT PATH. frontend/src/telemetry/report.ts
posts to /api/client-failures with a bare fetch and debugHeaders() rather than
through api/client.ts, so no X-Device arrives -- and that endpoint is the ONE
place in this API that reaches AppendThrottle.get_ident today, being the only
one that names AllowAny. So the per-device bucket inventory-tng-t9of built
cannot apply anywhere it is currently reachable. AppendThrottle.get_ident says
so in its own docstring and names this bead. Check why report.ts avoids the
client first -- it may be deliberate, to keep a report from recursing through
the thing that reports failures -- and if it is, carry the one header rather
than routing the call.

WHAT TO PIN: a test that a browser told "unknown" stops sending the old token,
and one that a revoked device still sees its held batch.

title: The admin still deletes an ItemIdentifier, which frees a string 6kyb protected
description:
Found by the review of PR #33, and its own issue because it predates that batch.

ItemIdentifierInline sits on the item change form and ItemIdentifierAdmin
(backend/src/inventory/admin.py) is registered as a plain SimpleHistoryAdmin, so
an identifier can be removed from either place. Nothing stops it: no model holds
a foreign key to ItemIdentifier, so nothing PROTECTs it.

WHY THAT MATTERS AND IS NOT MERELY UNTIDY. item_identifier_unique_normalised_value
makes the normalised string unique across the table, so removing a row FREES the
string. It can then be typed against a different item, and a barcode already
printed on an object -- or a label already on a shelf whose scan resolves through
it -- afterwards answers with the wrong item rather than with nothing. That is the
exact harm inventory-tng-6kyb made ItemIdentifier.item PROTECT to prevent, and
guides/administrator.md states it in those words. Answering wrongly is worse than
answering nothing, which is why this is P2 and ls6d is P3.

SIBLING, NOT DUPLICATE: inventory-tng-ls6d is the same shape on Label, and
inventory-tng-k2sg is the same shape on Item and is done. All three want the same
helper by now -- k2sg wrote has_delete_permission plus a get_actions that drops
delete_selected by name, and a third copy of that pair is the point at which it
should be extracted rather than retyped.

ARGUE IT RATHER THAN SWEEPING: k2sg was explicit that each model is its own
argument. The argument here has a wrinkle k2sg did not: an identifier typed
against the WRONG item is a real thing an administrator must be able to undo, and
today deleting it is how. So the fix is probably not a bare refusal -- it may be
that correcting the item field is the supported move and the delete is what goes,
or that a delete is right and the inline is not. Decide it, and say which in
guides/administrator.md's Delete section, which now carries decision 0024 beside
it.

WHAT TO PIN: whatever is decided, a test that the chosen path is the only one, and
a line in the guide. MAY_CASCADE in tests/test_models.py is where a deliberate
destruction is recorded with its reason.
close_reason: Closed

title: The frontend suite fails on node 26, and nothing says which node to use
description:
Two halves of one snag, hit on 2026-08-25 by an agent running the frontend
suite in a shell that had the system's node rather than this project's.

THE FAILURE. `npm test` under node 26 fails roughly 247 of 410 tests with
`Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'clear')` -- `window.localStorage`
undefined under jsdom 30. It fails identically on unmodified `main`, so it is
environmental rather than any branch's defect. mise.toml pins `node = "24"`,
CI pins 24 in two places in ci.yml, and frontend/Dockerfile builds on
`node:24-bookworm-slim`, so nothing that matters is currently broken -- this is
a trap for whoever's shell resolves node differently, and it cost an agent a
run to work out.

A LEAD RATHER THAN A DIAGNOSIS, and it needs reproducing before it is believed:
jsdom exposes `localStorage` only for a non-opaque origin, so a missing
`environmentOptions.url` on the vitest environment is the usual cause of it
being `undefined`. Why node 26 surfaces it and node 24 does not is the part
actually worth finding out, because the answer decides whether this is a
one-line config fix or a dependency bump.

ORDER MATTERS AND IS THE OPPOSITE OF THE OBVIOUS ONE. Do not raise the pin
first. The failure IS on 26, so pinning to 26 spreads it to CI and to every
contributor instead of fixing it. Fix the suite, prove it green on 24 AND on
26, and only then decide whether the pin moves. Node is a build and test
dependency only -- decision 0002 and frontend/Dockerfile's own comment, "There
is no Node runtime in production" -- so the pin has no production consequence
either way, which is an argument for being relaxed about moving it and none at
all for moving it first.

THE SECOND HALF, and it is the cheaper one: nothing in DEVELOPERS.md tells a
contributor what to do when their shell has the wrong node. `mise exec -- npm
test` works from any shell regardless of whether mise has activated in it, and
that sentence belongs beside the test command it rescues. mise.toml already
carries a `[tasks]` block, so a task is the other option and probably the
better one.

SCOPE, EXPLICITLY: the fix stays inside this repository. The project owner has
asked that nothing outside the repository root be changed -- no shell
configuration, no PATH, no mise global state. `mise exec --` is the answer for
exactly that reason.
design:
FIVE WAYS TO FIX THIS PER-REPOSITORY, since the project owner has ruled out a
system-wide PATH change: they want the toolchain controlled per repository, not
globally. All of these live inside this repository root. Measured 2026-08-25.

1. `[settings] activate_aggressive = true` IN THIS REPOSITORY'S mise.toml.
   VERIFIED, and it is the direct answer. mise has a setting for exactly this
   failure -- it pushes a tool's bin path to the FRONT of PATH rather than
   letting later modifications win. Measured with it set in the project file:

       node install dir  position 18 -> 4
