title: One GitHub listing per run, and one tracking-repo fixture
description:
Two findings from the /simplify pass on pull request 518, skipped there because
each is an interface change rather than a simplification of what that batch
wrote.

=== ONE. THE SAME LISTING IS FETCHED TWICE PER --check RUN ===

MEASURED on 2026-09-02 against 427 issues, so nobody re-derives it:

  gh issue list ... --json number,url        2.61s, 5 GraphQL requests
  gh issue list ... --json number,state      2.63s, 5 GraphQL requests
  gh issue list ... --json number,url,state  2.63s, 5 GraphQL requests
  whole `sync-issues.sh --check` run         5.93s

So the second listing costs 2.6s and five requests and buys ONE extra JSON
field. It is 44% of the run, it grows with the issue count, and this is the
scheduled path -- daily, plus every issue opened.

WHY IT HAPPENS. Question 1 is asked by delegating to pull-new-issues.sh --check,
which fetches `number,url` for itself. Question 3 is asked here and fetches
`number,state`. Neither can see the other's.

THE SECOND REASON, and it is the better one: two listings are two snapshots. An
issue closed between them is described by one and not the other, and nothing
would say so.

THE SHAPE. Fetch once with `--json number,url,state` and give
pull-new-issues.sh a way to be handed a listing it did not fetch -- a
`--listing <file>` flag, or stdin. That keeps question 1 owned by the script
that owns it, which is the property the current arrangement exists to protect,
while dropping to one round trip and one snapshot.

WORTH DECIDING FIRST: whether a script that can be handed its input is still the
script that owns the question. The argument for delegating at all was that the
refusal wording lives where a suite can read it; passing a listing in does not
change that, but passing the WRONG listing in is a new way to be wrong, and it
wants a guard.

=== TWO. THE TRACKING-REPO FIXTURE IS IN TWO SUITES AND HAS ALREADY DIVERGED ===

export-issues.test.sh and pull-new-issues.test.sh both build "a checkout that is
legitimately current": a remote, a root commit, `remote add`, `fetch`,
`reset --hard`, `branch --set-upstream-to`, then fall_behind and catch_up. Same
six lines, same two helpers, down to the commit messages.

THEY HAVE ALREADY DRIFTED: export-issues.test.sh's catch_up does not fetch,
pull-new-issues.test.sh's does. Both are right for their own caller, which is
exactly how this kind of copy stops being noticed.

The guard they exercise -- require_current_checkout -- was centralised on the
argument that the hazard belongs to the family. The fixture that proves it
should live in scripts/testlib.sh beside new_repo, for the reason testlib's own
header gives.

A third caller of require_current_checkout would make this urgent. There is not
one yet.

title: Two latent gaps in the drift check, and one vocabulary for the family
description:
Both raised by the code-review pass on pull request 518 and both deliberately
left. Neither can fire today; both are recorded rather than dropped because each
is a documented lesson the codebase learned once already.

=== ONE. drifted.py MATCHES ON ISSUE NUMBER WITHOUT SCOPING TO THIS REPOSITORY

scripts/drifted.py calls unsynced.ref_of (which only checks a ref begins
https://github.com/) and then unsynced.number_of, and compares that number
against a listing fetched with --repo "$REPOSITORY". It never checks the ref
belongs to that repository.

THE BUG CLASS IS ALREADY WRITTEN DOWN, in unsynced.py's own header: "An earlier
version matched a regex and had a real bug in it, because issue numbers are
per-repository and the pattern accepted any repository's issue as though it were
ours." number_of's docstring says it "is only ever asked of a bead already known
to be ours" -- and drifted.py is the first caller for which that is not true,
because it iterates every row of the export rather than a set already narrowed.

WHY IT CANNOT FIRE TODAY: all 430 external_refs point at
lotia/nycmesh-inventory-tng. It would take a bead linked to another repository's
issue, which nothing currently creates.

THE FIX IS THE ONE unsynced.py USES: compare whole URLs rather than numbers, or
narrow the rows before asking for a number. The scoring agent put it at 50
precisely because it is latent; the reason to do it anyway is that "latent"
described the earlier version too, right up until it did not.

=== TWO. --limit 1000 WITH NO FULL-PAGE GUARD

scripts/sync-issues.sh asks `gh issue list --state all --limit 1000` and does
not check whether the page came back exactly full. scripts/export-issues.sh does
check -- a named LIMIT and a refusal, added in response to an earlier review with
the comment "A FULL PAGE IS NOT AN ANSWER" -- so this is the same shape
reintroduced in a new caller rather than a pattern nobody had considered.

At 430 issues it is a long way off. It fails silently when it arrives: a
truncated listing makes drifted.py compare against a partial set and report
agreement it never verified.

=== WHY THESE ARE ONE ISSUE

Both are "the family knows something this caller does not", which is the argument
inventory-tng-ynxv.1 made about `refuse` and `count_lines` and which produced
scripts/repository.sh. The listing itself is now fetched in three scripts with
three slightly different flag sets; a `list_issues` beside require_current_checkout
would carry the limit, the guard and the stderr handling once. That is probably
the right shape for all three, and is worth deciding before adding a fourth
caller.

title: One refusal vocabulary for the checker family, and the pull half guarded
description:
Two findings from the /simplify pass on inventory-tng-ynxv, skipped there
because most of what they touch is not that batch's work.

=== ONE. A `refuse` FOR THE WHOLE FAMILY, NOT ONE SCRIPT ===

scripts/repository.sh gained a local `refuse` when the behind-upstream guard
moved into it: print to stderr, name the outermost script, exit 2. The same
four-line shape is written out by hand at export-issues.sh:86, :100 and :199,
pull-new-issues.sh's tool and repository refusals, and sync-issues.sh's -- most
of them on main before that batch, which is why they were left alone.

WHY EXIT 2 RATHER THAN report.sh's fail/stop, since that is the obvious
question: those exit 1, which this family means as "it looked and objected".
Exit 2 is "it could not look at all". The distinction is load-bearing --
issue-sync.yml and export-issues.sh both branch on it -- so the two vocabularies
are separate on purpose and `refuse` belongs beside need_tools rather than in
report.sh.

Also worth folding in: `count=$(printf '%s\n' "$x" | wc -l | tr -d ' ')` appears
four times across export-issues.sh and pull-new-issues.sh.

=== TWO. THE PULL HALF IS UNGUARDED ===

require_current_checkout now exists and only export-issues.sh calls it. Decision
0031 records the hazard as running both ways: a checkout that has not fetched
somebody else's external_ref will file a second ISSUE if it exports, and
pull-new-issues.sh will make a second BEAD if it pulls, because unsynced.py
offers an issue it can see no link for and the honest response is to pull it.
sync-issues.sh runs both halves and is guarded on neither.

THE COSTS ARE NOT EQUAL, which is why this was a separate call rather than an
oversight: an ordinary token cannot delete a GitHub issue, so a duplicate there
is permanent, while a duplicate bead can be deleted. That asymmetry justifies
guarding one half first. It does not justify leaving the other unguarded for
ever, and the guard is now one function call away.

WORTH DECIDING: whether pull-new-issues.sh --check should be held to it too.
Almost certainly not -- it runs in CI where the head is a pull request's and has
no upstream -- but that is the same reasoning the export half already recorded,
and it should be checked rather than assumed to carry over.
close_reason: refuse and count_lines are repository.sh's now and adopted at ten sites across three scripts; require_current_checkout is called by pull-new-issues.sh on the writing path, with a remote in its scene and five cases. --check and dry runs are not held to it, for the reason the export half already recorded. 0031 and DEVELOPERS.md say both halves are guarded.

title: testlib does not yet hold what five suites re-roll
description:
Found by the /simplify pass on inventory-tng-cwpa.6, which moved one of these
and left the rest because they are outside that diff.

WHAT MOVED. bead() -- one line of a bd export -- was written out in five
places. It is now in scripts/testlib.sh and four suites call it. That leaves:

* scripts/untriaged.test.sh:16 has a fifth copy, built in Python rather than
  bash, so it did not convert mechanically with the others.

WHAT DID NOT MOVE, and is the larger of the two. The PATH sandbox is written
out five times: the BORROWED=(...) list plus

  for tool in "${BORROWED[@]}"; do ln -sf "$(command -v "$tool")" "$BIN/$tool"; done

appears identically in export-issues.test.sh, pull-new-issues.test.sh,
check-setup.test.sh, bootstrap-dev.test.sh and landing-gate.test.sh. A sixth
suite needing one writes it a sixth time.

WORSE THAN THE REPETITION: no_bd/with_bd now exist in two suites with DIFFERENT
implementations -- one writes a stub inline, the other copies a saved binary --
so the drift the shared harness exists to prevent has already started.

THE SHAPE. A `borrow <tool>...` in testlib.sh that builds $WORK/bin and returns
its path, on the same argument workspace() and new_repo() were added under and
which testlib's own header makes: "so that a change to any of those is made
once instead of four times and forgotten in three".

WHAT IS NOT SHARED, deliberately: the `gh` and `bd` stubs themselves. Each
suite's stubs answer different questions -- export-issues.test.sh's gh has to
record what it was told to close -- and a stub general enough for all five would
be a second implementation of the tools rather than a fixture.

NOT URGENT. Nothing is wrong today; this is the fifth copy being the one that
makes the case, and it is filed rather than done because three of the five files
are untouched by the change that noticed it.
close_reason: borrow() in testlib replaces five sandbox builders in four spellings, and refuses a tool it cannot find rather than suppressing the lookup. untriaged.test.sh's Python fixture is gone; bead() gained an optional title. Left alone: with_bd differs between two suites because their bd stubs must differ -- that is a fixture, not drift.

title: Two assertions in unsynced.test.sh cannot fail
description:
Found by the code-review pass on inventory-tng-cwpa.6, which had the same
defect in three new suites and fixed it there. These two are on main already,
so they are outside that diff and are filed rather than smuggled in.

scripts/unsynced.test.sh:40 and :84 read

  assert "$(offer 60 12 | check)" 0 0 "" "issues already linked are not offered again"

and testlib's assert tests [[ "$output" == *"$want_text"* ]]. With want_text
empty that is true of every string, including the one the case exists to rule
out. Both status arguments are literals, so the exit status is not checked
either. Demonstrated: assert "anything" 0 0 "" "x" prints ok.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY UNTESTED. :40 is "a linked issue is never offered again",
which is the property the whole mapping exists to provide -- the check against
filing a second bead for an issue already pulled. It would stay green with the
membership test deleted.

THE FIX IS THE ONE cwpa.6 USED, so this is a transcription rather than a
design: assert on "<$out>" against the literal "<>", which is an exact
emptiness test rather than a substring one, and pass the real exit status
instead of a literal. Verified there that the new form fails on non-empty
input, which is the check the old form could not make.

WORTH DOING WHILE THERE: testlib.sh could refuse an empty want_text outright.
An assertion that cannot fail is never what somebody meant, and the pattern
reached four files before anything noticed. That is the deterministic version
of this fix and it is the one that stops it coming back -- but it is a change
to the harness every suite shares, so it is weighed here rather than assumed.
close_reason: testlib's assert and refute now refuse an empty substring, with exits for status-only cases. The guard immediately found a sixth site the grep had missed: landing-gate.test.sh's 'a collapsed branch with a receipt merges' had never checked anything.

title: docs/briefs/authorisation.md lags the artifact it is the offline copy of
description:
Found on 2026-09-01 while reconciling the published artifacts with main. Not
inventory-tng-2jzx's work: the mesh-posture sentence in that file was corrected
under 2jzx, and this is everything else in the same file that has gone stale.

THE RELATIONSHIP THIS BREAKS. docs/briefs/authorisation.md says of itself that
the artifact is "a presented version" and "this file is the copy that does not"

WHAT IS STALE, checked against main rather than assumed:

* Q1's "What survives. The allow-list is still worth having." The READ half of

title: stack_info=True on a structlog logger captures no stack at all
description:
Found by the code-review pass on the batch that landed inventory-tng-0qys, and correctly not folded into it: 0qys is about DRAWING a captured stack, and this is about there being nothing to draw.

WHAT HAPPENS. Every logger this application uses is a structlog one. structlog.stdlib.BoundLogger leaves stack_info in the event dict rather than passing it to the stdlib call, and StackInfoRenderer is deliberately absent from SHARED -- logs.py:193 says why, and the reason is good: ProcessorFormatter has already formatted record.stack_info for FOREIGN records, and running the renderer again re-captures the stack from inside the logging machinery, so the frames a reader wants arrive under seven frames of logging/__init__.py.

Measured on this branch:

  structlog.get_logger('inventory.ledger').error('boom', stack_info=True)
  -> {"stack_info": true, "event": "boom", ...}

The boolean, not a stack. So a developer who writes stack_info=True gets a field saying they asked, and never the frames they asked for -- in the JSON and in the console alike. A stdlib record arriving through ProcessorFormatter does carry the formatted string, which is the case 0qys fixed the drawing of.

WHY IT IS A DECISION AND NOT A PATCH. The obvious move -- add StackInfoRenderer to SHARED but not to FROM_LIBRARIES -- is exactly what logs.py's comment warns against for the foreign chain, and it needs checking that the frames it captures on the NATIVE path are the caller's rather than structlog's own. That is a measurement plus a judgement about what stack_info promises, not a mechanical fix.

WORTH SETTLING EITHER WAY. If the renderer belongs on the native chain, add it and hold it with a test that asserts the top frame is the caller's. If it does not, then stack_info=True is a request this project cannot honour, and the honest thing is to say so where somebody would type it -- logs.py -- rather than leave a field that looks like it worked.

Note the console now draws the boolean as stack_info=True beside the message rather than as a bare line reading True, which is inventory-tng-0qys's own fix for the regression this bead describes the cause of.

title: The chart's Jobs get no writable path, where compose gives their analogue two
description:
Found by the simplify pass on the batch that landed inventory-tng-pmd, and deliberately not folded into it: pmd is about gunicorn's control socket on the long-running backend, and this is about what a run-once manage.py needs. Different question, different answer.

WHAT IS ASYMMETRIC. infra/helm/inventory-tng/templates/migrate-job.yaml and administrator-job.yaml run the backend image with readOnlyRootFilesystem: true and declare no volumes and no volumeMounts at all. compose.yaml's analogue of them -- the seed service, one 'manage.py seed_demo_data' under the same hardening -- is granted BOTH /tmp and /home/app.

So the two ways this project runs a one-shot management command disagree about whether it may write anywhere, and only one of them has been thought about.

WHAT TO ESTABLISH FIRST, because the answer is not obviously 'grant both'. A Job that writes nothing needs nothing, and an emptyDir it never touches is clutter rather than safety. Find out what 'manage.py migrate' and 'manage.py ensure_administrator' actually open on this image -- measure it, the way pmd's own claim was measured against postgres:18 -- rather than copying the Deployment's list across.

WHY IT IS NOT MERELY THEORETICAL. A Job that cannot write fails the release, not a request: migrations run in a Helm pre-install/pre-upgrade hook, so the failure mode is an upgrade that stops rather than a pod that logs an error and serves anyway. That is a worse failure than the one pmd fixed, and it is the reason this is filed rather than left.

AND THE TEST THAT SHOULD HAVE CAUGHT IT. test_chart.py's test_the_chart_grants_the_same_writable_paths_the_compose_stack_does compares only the backend Deployment against compose's backend service. backend/src/inventory/tests/charts.py already has workloads(), which exists for exactly this -- its docstring says a chart that grew a CronJob would otherwise be held by whichever test somebody remembered, and test_every_container_the_chart_renders_declares_what_it_needs already iterates it. Widening that comparison to workloads() is the first thing to do here, and it should go red before anything is changed.

title: A marker inside an HTML code block still counts as posted
description:
Found by the code-review pass on PR #84, in the commit that closed inventory-tng-1tyo. carries() in scripts/review_cycle.py knows two ways of SHOWING code -- a fenced block and four-column indentation -- and 1tyo made both of them right, including fences nested inside longer ones. It does not know the third: Markdown passes HTML blocks through verbatim and GitHub allows 
 in
comments.

VERIFIED against the function as merged:

  
\n\n
          -> counted
  
\n\n   -> counted
  > ```\n> \n> ```   (blockquoted)         -> not counted

The last is a pre-existing false NEGATIVE and safe; the first two are false
positives of the inventory-tng-egh4.1 shape, which is what 1tyo exists to have
closed.

REACHABLE WITHOUT ANYTHING ADVERSARIAL. The one context where people reach for

 instead of a fence is writing about markup that would otherwise be eaten
-- which is exactly what somebody documenting the marker rule is doing.

WHY IT WAS NOT FIXED IN THE REVIEW. CommonMark defines seven kinds of HTML
block with different closing conditions, and a parser that gets it half right
on a REQUIRED check fails in the worse direction: refusing evidence somebody
really did post. That is a bigger harm than the one being closed.

DECIDE IT WITH inventory-tng-bahi, which is the other open question about what
this reader accepts. The cheap answer may be better than the correct one: treat
a line matching
close_reason: Closed

title: scripts/*.py escape the ruff rules the build enforces everywhere else
description:
Noticed while landing inventory-tng-2o3x, and not caused by it -- the errors are on main and predate that batch.

CI's Backend job runs ruff over backend/ only, so the Python under scripts/ is never linted. Measured on origin/main's copy of scripts/check-docs.py:

  E401   line 14, multiple imports on one line
  I001   line 14, import block un-sorted
  ANN201 line 112, missing return type on runs()

ANN is the one that matters. AGENTS.md states that every function is annotated and that ruff's ANN rules fail the build on a missing return type -- and for scripts/ that is simply not true. A rule the documentation calls enforced, which one directory quietly escapes, is worse than one that was never claimed: it is believed.

WHAT TO DECIDE, because it is not obvious and should not be settled by whoever happens to fix the lint. scripts/ is deliberately stdlib-only and virtualenv-free -- review_cycle.py and ci-check-names.py say so in their headers, because they run from a workflow step and from bash scripts that have neither. Running the backend's ruff over them coples a directory that is meant to stand alone to backend/pyproject.toml. Either that coupling is accepted, or scripts/ gets a ruff configuration of its own, or the claim in AGENTS.md is narrowed to say where it holds.

Worth checking how many files are affected before choosing: this was found in one file, by accident.

title: check-docs.sh dies on any binary file in the tree
description:
Any undecodable file anywhere in the working tree takes the duplication
checker down, and it reports the failure as "the reader failed, so nothing was
checked" rather than as a file it should have skipped.

SEEN, not theorised: a stray trace.pb and a traces/ directory of parquet files
were left in the repository root by a profiling run during a session. Every
scripts/check-docs.sh invocation then ended in

  UnicodeDecodeError: utf-8 codec cannot decode byte 0xb5 in position 19
  check-docs.sh: the reader failed, so nothing was checked.

The corpus is built by subtraction -- an exclusion list of binary and font
EXTENSIONS -- so anything with an unlisted extension is read as text. .pb and
.parquet are not on the list, and no list of extensions ever will be complete.

THE FIX IS TO STOP GUESSING FROM THE NAME. Read the bytes and skip what does
not decode, which is the question actually being asked: this file cannot
contain repeated English prose. The extension list can then shrink to a
performance hint rather than a correctness one.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THE ANNOYANCE. The failure direction is right -- it
refuses rather than passing silently -- but the checker runs in CI as a
required job, so one stray artifact in a contributors tree blocks their
push for a reason that has nothing to do with their change, and the message
does not name the file.
close_reason: Closed

title: The stop hook is still wrong when nothing has been recorded at all
description:
Raised by the /simplify pass on PR #82 (inventory-tng-gfkr), which made the
stop hook truthful about a cycle that had been RECORDED and refused. It is
still wrong about one that has not been recorded at all.

WHAT IS LEFT. `stop_mode` computes the missing stages from the receipts file
and from nothing else. With no receipt, receipt_status returns both stages
whatever the pull request carries -- so an agent that has posted the simplify
marker and is waiting for a person is told to run simplify.

WHY IT IS WORSE THAN IT SOUNDS: THE NUDGE IS SPENT FIRST. The once-per-head
bookkeeping is written before the message is assembled, so that head gets one
refusal and it is the false one. Waiting for a person is the natural place to
stop -- the branch is blocked on a human, and the skill puts `record` after a
rebase and a push -- so this is the ordinary path rather than an edge.

THE DEEPER FIX IS AVAILABLE AND CHEAP IN CALLS. stop_mode already makes the
round trip: gh_json pr view --json number,state,isDraft,headRefOid,
statusCheckRollup. Adding comments,reviews costs bytes rather than a call, and
the scene reader could then compute missing stages from the pull request
instead of from the cache. That needs marked() lifted out of record_receipt's
inline python into a shared source string under the same no-apostrophe rule --
about thirty lines, no new dependency, since the stop path already requires
python3 and gh.

WHAT IT BUYS BEYOND CORRECTNESS: a state the receipt cannot express at all,
"both passes ran and nothing recorded them", which is a third row in the
outstanding block rather than two stage lines.

WHY IT WAS NOT TAKEN ON #82. inventory-tng-x0jp proposes holding the whole
attestation as a required CI check and says taking it deletes most of
scripts/landing-gate.sh, including this path. Doing the gh-side computation now
is work x0jp would throw away. So this issue is really a question for whoever
picks up x0jp: settle x0jp first, and if it is declined or deferred, do this.

MEANWHILE the smaller half of the same complaint is worth knowing: the once-per-
head nudge could be spent on a message the gate later discovers was wrong, and
nothing re-arms it. Moving the bookkeeping to after the message is assembled
does not fix the falsehood, but it would stop the false one being the only one.

title: 0020 assumes an agent can always finish a branch alone
description:
Raised by the /simplify pass on PR #81 (inventory-tng-d854), which changed
the landing gate to say that `/code-review` is a person's to run and
`/simplify` is an agent's.

0020 "Who merges" is written on the premise that the bar is the same for both
populations -- "written once and identical for both" -- and that "a branch that
does not meet the bar is one to finish. It is never one to ask an exception
for."

d854 introduces a branch state an agent structurally CANNOT finish alone. Not
through lack of skill or permission, but because the harness refuses it the
command. That is not an exception being asked for and it is not a branch left
unfinished; it is a third thing 0020 does not have a word for.

WHY IT IS ARGUABLE RATHER THAN OBVIOUS. 0020 is about MERGING, and the review
cycle sits upstream of the merge bar -- so it is defensible that nothing in
0020 is contradicted, only that its surrounding prose now reads as though an
agent can always get to the end by itself. Somebody should decide which
reading is right rather than leaving the two to disagree quietly.

THE PRECEDENT IS EXPLICIT. inventory-tng-83cn settled the same shape for its
own change and wrote the rule down: "if this changes that answer, 0020 gets an
amendment rather than being left to disagree with the code." This is that
condition, so the amendment is owed or the reasoning for declining it is.

Small either way: an amendment paragraph, or a note on 0020 saying the case was
considered and the record stands.

title: Give a GitHub-born bead a real identity
description:
Phase 4. A bead pulled from GitHub arrives as inventory-tng-1788173271772-1-17c29583, typed task, priority 2, with no parent and no dependencies -- measured, not supposed.

That is a reasonable default and a poor permanent state: the id is unreadable in a commit message, the type is a guess, and nothing connects it to the epic it belongs to.

So the arrival needs a triage step -- retype it, prioritise it, give it a parent, and decide whether it is a duplicate of something already tracked. bd find-duplicates exists and is worth trying here rather than reading 73 open beads by hand.

WHETHER THE ID CAN BE CHANGED IS THE OPEN QUESTION. If bd can rename an issue while preserving external_ref, triage can normalise it. If it cannot, the choice is to live with synthetic ids for externally-filed work, or to close the arrival and refile it -- which loses the GitHub link and is probably worse. Find out before designing the rest of the step.
notes:
=== THE OPEN QUESTION IS ANSWERED, 2026-08-31 ===

This issue asked whether a bead's id can be changed while keeping its GitHub link, because if it cannot the choice was to live with synthetic ids for externally-filed work or to close and refile, losing the link.

IT CAN. `bd rename <old> <new>` exists and preserves external_ref. Tested: a bead was created, pushed to GitHub (issue 66), renamed, and the ref still pointed at issue 66 afterwards. Both were deleted after.

It also updates references to the old id in other issues' descriptions, titles and notes, and rewrites dependencies pointing at it -- so a renamed arrival does not leave dangling text behind.

SO TRIAGE CAN NORMALISE. An arrival comes in as inventory-tng-1788173271772-1-17c29583, typed task at priority 2, with no parent. The step is: read it, rename it to something a commit message can carry, set the type and priority, give it a parent, and check bd find-duplicates for something already tracked.

WHAT IS STILL A PERSON'S. All of the above is judgement -- what kind of work is this, how urgent, whose epic, is it a duplicate. Nothing here should guess at those. What could be automated is only the LISTING: which beads carry an external_ref, have a synthetic id, and have never been triaged. That is worth doing if arrivals become frequent, and is not worth doing before there are any.
=== BUILT 2026-08-31 ===

bd find-duplicates was worth trying, as the description said, and is not the right tool. Run against this tracker it returns fifty pairs comparing every bead with every other -- it answers 'what looks similar in here' rather than 'does this arrival duplicate something', and there is no way to scope it to one issue. bd search is what fits: single term, substring match, and it found the right bead on every term tried.

So the helper offers search terms rather than running a comparison: the longest, least common words from the arrival's title, which is what a person would have picked by eye.
=== THE JUDGEMENT, WRITTEN DOWN, 2026-08-31 ===

The project owner, on reviewing this: capture the judgement part before closing.

Right, and the gap was real. untriaged.py finds arrivals and prints commands; deciding what the thing IS was left entirely to whoever ran it, which meant it lived in one person's head and was not a process at all.

docs/triage.md now carries it: read it as a report rather than a request; the five decisions (duplicate, kind, urgency, whose work, what to call it); how far to go rewriting a body somebody else wrote; what must never be pasted in, under 0029; and when closing is the complete answer rather than a failure to triage.

The two parts most worth having written down, because both are the tempting mistake rather than the obvious one:

- DO NOT FABRICATE THE REST. Beads here are arguments -- measured, read rather than assumed. An arrival is two sentences from somebody who owed us none of that, and writing the bead you wish you had received produces confidence nothing backs. Keep what they said, add what you checked with the date, say what is unknown.
- AN ARRIVAL HAS NO SPECIAL CLAIM ON URGENCY. Inflating a priority to be welcoming is how the scale stops meaning anything. Thank them on the issue, which is where thanks belong.

title: gnhl's commit message describes the surface it opened before it was corrected
description:
Commit 8cd81a1 on main is inventory-tng-gnhl. Two passages in its message
describe the state before 8b5f615 corrected it, and `fixup!` does not touch a
base message when it collapses, so both landed unchanged.

=== WHAT IT SAYS, QUOTED RATHER THAN PARAPHRASED ===

The surface it claims to have opened:

  "VOLUNTEER_ACCESS=open answers callers with no account on the endpoints a
  volunteer uses: the two appends point 3 names, and the reads without which
  neither means anything -- the catalogue and its balances, the pick-list, the
  label map the client prefetches, and the resolver for one scanned code."

And how it says it was checked:

  "Mutation-checked by giving ItemDetailView the open list and watching it
  fail."

=== WHY EACH IS WRONG ===

THE SURFACE SENTENCE IS THE AMBIGUITY THAT CAUSED THE BUG. "The label map the
client prefetches" names two plausible endpoints, and gnhl was implemented by
reading that sentence rather than the client, so the wrong one was picked:
LabelSheetView was opened and LabelListView, which scan/labelCache.ts actually
prefetches, was not. ItemDetailView was missed entirely -- scan/applyCode.ts
falls back to it for a sticker minted since the last prefetch -- and
CategoryListView was opened although nothing outside the admin screens fetches
it. 8b5f615 corrected all four. The message still reads as though the sentence
were the specification, which is exactly how it misled once already.

THE MUTATION-CHECK SENTENCE IS NOW FALSE IN THE WORST DIRECTION. ItemDetailView
is IN the open list as of 8b5f615, so a reader who checks the claim finds the
opposite of what it asserts: the message describes the FIXED state as the
deliberate mutation. A claim about how something was verified is the one part
of a message a reader is most entitled to trust.

=== WHAT CANNOT BE DONE ===

Rewriting main. The commit is merged and published, and per AGENTS.md anything
touching main directly asks first; a history rewrite to correct prose is not a
trade this project should make. This issue exists BECAUSE the cheap fix is
gone, not to propose it.

=== WHAT THE RECORD ALREADY HOLDS ===

The correct account is written down twice, and both survive:

* backend/src/inventory/tests/test_volunteer_flow_reaches.py -- its module
  docstring lists all four mistakes and says why nothing in the suite noticed:
  the capabilities audit asks whether an OPEN view is argued, never whether a
  view the client NEEDS is open.
* PR #57 comment 5475992075, which flagged the reword before the merge and was
  not acted on.

So nothing is unknown. What is wrong is that the commit a reader reaches first
-- by bisect, by blame on views.py, by git log on the permission classes --
contradicts both.

=== WHAT COULD BE DONE, IF ANYTHING ===

Three honest options, smallest first, and picking "none" is a legitimate close:

1. NOTHING, ARCHIVED. The docstring and the PR comment are the durable record
   and a reader who follows either gets the truth. The cost is that they must
   first doubt the commit message enough to look.
2. A GIT NOTE on 8cd81a1 saying which two passages are superseded and by what.
   It attaches to the commit itself, so git log --notes and blame-driven
   reading both surface it at the point of confusion. The cost is that notes
   are not fetched by default, so most clones will not see it.
3. A LINE IN THE TEST DOCSTRING naming 8cd81a1 explicitly, so the file that
   already tells the story says which commit message it is correcting. Cheapest
   and most likely to be read, since anyone touching this surface runs into
   that test.

WHAT THIS IS NOT: a process issue about fixup discipline. That a `fixup!` leaves
the base message alone is how git works and is not news. If a guard is wanted so
the next collapse does not repeat this, that is its own issue and should be
argued on its own merits rather than smuggled in here.
acceptance_criteria: One of the three options is chosen and recorded. Closing as 'nothing, archived' is a valid outcome and needs the reasoning written on the issue, not just the status. If option 2 or 3 is taken, the wording names 8cd81a1 and both superseded passages.

title: Four rate limits reach the pod unchecked
description:
Noticed while doing inventory-tng-81f7.1. APPEND_BURST_RATE, APPEND_SUSTAINED_RATE, CLIENT_REPORT_RATE and DEVICE_ENROLMENT_RATE are rendered by the chart into the backend's environment and nothing asserts that they arrive, or that the chart reads the operator's value rather than hard-coding one.

Every throttling test sets the rate directly through settings, so all of them stay green while a cluster runs with whatever settings.py fell back to. A limit that does not reach the container is not a limit, and the failure is silent in the permissive direction.

ANONYMOUS_READ_RATE got that pair of assertions when it landed (test_anonymous_reads.py). The other four should have the same, and the sensible shape is one parametrization over the rate settings rather than four copies -- the same argument inventory-tng-aoji.3 made about the posture settings, and possibly the same mechanism.

title: One guardrail per setting, rather than one test module per setting
description:
Raised by the simplify pass on PR #55 (inventory-tng-81f7.5). Not fixed there because the fix edits three test modules and so belongs to no one of them -- the third row of DEVELOPERS.md#one-review-pass-findings-filed-per-issue.

THE PATTERN. This repository has a named rule for an operator-facing setting, from decision 0021 point 11: the careful value is the code's default, the intended value is written explicitly in every shipped file, the chart renders it, the two example values files state opposite answers, and a startup line is printed when the setting is the adapted one. Holding a setting to that rule currently means hand-writing about six tests.

IT IS NOW WRITTEN TWICE. test_second_factor.py does it for REQUIRE_SECOND_FACTOR and test_roster_visibility.py does it for PUBLIC_VOLUNTEER_DETAILS, and roughly a hundred lines of the second are the first with four strings changed -- three test functions even keep their original names. The copy had already drifted once before review caught it: the chart test asserted the rendered STRING rather than what environ parses back out of it, which is the weaker property, and was corrected in 81f7.5's own fixup.

THE SPECIFIC DUPLICATIONS, all now at three copies rather than two:

1. The settings-module reload idiom -- import_module, MonkeyPatch.context, setenv, reload(module).ATTR, finally reload -- is verbatim in test_trusted_origins.py, test_second_factor.py and test_roster_visibility.py. The fragile half is the finally, which restores module state for every test after it; a copy that forgets it poisons the session rather than failing itself.
2. SHIPPED = ('compose.yaml', '.env.sample') is declared in the same three modules, each with a comment pointing at one of the others. It belongs beside NGINX_TEMPLATE and BACKEND_DOCKERFILE in tests/helpers.py, which exists for exactly this reason and says so.
3. test_each_example_states_the_answer_it_is_named_for exists twice with the same name and the same body.

WORTH NOTING, NOT NECESSARILY FIXING: backend/src/inventory/serializers.py, and two places in middleware.py, each hand-roll 'get the user off a request that may not be there'. permissions.py centralised the is_staff half and says in its docstring why -- 'every reader of it needs this dance; doing it here means the views do not' -- but stopped short of the is_authenticated half. And settings.py now has three copies of 'call announcement(), print it to stderr if non-empty'.

WHAT GOOD LOOKS LIKE. A table-driven guardrail taking (setting name, chart value, code default, shipped files, example expectations, announcement module) and generating the checks, so a new operator-facing setting is a row rather than a module -- and so the rule is enforced for settings nobody remembered to write a module for. The behavioural tests stay per setting; it is only the six structural ones this covers.

title: Read an item's movements back as a journey
description:
The implementable slice of inventory-tng-35zr, and deliberately the one that needs NONE of that issue's open decisions.

WHY THIS FIRST. The rows for a journey already exist -- StockMovement carries from_location and to_location, the ledger is append-only, and warehouse -> a volunteer's custody -> hub is recordable today. What does not exist is anything that reads them back as a story. So this is a READ, over data already being written, and it prejudges nothing about end-user locations, retirement or MeshDB.

It also makes the gap visible to everybody rather than to whoever read the parent issue: a journey that stops at a NULL destination will look stopped, on a screen, which is a better argument for fixing it than a paragraph.

=== WHAT IT IS ===

Given an item, the movements that carried it, in order, as a sequence a person can read: when, how much, out of where, into where, under which transaction kind and by whose hand. The ledger already holds every one of those.

=== WHAT TO DECIDE WHILE BUILDING IT, none of which blocks starting ===

* WHOSE JOURNEY. An Item is a TYPE, not a unit -- there are no serial numbers -- so this cannot be "where did THAT router go". It is "how has this product moved", which is still useful and is a different sentence. Say which one the screen promises, in the screen, or somebody will read it as the first.
* HOW FAR BACK. A catalogue row with three years of movements is not a list anybody reads. Paginate from the most recent, like every other collection here.
* WHOSE EYES. Custody locations are named after people, so a journey through one names a volunteer -- which is the surface inventory-tng-81f7 is about. Until that is settled, this belongs behind the administrator's login rather than on the volunteer's side.

=== WHAT IT MUST NOT DO ===

Not invent a status. The parent issue is where "installed", "retired" and "in use" get decided; a screen that infers them from the shape of the last movement would be a second model nobody agreed to, and it would be wrong the day the real one lands.

=== DONE MEANS ===

An administrator can open an item and see how stock of it has moved, most recent first. A journey that currently ends at a NULL destination shows that it does, rather than hiding it.

title: A stream epic and a batch epic are recorded the same way
description:
check-batch.sh reads the parent epic of the issues a branch lands as the batch, and then requires every child of that epic to have landed. That is right for a batch and wrong for a stream.

WHERE IT BITES. inventory-tng-dzwu is a stream -- the local development experience -- and its two children are deliberately separate pull requests: a plan, then the implementation of what the plan decided, so that the plan can be disagreed with before anything is built. Landing the plan alone is refused:

  in the batch but not landed here: inventory-tng-dzwu.2

The same shape applies to inventory-tng-nb8, which is titled EPIC and has landed children in several batches over weeks while others stayed open.

WHAT WAS DONE INSTEAD, and why it is a workaround rather than a fix: the plan was given a batch epic of its own (inventory-tng-qzv7) and the stream kept the implementation. It works, and it means a stream now needs a throwaway epic per pull request, which is bookkeeping the tracker should be doing rather than a person.

WHY IT IS NOT URGENT. Nothing is unsafe: the refusal is in the careful direction, and the workaround is cheap and visible. What it costs is that the batch epic stops meaning one thing -- some are batches, some are containers holding batches -- and the next person has to work out which they are looking at.

WHAT A FIX MIGHT BE, and this is a sketch rather than a decision:

* A stream is marked as one, and check-batch reads through it to whichever epic actually holds the landed set. One field, and epics stop having two meanings.
* Or membership stops being parenthood: a label naming the batch, so an issue can be in a stream and in a batch at once, which is what is actually true.

The second is closer to the truth and a larger change. Whichever, DEVELOPERS.md's description of membership moves with it, and scripts/check-batch.test.sh wants a case for a stream epic whose other children have not landed.

title: A theme drift failure does not say how to fix it
description:
Found by the review pass on PR 48 (inventory-tng-u1am), and deliberately not fixed there rather than widening the batch.

frontend/scripts/theme-css.test.ts compares the committed backend/src/inventory/static/accounts/theme.css against what the theme resolves to. When they differ -- which is what happens after any edit to frontend/src/theme.ts, and after a @mui/material bump inside ^9.3.1 -- vitest prints a toBe diff of roughly 400 lines of CSS custom properties.

The diff is correct and useless. The one thing the reader needs is the command:

  cd frontend && npm run theme:css

WHY IT IS WORTH FIXING RATHER THAN LIVING WITH. The failure is EXPECTED in normal work: it is the reminder that the generated file has to be regenerated, not a sign that anything is wrong. A reminder that buries its instruction under 400 lines of noise trains people to skip reading it, and the next step after that is somebody deleting the test because it 'keeps breaking'. That would leave the sign-in pages carrying last year's palette with nothing failing, which is the exact state inventory-tng-u1am's design argued against.

WHAT TO DO. Assert with a message rather than a bare toBe -- vitest takes one as the second argument -- naming the command and the file. Keep the comparison itself: it is what makes this a projection rather than a copy.

Belongs to the developer-experience stream in spirit; filed on its own because it is a two-line change to one test and needs nothing else.

title: Ask the database for every fold once, instead of one insert at a time
description:
Raised by the simplify pass on PR 39, and declined there because it is a rewrite of mint() rather than a fix to it.

_identifiers.mint() discovers PostgreSQL's fold for a value by trying the insert and reading the refusal (_hold). That is correct, and decision 4 of docs/decisions/0026-what-makes-two-strings-one-identifier.md is why the refusal is an answer. But it means the authority is consulted one row at a time, and almost every piece of machinery in that loop exists only because of it: the savepoint around each insert, the answering dict keyed by a union of two folds, the predicted/minted_now pair, and the two-branch folds_disagreed counter.

One query up front would replace all of it -- something of the shape SELECT v, <Canonical(v)> FROM unnest(%s::text[]) AS v, giving the database's fold for every value in a single round trip. Then answering is keyed by one fold, _hold goes, the savepoints go, and the disagreement count is a set difference computed before the loop rather than accumulated inside it.

NOT URGENT. This is an offline importer over roughly 6000 rows, run occasionally, not a request path. The cost is two extra statements per identifier on the happy path.

WATCH THIS IF YOU DO IT: mint() uses objects.create() per row on purpose, because bulk_create does not fire the signals django-simple-history writes history from. Folding the values in bulk must not turn into inserting them in bulk.
acceptance_criteria:
The database's fold for every value is obtained in one round trip, and no insert is attempted in order to discover it.

Every history row the current importer writes is still written.

The report still distinguishes what this run added from what was already there, and still counts the times the two folds disagreed.

title: Spell each catalogued thing the way its maker does
description:
Decision 7 of `inventory-tng-65l`, carved out of it because no code change
makes it true. The research found that "the spelling the manufacturer intends"
-- the project owner's own words for what they wanted -- is NOT true of this
catalogue, is wrong in at least six places, and contradicts itself in two more.

THIS IS A DATA TASK AND TOUCHES NO CODE. Established 2026-08-25 by reading
every file that names a catalogue string:

* Nothing at runtime branches on `Item.name`. Not a serializer, not a view, not
  a filter, not a component. It is a column value that gets displayed.
* `Label.code` is an opaque Crockford token and the model says why: "The token
  means nothing on its own, so renaming an item cannot break a label." A
  thousand stickers on shelves survive any rename here.
* What DOES name these strings is the one-off loader -- `sheet/items.py`'s
  `ALIASES`, its four tests, `_quantities.py`, and
  docs/briefs/sheet-classifiers.md whose figures a test pins against
  `profile_sheet` -- plus illustrative fixtures that merely happen to use real
  product names (`test_ledger.py`, `test_models.py`, docs/data-model.md, and
  `frontend/capture/scene.ts`'s MEASURED_ITEM). None of the fixtures has to
  match the catalogue.

SO IT IS BLOCKED ON inventory-tng-2dg, DELIBERATELY, and that is what keeps it
a data task. Renaming BEFORE the import would mean editing `ALIASES` values in
lockstep and churning a brief whose figures are under test while the migration
is being validated. It would also be wrong in kind: `ALIASES` records
judgements about a 2022-2026 workbook -- its docstring reasons that `TP-Link
SFP-RJ45` means the catalogue's `SFP-RJ45 Module` and not a typo for its
`Tp-Link`, "which is a router" -- and rewriting it to name products by
spellings that did not exist when those rows were typed makes the migration
artifact describe a world that never happened. After the import, `ALIASES` is
spent and the names are ordinary data.

SPELLING DOES NOT AFFECT FINDABILITY, only what a volunteer reads. Case is
folded on both sides of every comparison, and after `inventory-tng-gz2` a
search runs against identifiers rather than the name. So nothing breaks if this
is never done; the catalogue simply goes on being wrong in public.

## Two decisions, not one

They were bundled in 65l and should be settled separately, because one is
checkable and the other is a house convention.

### 1. Manufacturer spellings -- objective, verify against the vendor's page

PROPOSED, awaiting the project owner's confirmation. Each is thirty seconds to
check and should be checked rather than taken on trust.

    Tp-Link                    -> TP-Link Archer A7
    OmniTikPOE                 -> OmniTIK 5 PoE ac
    Hex POE                    -> hEX PoE
    Netpower 16P               -> netPower 16P
    Netpower 15R               -> netPower 15R
    ToughCable                 -> TOUGHCable
    RJ45 ToughCable connectors -> TOUGHCable RJ45 connectors
    LiteBeam                   -> unchanged, already correct

Two of those carry a second change beside the case and can be taken as case-
only instead:

* `Tp-Link` is a BRAND used as a product name. `ALIASES` maps `archer 7` and
  `archer a7` onto it, so the model belongs in the name.
* `OmniTikPOE` -- the repository already disagrees with itself, since
  `seed_demo_data.py` says `OmniTik 5 PoE ac`.

ONE TO CHECK RATHER THAN APPLY: MikroTik ships a netPower 16P and a netPower
15FR. Whether the catalogue's `15R` is a truncation of 15FR is a question for
somebody who can look at the hardware.

### 2. House style -- no manufacturer to appeal to

Nothing external settles these. The value is picking A rule, once.

* RJ45 or RJ-45. The catalogue holds `RJ-45 Coupler (Indoors)` beside `RJ45
  passthrough` and `SFP-RJ45 Module`; unhyphenated is already the majority.
* `Ubiquiti J-Pole` against `Jpole Umount Extender`. One spelling, in both --
  and `Umount` is likely `U-mount`.
* The masts: `mast straight`, `Mast telescope`, `Non-pen Mast` are three
  different shapes. A pattern such as `Mast, straight` / `Mast, telescopic` /
  `Mast, non-penetrating` makes them sort together, which is what matters in a
  pulldown.
* `W-mounts` is plural where the rest of the catalogue is singular.

## Scope limit worth stating

The full 52 catalogue names are in the workbook, not in this repository. The
list above is drawn from the dozen that `sheet/items.py` encodes plus those
65l's research named. A complete audit means reading the catalogue tab of
`ignored/NYC Mesh - Inventory Sheet.xlsx` -- which also holds the volunteer
roster `inventory-tng-81f7` exists about, so whoever does it reads that one tab
and nothing else.

## Acceptance

The catalogue names match what the manufacturer publishes, or a house-style
rule that is written down; the rule lives in a document rather than in
somebody's memory; and no code changed, because if code had to change the
sequencing above was got wrong.

title: Two volunteers can share an address in different case, and one search returns both
description:
Found by the codebase strand of inventory-tng-65l, 2026-08-22, finding 6. Checked against inventory-tng-24q.6, which is a different fault -- that one is the importer minting a second row when a sheet_key stops appearing.

VolunteerFilter searches email__iexact. The constraint volunteer_unique_email_when_present is case-SENSITIVE. So the two disagree about what one address is: Ada@example.org and ada@example.org can both be stored, and a search for either returns both rows.

Which way it should be settled is the decision this carries. Folding the constraint would need the same treatment decision 0026 gives ItemIdentifier -- a normalised column and a unique index over it, not a Python-side check -- and it would surface any pair already stored, so it inherits that record's migration rule about reporting rather than dying part way through.
acceptance_criteria: Storage and search agree about whether two addresses are one address, and whichever way it is settled, an existing pair differing only in case is found and reported rather than discovered by a failing migration.

title: people.py claims a parity with the identifier column that does not exist
description:
Found by the codebase strand of inventory-tng-65l, 2026-08-22, finding 5. Not fixed there because it is nobody's issue yet.

inventory/sheet/people.py: addressed() says it uses lower rather than casefold 'matching the Lower(Trim()) column the identifier tables normalise with', and spelled() folds the same way on the same claim.

But Volunteer.sheet_key and Volunteer.email have plain case-SENSITIVE unique indexes and no generated column. There is no Lower(Trim()) column on either. Python is the only fold in play, so there is no drift risk and no bug in the behaviour -- the claim of parity is simply untrue, and it is the kind of untrue that gets believed and built on.

Note the reference to the identifier column will also be stale once decision 2 of docs/decisions/0026-what-makes-two-strings-one-identifier.md lands, because the expression stops being Lower(Trim()).
acceptance_criteria: The docstrings say what is actually true: these two fold in Python only, against case-sensitive unique indexes, and the reason for lower over casefold stands on its own rather than on a parity that does not exist.
close_reason: Closed

title: Three test helpers living in five files
description:
Found by the simplify pass on PR #37, and its own issue because no issue in that batch owns all the call sites -- the third row of DEVELOPERS.md's triage table.

TWO HELPERS, COPIED. `const answering = (body, status = 200) => new Response(JSON.stringify(body), { status })` is now written out in four files: administrator.test.tsx, vocabularies.test.tsx, printing.test.tsx and merging.test.tsx. Three of the four dropped the sentence the first one wrote about what the default 200 is for. api/testFixtures.ts already holds `page()` and says in its own docstring why the API's shapes belong there rather than beside one screen's fixtures; this is the same argument.

And the MUI select idiom -- `fireEvent.mouseDown(combobox)` then `fireEvent.click(await screen.findByRole("option", ...))` -- is now written twenty-two times across five files. The `screen` rather than `within(dialog)` is not a style choice: the option list is portalled out of the dialog, and a copy that uses `within` fails with a "not found" that says nothing about why. That reason is written down in exactly one of the twenty-two.

WHAT TO DO. `answering` beside `page()` in api/testFixtures.ts. A `pickOption(container, label, option)` in testHarness.tsx, carrying the portal comment, beside `writes`/`theWrite`/`stubSession`/`callsTo` which are already there for this reason.

WHAT TO PIN. Nothing new: every call site is in a test that already passes, which is what makes the extraction safe and what makes it worth doing while they are green.
close_reason: Closed

title: One select over a paged collection, not three
description:
Found by the simplify pass on PR #35, and its own issue because it exists only as the composition of inventory-tng-2oba.1 and code that batch did not touch -- the third row of DEVELOPERS.md's triage table.

THE DUPLICATION, and there are now three of it. frontend/src/batch/LocationPicker.tsx, the Category field of frontend/src/admin/CreateItem.tsx, and the item field of frontend/src/admin/PrintLabels.tsx are the same control written three times: useResource over a Page<T>, an empty-string value because a select with no value is uncontrolled, String(id) on each MenuItem, disabled when the list is empty, and the read's error as helper text. Category, Location and Item are all {id, name}, so nothing generic is needed to hold them.

AND TWO OF THE THREE NOW KNOW SOMETHING THE OLDEST DOES NOT. CreateItem and PrintLabels tell three states apart -- reading, none yet, could not be read -- because saying "none yet" while the request is in flight sends somebody off to make a row that already exists. LocationPicker conflates all three: while the request is in flight, and when there are genuinely no locations, and when the read failed, it draws a disabled empty select and says "Or scan the code on the wall." That is on the VOLUNTEER's critical path, which is why it has not been changed from a batch about administration.

WHAT NOT TO DRAG IN. MergeVolunteers.tsx renders two selects over a list it was handed -- no fetch, no error, no in-flight state -- so it is not this shape and folding it in would put a paged-collection reader inside a component that does not need one. Its own local `Which` is the right size for it.

WHAT TO DO. Lift the shared body into one component taking the path, the label, the value, the change handler and an empty-state sentence, and have the three call it. The tri-state helper text goes with it, which is what closes LocationPicker's half.

WHAT TO PIN. LocationPicker's three states, which nothing asserts today. administrator.test.tsx and printing.test.tsx already have the shape of those tests, including holding the response open so the in-flight state actually renders.

title: Nothing prunes an old Device row, so an address is kept for ever
description:
Raised by the review of PR #34 and filed rather than folded in, because a
retention rule is a decision about how long this project keeps something rather
than part of building the thing that keeps it.

WHAT IS THERE NOW. inventory.models.Device holds one row per browser that has
enrolled, with enrolled_from -- the address the credential was asked from --
and nothing ever removes one. A row for a phone somebody replaced two years ago
sits there with an address on it.

WHY THAT IS WORTH A BEAD RATHER THAN A SHRUG. This system otherwise refuses to
record a caller's address at all: inventory_tng/redaction.py drops gunicorn's
%(h)s from the access line on the argument that it identifies a person, and
docs/observability.md carries the same position. docs/data-model.md now says
plainly that Device is the one table contradicting it, and inventory-tng-t9of
argued the column in: minting answers everybody, so credentials asked for in
bulk are the abuse shape, and the column is what makes that findable. That
argument is about the RECENT past. It says nothing for a row from 2026.

WHAT TO DECIDE, and it is genuinely a decision:

  * How long an address is worth keeping. Long enough to answer 'where did
    this burst come from' is days or weeks, not years.
  * Whether the ROW goes or only the ADDRESS. They are different: nulling
    enrolled_from on an old row keeps revocation working for a device still in
    use, where deleting the row un-revokes a revoked one -- DeviceAdmin says
    why that matters and decision 0024 is the general argument. Almost
    certainly the address and not the row.
  * Whether a revoked row is ever collected at all. A device cut off for cause
    is the one somebody may want to look up later.

SHAPE: a management command, run from a cron or by hand, that nulls
enrolled_from on rows older than a configured age and says how many it touched.
ReportingCommand is the base and _telemetry.running is how it reports. NOT a
signal or a save-time sweep -- a rule that runs when somebody happens to enrol
is a rule that does not run when nobody does.

AND SAY IT WHERE IT WILL BE READ: docs/data-model.md's Device section names
this bead already, so whatever is decided replaces that sentence; docs/
deployment.md#cutting-off-a-device is where an operator would look for the
command.

title: The jsdom storage repair is a two-name allowlist; a custom environment would fix the class
description:
Raised by the simplify pass on PR #33, and filed rather than folded into
inventory-tng-s6w3 because it trades a repair proven green on two node versions
for a better-shaped one, and that is a judgement worth making on its own.

WHAT IS THERE NOW. frontend/src/test-setup.ts calls restoreStorageFromJsdom(),
which copies jsdom's localStorage and sessionStorage onto the test global when
node's own are undefined. It works -- 423 tests green on node 24 and node 26 --
and it compensates for one instance of a general fault rather than removing it.

THE FAULT, IN ONE LINE OF VITEST. node_modules/vitest/dist/chunks/index.*.js,
getWindowKeys:

    if (skipKeys.includes(k)) return false;
    if (k in global) return keysArray.includes(k);
    return true;

keysArray is [...additionalKeys, ...KEYS]. KEYS holds Storage and StorageEvent
and NOT localStorage or sessionStorage, and the jsdom environment calls
populateGlobal with no additionalKeys. So any window key node has already put on
globalThis is skipped, silently. Node keeps promoting web globals; every future
one that jsdom also provides fails the same way, and the symptom is hundreds of
tests failing at once naming nothing.

THE DEEPER FIX, VERIFIED ON THE MACHINE. builtinEnvironments and populateGlobal
are exported (from vitest/runtime; the vitest/environments spelling still works
and warns). A small environment module deletes the offending globals and
delegates:

    for (const k of [...]) delete global[k];
    return builtinEnvironments.jsdom.setup(global, options);

delete works: node's localStorage descriptor is configurable, and after the
delete 'localStorage' in globalThis is false. vite.config.ts then names that
module as test.environment. The storage objects end up on populateGlobal's own
getter and teardown path rather than a second defineProperty vitest does not
know about, and frontend/src/test-setup.test.ts becomes the test of the
environment rather than of the patch.

ROUTES CHECKED AND RULED OUT, so nobody re-derives them:

  environmentOptions.jsdom  -- spread into the JSDOM constructor, cannot affect
                               what vitest copies onto the global
  setupFiles ordering       -- setup files run strictly after environment.setup
  server.deps               -- unrelated
  poolOptions execArgv with --no-experimental-webstorage -- DOES work on node 26
                               and is accepted on 24, but node < 22.4 does not
                               know the flag and the worker dies on it, which
                               trades one version cliff for another

WHAT MAKES THIS RISKY, and it is the reason for the bead. test.environment stops
being a builtin name and becomes a local module resolved through a vitest export
whose sibling spelling already deprecation-warns. Getting it wrong is a suite
that will not start rather than one that fails a test. So: prove it on node 24
AND node 26 before believing it, exactly as s6w3 had to.

title: check-docs.py reports a file against itself when a path arrives twice
description:
Found by the review of PR #33 and filed rather than folded in, because it
predates inventory-tng-hoc6 and hoc6 only changed the flags on the line that
feeds it.

scripts/check-docs.py keys `seen` on the twelve-word run and re-initialises
`shingles[name]` for each occurrence of a name, so a path passed twice collides
with its own first pass and lands in hits[(name, name)]. The report is then
'a.md and a.md say the same thing' for every passage in every file -- which is
not a fault a reader can act on, and it buries anything real in the same run.

HOW A PATH ARRIVES TWICE: `git ls-files` prints one line per unmerged stage, so
a conflicted merge or rebase makes every conflicted path appear two or three
times. The checker then objects at length about something that has nothing to
do with the conflict, at the moment somebody is least able to spare the
attention. Same shape as scripts/check-setup.sh, whose own comment already
notes the per-stage rows and takes head -n1 for exactly this reason.

THE FIX IS SMALL and there are two places to put it: dedupe the enumeration in
check-docs.sh, or ignore a name already read in check-docs.py's loop. Prefer the
reader, because it also covers a caller passing the same path twice on the
command line, which the entry point offers.

A TEST IS THE POINT: the same file named twice on one invocation must not be
reported. That is one line in scripts/check-docs.test.sh using `assert`, which
already exists for cases the `check` shape does not fit, and it needs no
conflicted repository to set up.

Worth asking the same question of scripts/check-telemetry.py, which reads a
corpus the same way.
close_reason: Closed

title: check-docs.sh reads only tracked files, so a new file passes here and fails in CI
description:
scripts/check-docs.sh:66 enumerates with `git ls-files`, which lists TRACKED
files only. A documentation file that has been written but not yet committed is
invisible to it, so the check passes locally, the commit lands, and the
Documentation job fails on a file the author already ran the checker against.
Hit twice in one sitting on 2026-08-25 while landing `inventory-tng-p7ic`.

`git add -N` before running it is the workaround and it is the wrong fix: it
asks every contributor to remember a flag in order to make a checker honest.

THE FIX IS ONE FLAG ON THE ENUMERATION:

    git ls-files --cached --others --exclude-standard

`--others` adds untracked files and `--exclude-standard` keeps .gitignore
honoured, so the set becomes exactly what CI will see once the work is
committed -- which is what the checker was always claiming to test.

CHECK THE SIBLINGS IN THE SAME CHANGE rather than filing this again in a month:
scripts/check-telemetry.sh and anything else under scripts/ that walks the
repository this way. Rule 1 applies to the prose that explains the enumeration
too -- say it once, wherever it belongs, and link.

A TEST IS THE POINT, not the flag: a new, uncommitted, non-ignored file with a
deliberate violation in it must make the checker fail. Without that this
regresses the next time somebody tidies the pipeline.
close_reason: check-docs.sh and check-telemetry.sh now enumerate with --cached --others --exclude-standard, so an uncommitted file is checked; four cases pin it

title: A hard delete that takes real hoops to reach, for when one is genuinely needed
description:
Asked for by the project owner on 2026-08-25: with `inventory-tng-6kyb`
landed and the admin's Delete going away, is there a "only use this if you
REALLY know what you are doing" path that still exists but is hard to reach?

ARGUE WHETHER IT IS NEEDED BEFORE BUILDING IT, and that is most of this bead.
Three cases are worth separating and only one of them wants this:

* A row created by mistake a minute ago, with nothing recorded about it. That
  ALREADY deletes -- `PROTECT` only refuses once an identifier, a price, a
  label or a movement exists. No new mechanism needed.
* A row that should stop appearing. That is `Item.active`, it is built, and it
  is what `guides/administrator.md` tells an administrator to use.
* A row that must genuinely leave the database -- a corrupted import, a legal
  erasure. Rare, irreversible, and destroys ledger history that the append-only
  design exists to keep. This is the only case, and its rarity is the argument
  for what shape it takes.

THE SHAPE THAT FITS: a management command, not a screen and not an admin
action. The hoop is then having a shell on the server, which is a real gate
this project already relies on, cannot be reached by a mis-click from a phone,
and leaves the destructive path out of every interface a volunteer or an
administrator ever sees. Decision 0014's argument for one interface is about
where ordinary work happens; this is deliberately not ordinary work.

IT MUST PRINT THE BLAST RADIUS AND DEFAULT TO NOT DOING IT. `--dry-run` as the
default, naming every row that would go -- how many identifiers, which of them
are printed kinds, how many offers, how many labels, how many movements -- and
a second explicit flag to proceed. A confirmation that does not say what is
about to be lost is a confirmation nobody reads.

WORTH KNOWING: `MAY_CASCADE` in backend/src/inventory/tests/test_models.py is
the existing place where a deliberate destruction is recorded with the reason
that makes it acceptable. It is empty after 6kyb. Whatever this builds should
not quietly reintroduce a cascade behind its back -- the command should delete
what it names, having said so, rather than relying on the database to sweep.
close_reason: NOT BUILT, deliberately. Argued in docs/decisions/0024-no-hard-delete.md: the ledger's triggers refuse DELETE so the case that wants this cannot be served by any application command; PROTECT is Django's rather than Postgres's so manage.py dbshell already IS the proposed hoop; the blast-radius printout is the only added value and a command nobody should run is one nobody has exercised; and erasure is a Volunteer/history question, not an Item one. Retirement and compensating movements are what the application offers.

title: CI's postgres healthcheck probes a role that does not exist
description:
.github/workflows/ci.yml runs its postgres service container with
POSTGRES_USER=inventory and POSTGRES_DB=inventory_tng, and probes it with a
bare `--health-cmd pg_isready` (lines 31 and 99, the Backend job and the
Integration job).

The postgres entrypoint runs initdb --username="$POSTGRES_USER", so the role
created is `inventory` and the role `postgres` is never created. A bare
pg_isready inside that container defaults -U to the OS user it runs as, which
is `postgres`, so every probe is answered `FATAL: role "postgres" does not
exist` -- and pg_isready reports the server as accepting connections and exits
0 anyway, because a server that refuses a role is a server that is accepting
connections.

This is the same class of defect as inventory-tng-6h2, which fixed the compose
stack's probe, but it is NOT the same line: compose had `-U` and no `-d`, and
CI has neither. The fix here is to give the probe both, matching the service's
own env:

    --health-cmd "pg_isready -U inventory -d inventory_tng"

Consequence today is log noise in a throwaway container rather than a broken
build, which is why it is P3. What makes it worth fixing is that the probe
passes for a reason unrelated to the thing it claims to check, so a genuinely
misconfigured service container would also go green.

Noticed by the second review cycle on PR #32. Pre-existing; ci.yml is untouched
by that branch, so by DEVELOPERS.md#commits it is its own issue and its own
commit.
close_reason: Closed

title: compose.yaml is parsed inline in four test modules
description:
backend/src/inventory/tests/test_shipping.py has a compose() function that yaml.safe_loads compose.yaml; test_telemetry.py open-codes the same load; and inventory-tng-6h2 added a third in test_database.py. A FOURTH arrived with inventory-tng-pmd, in test_chart.py, which reuses tests/helpers.py's shipped() for the path but still parses the file itself.

Three parse sites means three places to fix if the file moves, is split into compose.yaml plus an override, or grows a construct safe_load refuses. Four means four, and the count grows every time a test wants to hold the chart or the settings against the stack -- which is a thing this suite does more of, not less.

tests/charts.py is the precedent for lifting exactly this out: it exists as an importable non-test_ module holding CHART and render() because two tests asking the same question with two answers is the drift they exist to catch. The same argument applies here.

FIX: one compose() in tests/helpers.py (or a small tests/stack.py), called by all four. Noticed by the simplify pass on PR #32; pre-existing.

title: One tracker fixture, not twenty copies of it, in check-commit.test.sh
close_reason: Closed

title: Print a sheet of labels
description:
print_label maps to LabelListView POST, and /api/labels/sheet already renders a printable sheet of stickers server-side. Nothing in the application asks it to, so the one capability whose backend is completely finished is the one with no way to use it.

BLOCKED ON THE NAVIGATION DECISION, deliberately, and it is the only child of inventory-tng-2oba that is. A sheet spans items and belongs to no row, so unlike the other four this one cannot be placed by decision 0014 point 1 -- it is the case that decision has to cover. Building it first would settle the navigation shape by accident for inventory-tng-ayu and inventory-tng-3ez as well.

WHAT IT NEEDS ONCE PLACED: choosing what goes on the sheet (which is where inventory-tng-3ez's narrowing meets it), asking the endpoint, and handing the result to the browser to print. The rendering is not this project's problem, which is what makes the issue small once the placement is known.

ACCEPTANCE. An administrator can print a sheet of stickers without opening Django's admin or calling the API by hand; the control is drawn from the capability; the placement follows the decision rather than inventing one.
close_reason: Closed

title: DECISION: what makes a review current enough to count as evidence
description:
Found by the /code-review pass on PR #30, as the half of one finding that is a decision rather than a defect. The pagination half of that finding was fixed on the branch.

WHAT THE GATE DOES NOW. scripts/landing-gate.sh record accepts, as evidence that the code-review stage ran, ANY review submission on the pull request, and as evidence that simplify ran, any comment carrying the marker. It stores each one's id, author, timestamp and -- for reviews -- the commit it was submitted against. Nothing reads that commit back.

WHAT IS CORRECT ABOUT THAT AND MUST NOT BE 'FIXED'. The reviewer's scenario -- review at head A, fix the findings, force-with-lease to head B, record at B citing the review of A -- is the documented cycle working exactly as intended. A review is OF the code before the fixes; requiring review.commit to equal the head would refuse every honest cycle and admit only one that reviewed its own fixes. So 'tie the evidence to the merged head' is the wrong answer and it is worth writing that down before somebody implements it.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY OPEN. Two things count that arguably should not:

  * A review left in a PREVIOUS cycle. Push, review, push again -- the head check forces a re-record, but the re-record is satisfied by the old review. The findings were answered, so this is usually fine; it stops being fine when the second push is a rewrite rather than a fix.
  * A review that is not a review of this batch at all: a bot approval, a drive-by comment, a 'changes requested' that is still outstanding. Any of them satisfies the code-review stage.

CANDIDATES, none obviously right. (a) require the evidence to be newer than the branch's first commit, which catches the stalest case and nothing else; (b) require at least one review whose commit is an ANCESTOR of the head being merged, which is the real relation and costs a git call per review; (c) refuse while any review is in CHANGES_REQUESTED, which is a different rule wearing this one's clothes and may belong to branch protection instead; (d) leave it, and have status print each review's commit so an auditor can see what was reviewed.

WHY IT IS FILED RATHER THAN GUESSED. Each candidate changes what the gate refuses, and the gate is what AGENTS.md rests merging-without-asking on. 0020 already records how much may rest on a client-side guard; this is the same trade one level down. It blocks nothing.

title: One place that knows where the hooks are, not two
description:
Found by the /simplify pass on PR #29 (inventory-tng-nt1f), and filed rather than applied because it is a shared-helper extraction across two scripts that both have their own test suites, and both are correct as they stand.

scripts/bootstrap-dev.sh and scripts/check-setup.sh now ask the same question in two places: where this repository keeps its hooks, and whether git is actually pointed at them. Both compute the main checkout's hooks directory the same way (dirname of readlink -f of git rev-parse --git-common-dir, plus .beads/hooks), both read core.hooksPath across EVERY scope rather than local alone, and both compare by -ef rather than by spelling because beads writes an absolute path and bootstrap writes a relative one.

The duplication is deliberate and is acknowledged in the code -- bootstrap-dev.sh says "the same question scripts/check-setup.sh asks so the two cannot answer differently". That comment is the finding: two spellings of one predicate is how they come to disagree, and the comment is doing the work a shared file should be doing.

THIS REPOSITORY ALREADY HAS THE PATTERN, which is why this is worth doing rather than tolerating. scripts/message-rules.sh exists for exactly this reason and says so: check-commit.sh sources it "so that check-batch.sh can apply the same ones without reading this script's output". scripts/report.sh, scripts/trailers.sh and scripts/testlib.sh are the same idea. A scripts/hooks-path.sh sourced by both would be the fourth of a kind rather than a new invention.

WHAT IT WOULD HOLD: the hooks directory name, the main-checkout resolution for a linked worktree, and the "is git pointed here" predicate returning enough for each caller to phrase its own message -- bootstrap must repair and check-setup must deliberately NOT repair, so the extraction is the question, not the response to it.

WHY IT WAS NOT DONE IN #29: the code is correct, tested (bootstrap-dev.test.sh 40 assertions, check-setup.test.sh 22) and documented, and this refactor touches the thing that guards every commit in the repository. It deserves its own change and its own test run rather than riding out on the change that introduced it.
design: Follow scripts/message-rules.sh exactly: a sourced file holding the rules, with each caller keeping its own reporting. Note the two callers differ in what they do with the answer -- bootstrap repairs, check-setup refuses to -- so what is shared is the question and not the handling.
acceptance_criteria: bootstrap-dev.sh and check-setup.sh derive the hooks directory and the is-git-pointed-at-it answer from one sourced file; neither restates the worktree resolution or the scope handling; both test suites still pass; and a change to where hooks live is a change to one file.
close_reason: Closed

title: Weigh CONN_MAX_AGE against a failover that leaves stale handles
description:
Deliberately left out of inventory-tng-39ng, and recorded here so the argument
outlives that bead being closed.

CONN_MAX_AGE is 0 -- backend/src/inventory_tng/database.py reads DATABASE_URL
through django-environ, which returns none, so Django's default stands. Every
request therefore opens a fresh PostgreSQL connection: a TCP handshake plus
authentication, per request, per gunicorn worker, on a deployment where three
sync workers per pod are the whole of the capacity. Raising it is the ordinary
Django answer and it is measurably cheaper.

WHAT MAKES IT A DECISION rather than a setting. A persistent connection is held
across requests by a worker that is not looking at it, so a database that moves
underneath -- the failover 39ng is about -- leaves each worker holding a handle
to an address that no longer answers. Django checks a reused connection's health
before handing it back (close_if_unusable_or_obsolete), but the check is not
free of the same blackhole problem the connect had: a dead handle is discovered
by writing to it. 39ng's connect_timeout bounds the DIAL and says nothing about
a socket already open, which is what makes this a second piece of work rather
than a bigger version of the first.

WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: a number for CONN_MAX_AGE, and evidence about what a
worker holding a stale handle actually does when the database address moves --
